div.p: Prologos.-Hermes enters. He first gives a résumé of those incidents of the story which precede the action of the play, and then so far anticipates the catastrophe as to announce what are Apollo's intentions with regard to Ion. Anxious that the young man should, though late, have his rights as heir to the Athenian throne, he will cause Youthos to be persuaded that Ion is his own son, and as such to take him back to Athens. When arrived there, Ion will be recog- nized by Kreousa and all will be well. Having thus made matters clear to the audience, the god retires to watch the progress of the play from the laurel- bushes of the sacred garden. His departure is followed by the entrance of Ion, who comes forward and delivers a long monody of great beauty. (See sketch at v. 82.)

The long syllable preceding οὐρανόν violates the law of the final cretic, and most edd. accordingly suspect the text. It may, however, be doubted whether the verse, as we have it, is not genuine: cp. Phoen. 747 ἀμφότερον· ἀπολειφθὲν γὰρ οὐδὲν θάτερον, where no alteration is possible. Such passages as Soph. El. 376, 449, O.C. 115, 664, 1022, 1543, which have been supposed to offer parallels to the present case, do not contravene the rule as properly understood. In all of them the concluding words of the line are to be taken closely to- gether. -"Ατλας (τλάω) properly = sustainer.

ὁ... ἐκτρίβων, 'who wears. Besides its ordinary mean- ing of wear away, the word also suggests here the idea of continually bearing (i.e. wearing). The subst. τρίβων (cloak) offers a curious parallel to this extension of the primary signification. The English wear, on the other hand (✓ WAS, cp. ἐσ-θής, vestis), first means to wear on the body, and second- arily to wear-out by so doing.-θεῶν... θεῶν : the repetition is intentional and points the sense.

μιᾶς, slightly emphatic: of one of the goddesses begat Maia. This use of els as a substitute (though not a synonym) for τις is rare: but cp. Bacch. 917 πρέπεις δὲ Κάδμου θυγα- τέρων μορφὴν μιᾷ (cuivis) : Ar. Αν. 1292 πέρδιξ μὲν εἶς (=εἰς τις) κάπηλος ὠνομάζετο. So in Latin, Plaut. Pseud. 4. 1. 38 ibi una aderit mulier lepida. The goddess was Pleïone, and Maia was one of the Pleiads. -ἐγείνατο from γείνομαι : this tense is transitive; the pres. and imperf. are intransitive.
λάτριν. In Aesch. P. V. 941 Prometheus contemptuously calls him τὸν Διὸς τρόχιν.
ὄμφ. μεσον, mid-centre. See Introd. § 2.

Φοίβος, i.e. the Bright or Radiant god. In Homer at least the name must be understood to express the radiance and bloom of youth, since Apollo was not identified with Helios till considerably later. -ὑμνῳδεῖ : see Introd. § 3.
καὶ μέλλοντα. According to the well-known rule this should be καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα. Paley cp. Aesch. Αg. 324 τῶν ἁλόντων καὶ κρατησάντων : Hel. 923 τά τ' ὄντα καὶ μή.

ἄσημος. The word is primarily used of unstamped or uncoined metal: then derivatively of anything lacking definite character, such as unintelligible sounds, ambiguous oracles, an unblazoned shield, an unknown or insignificant person or place, as here. οὐκ ἄσημος is of course a strong μείωσις for έπιση- μοτάτη. The poet is thinking of the Athens of his own day, of which Pericles said τὴν πᾶσαν πόλιν τῆς ῾Ελλάδος παίδευσιν εἶναι. A portion of Milton's fine and enthusiastic descrip- tion (Par. Reg. 4. 237) may find a place here :- 'Behold Where on the Aegean shore a city stands, Built nobly; pure the air and light the soil; Athens the eye of Greece, mother of arts And eloquence, native to famous wits Or hospitable, in her sweet recess, City or suburban, studious walks and shades'.

χρυσολόγχου. The allusion is to the gilded point of the spear of the colossal bronze statue of Athena Promachos on the Acropolis, which was a conspicuous object at a distance of several miles. The statue, one of Pheidias' greatest achievements, was erected in commemoration of the victory at Marathon and its cost defrayed out of the spoil taken on that occasion.-Παλλάδος : cp. Soph. O.C. 107 ἴτ᾽, ὦ μεγίστης Παλλάδος καλουμέναι | πασῶν ᾿Αθῆναι τιμιωτάτη πόλις.

᾿Ερεχθέως. Erechtheus, otherwise called Erichthonios, was the son of Hephaistos and Ge or Atthis. Soon after its birth Athena placed the child in a chest together with two serpents, to be its protectors. She then gave the chest to Aglauros, Pandrosos and Herse, daughters of Kekrops, for- bidding them to open it. They did so, however, and seeing the serpents, were terrified into madness and flung themselves over the cliffs of the Acropolis. Erechtheus, when he grew up, expelled Amphiktion and seized the government of Athens. He established the worship of Athene there, building her a temple in which he placed the original palladium or wooden image of the goddess, and instituting the Panathenaic festival. He himself was worshipped in the Erechtheion jointly with Athene, and was even identified with Poseidon under the name of Poseidon Erichthonios. Erechtheus, however, divided the honour of being the most ancient Attic hero with Kekrops mentioned above. This Kekrops, an autochthonous being, half man and half snake (τὰ πρὸς ποδῶν δρακοντίδης Ar. Vesp. 438)-a shape given also to Erechtheus by one form of the legend-was the eponymous hero of the portion of Attica called Kekropia. He too is called the first king of the country and, as well as Erechtheus, is said to have decided the dispute between Athene and Poseidon for the possession of the Acropolis. On the whole, however, Erechtheus holds the first place both in the legends and in the estimation of later times. His temple on the Acropolis, which still remains, is one of the finest specimens of the architecture of the Pheidian period.

ἔνθα προσβόρρους κ.τ.λ. The rocks on the south side of the Acropolis were equal in length with those on the north, but the latter appear to have obtained the name of the Long Cliffs par excellence because an uninterrupted view of them in their entirety could be more easily gained from the sur- rounding country. The cave of Pan (Paneum) which is here more particularly alluded to, is still to be seen. It lies at the base of the cliffs at the N.W. corner of the Acropolis.
For the double gen. cp. Soph. Phil. 489 πρὸς τὰ Χαλκώδοντος Εὐβοίας σταθμά.
ἄνακτες : lords of the land, meaning merely the inhabitants. So Soph. O.C. 831, but not v. 1222 infr. In Aesch. Pers. 370 rowers are called κώπης ἄνακτες.
ἦν φίλον, placebat: the god so willed.
γαστρὸς διήνεγκ᾿ ὄγκον : she bare to the end the burden of her womb. Cp. Hdt. 1. 25 τὸν πρὸς Μιλησίους πόλεμον διενείκας.

οὐπερ, the very place where; -περ gives emphasis to the word to which it is attached, e.g. ὥσπερ, exactly as; καίπερ, although (a strengthened καί); ἐξ ὅτουπερ (Dem.), where the indefiniteness of ὅτου is emphasized: Soph. Εl. 386 ὅταν περ...μόλῃ, the very moment he returns.

ὡς θανούμενον, to die, as she thought. Note this force of ὡς with the participle, and cp. Lysias Eratosth. § 13 κινδυνεύειν ἐδόκει, ὡς τοῦ γ᾽ ἀποθανεῖν ὑπάρχοντος ἤδη, I re- solved to risk the attempt (to escape), reflecting that, as it was, I stood to die: Soph. Aἱ. 281 ὡς ὧδ᾽ ἐχόντων τῶνδε, οη the understanding that this is so.

κοίλης...κύκλῳ: in the lightly-rocking embrace of a sheltering cradle. κύκλῳ merely implies that the cradle was semi-cylindrical in shape. L. and S. take εὐτρόχῳ=on wheels; but this is very unlikely, and beyond this passage there is apparently no evidence for supposing the ancient cradles had wheels any more than modern ones. 20 ff. See on v. 10.
παραζεύξασα, attaching.
Αγλαυρίσι. Aglauros was the wife of Kekrops, and one of the daughters bore her name. The name is variously spelt in Mss. as "Αγραυλος and "Αγλαυρος. The latter is perhaps more correct.
ἐκεῖ, at Athens, as opposed to here, at Delphi.
ὄφεσιν. The snakes were worn on the neck: cp. v.
χλιδήν, rich stuff; cp. v. 1417 ff. The word means
daintiness, luxury; 2. the outcome of this, insolence ;3. luxuries, such as costly ornaments and apparel; 4. personal charms, such as beautiful features or shape, or hair.

προσάψασ᾽ ἔλιπεν κ.τ.λ. : attached to the child before she left it as destined for the tomb. As very commonly in a Greek sentence, the participle expresses the chief idea, the main verb only an attendant circumstance: cp. Thuc. 7. 14 ἀφ᾽ ὧν [νεῶν] ἔχοντες ἤλθομεν, from the ships which we had when we came. -ὡς θανουμένῳ (mark the case) gives the reason for her so apparelling the child. It was customary to place ornaments on those about to be buried.

αὐτόχθονα refers to the legends of Erechtheus and Kekrops, from whom the Athenians claimed descent (see on v. 10); but in fact Attica had suffered fewer changes of inhabitants than any other parts of Hellas, owing, as Thucydides tells us (1. 2.), to the poorness of its soil.
πλεκτὸν κύτος, the osier-woven casket. κύτος is used of any hollow receptacle, and in Soph. Trach. 12, ἀνδρείῳ κύτει, even of the human body.
κρηπίδων, the steps, so called as forming part of the basement of the temple.

κυρεῖ δὲ κ.τ.λ. : And it happens, when the orb of the coursing sun appears, that the Prophetess, etc. The hap marked by κυρεῖ is the god's placing the child on the temple- steps just before the entrance of the prophetess at sunrise. It is not meant that she happened to come in at sunrise on that day contrary to her practice. Like Ion she would always begin her duties to the sun-god at his rising. For ἅμα cp. v. 122.
ἐθαύμασ᾽ εἰ τλαίη: wondered whether any had dared. With ἔτλη the meaning would have been, was amazed that any had dared, expressing conviction.
ὠδῖνα, offspring, as often.
θυμέλας, the temple-steps. Cp. v. 114 and ἐσόδους, υ.

θυμέλη (√ θυ, cp. πι-μ-ελή) appears properly to mean sacrificing-place, i.e. the platform at the top of the steps of an altar, on which the sacrificing priest stood. The obvious re- semblance easily accounts for its transference to the platform of a temple. There is a further extension of the meaning Ι.Α. 150 ἐπὶ Κυκλώπων ἱεὶς θυμέλας, where the massive masonry of the ancient buildings of Mykenae is referred to.
οἴκτῳ: causal.

μὴ ᾿κπεσεῖν : consecutive inf. The uses of ἐκπίπτω, which commonly serves as a passive of ἐκβάλλω, are interest- ing:-(1) to be thrust forth, banished, e.g. τυραννίδος, or absol.; cp. Thuc. 1. 2. οἱ πολέμῳ ἢ στάσει ἐκπίπτοντες: (2) to be cast ashore, cp. Od. 7. 283 ἐκ δ᾽ ἔπεσον θυμηγερέων : (3) to rush, or sally forth: (4) of actors, to be hissed off, explodi, cp. Dem. de cor. § 265 ἐξέπιπτες, ἐγὼ δ᾽ ἐσύριττον.
τὸν σπείρ. κ.τ.λ.: and knows not Phoibos for his father; lit. that his father is Phoibos.

ἀμφὶ βωμίους τροφάς... : 'he used to wander about the altars of his boyhood's home in childish play.' τροφάς is τροφας doubtless, as Paley says, for τόπον ὅπου ἐτρέφετο, but I should prefer to take the word of his bringing-up in the widest sense rather than merely of his maintenance from the altar- offerings: cp. Hec. 599 ἆρ' οἱ τεκόντες διαφέρουσιν, ἢ τροφαί ; For the meaning given to τροφάς Paley cp. Med. 68 πεσσούς προσελθών (the place where the game was played; but see Dr. Verrall's note ad loc.), and ἐν τυρῷ, ἐν μυρρίνῃ and the like in Aristophanes. The use with abstract substantives is more rare, but he gives also ψῆφον παρ' αὐτήν, Ι. T. 969 (close by the place of voting) and ματέρος ἀνθονόμους ἐπωπάς, Aesch. Supp. 533, the flowery meads where my mother was watched.
ἔθεντο χρυσ.: made him treasurer. This use of τίθημι as a factitive verb is one of its commonest : cp. vv. 105, 109,
καταζῇ, continues to live; so Plat. Symp. 192 в καταζῆν ἀγάμοις. Cp. Hdt. 9. 93 κατακοιμήσαντος τὴν φυλακήν, having slept through his watch.
Χαλκωδ. Chalkodon was an ancient and famous king of the Chalkidians in Euboea, who are called in Hom. Abantes from Abas father of Chalkodon: cp. 11. 2. 541 Χαλκωδοντιάδης μεγαθύμων ἀρχὸς ᾿Αβάντων.
πολέμ. κλύδων: storm of war.

ὃν ξυμπονήσας... : Because he lent them aid therein, and helped to sweep away that storm. For ξυνεξελών cp. Med. 904 χρόνῳ δὲ νεῖκος πατρὸς ἐξαιρουμένη: Thuc. 4. 83 μὴ ὑπεξελεῖν τῷ Περδίκκᾳ τὰ δεινά, i.e. remove them from his path.
ἀξίωμα, dignity, honour. The gen. may be defini- tive or possessive: cp. Or. 9 κοινῆς τραπέζης ἀξίωμ᾽ ἔχων ἴσον.

Αἰόλου, Aiolos was son of Hellen, son of Zeus. It is strange that Eur. here makes Xouthos son of Aiolos since the legends, as we have them, make Aiolos, Doros and Xouthos brothers. There is also some confusion in calling Xouthos an Achaean, as Achaios was, according to the legends (cp. v. 1592) a son of Youthos and Kreousa and brother of Ion.
χρον. σπ. λέχη, though married long.

οὐ λέληθεν κ.τ.λ. : he has not been (so) forgetful as it appears; lit. it has not escaped his memory, as it seems to have done. λέληθεν is impersonal; cp. Xen. Hier. 2. 5 τὸ πλῆθος περὶ τούτου λεληθέναι οὐ θαυμάζω : Plat. Legg. 903 C σὲ δὲ λέληθε περὶ τοῦτο αὐτὸ ἡ γένεσις ὡς ἕνεκα ἐκείνου γίγνεται πᾶσα, ὅπως κ.τ.λ.
τε...τε: that the boy may have his rights without exposure of the secret. Cp. υυ. 257, 309.
κτίστορα, founder. Ion is to be the eponymous hero of the Ionian settlement in Asia Minor: see v. 1584.

θήσεται, will cause; an extension (following the analogy of ποιεῖν) of the factitive use noticed on v. 54. --- ὄνομα, adverbial. - κεκλῆσθαι : note the tense, which imports that the name will be a permanent one.
δαφν. γύαλα, laurel-planted close, i.e. the grove of sacred laurels which lay on one side of the temple: cp. v. 115 ὑπὸ ναοῖς, and v. 220 n.

ὡς ἂν...τὸ κρανθέν. Paley says, "That he may hear the oracle which is to be delivered to Xuthus and Creusa." But he already knows what is to be the purport of this (vv. 69 sqq.); and if he did not, the interior of the temple would offer him a better position for learning than the garden out- side. It is better to take κρανθέν in the sense of accomplished, done. Hermes (who, it is to be observed, takes no part in the action of the play) offers by these words an explanation of his presence on the scene. Being interested in Ion, and knowing Apollo's intentions concerning the lad, he has come to see the matter out, to learn all (ἐκ-μάθω) that is (actually) done about the lad. Observe that κρανθέν is pure (timeless) aorist, = ὅ τι ἂν κρανθῇ.

λαμπρὰ θῇ. It is not clear whether the laurel branches are to be used for sweeping the pavement (cp. vv. 115, 114), or for decoration of the πυλώματα : perhaps both methods of brightening' the temple-entrance are intended. -πυλώματα, the portals, including not only the doors but also the pave- ment in front to the top of the steps. This space was in the case of the Parthenon flanked on each side by an open screen of bronze-work, so as to form a sort of vestibule.
Ἴωνα is in apposition to ovoga which is cognate acc. with ὀνομάζω.

Ion's Monody. - 'The sun's chariot now returns chasing away the stars, and the mountain's peaks are burning beneath his wheels. The incense floats up to the temple roof and the priestess prepares for her task. Ye servants of the god, bathe you in Kastalia's stream and so approach the shrine; and beware of uttering ill-omened speech to those who would consult the oracle. My task, as ever, shall be to make bright with flowers and branches of the bay this portal, and to keep off the flocking birds. Come, to thy work, my laurel-branch, wherewith I sweep the temple floor as each day dawns.-Hail, O Healer! Blessed be thou, O Leto's son ! Fair is my task and noble, to serve not men but gods. Phoibos I call my father, for he it is that feedeth me. Blessed be thou, O Leto's son ! - But I must cease my sweep- ing and for my hands are pure-pour out the water from the golden ewers. Oh, that I might ever serve Phoibos thus ! Ha, the birds! Come not near, or mine arrows shall slay you. Nay, go elsewhere and make homes for your young; twould hurt me to take your lives, for ye are the gods messengers to men. Leave me to my labours in the service of those that nurture me.' 82 sqq. ἅρματα κ.τ.λ. 'Lo, his bright chariot and steeds four! The Sun now makes light o'er the earth; and before his fire there the stars flee into the vasty night of space, and Parnassus' untrodden peaks kindling into flame receive for mortals the wheels of light. Both τάδε and τῷδ are used δεικτικῶς. -πυρί is a causal dat. - τεθρίππων. τέθριππος is properly an adj., but both τέθριππον and τέθριππα are used as substantives = a chariot and four. Here τεθρίππων is a de- fining gen., and ἅρμ. τεθρίππων = lit. his chariot, viz. his four- horse. Musgrave proposed κάμπτει for λάμπει, with no stop at τεθρίππων. This would be a great improvement, and it is unfortunate that it lacks Mss. authority. κάμπτειν is properly said of a man who turns back along the second half of the δίαυλος after doubling the καμπτήρ at the end farthest from the starting point. Thus the word is correctly used of the sun's course through the heavens, as that is his home-journey: cp. Alc. 596 ἀμφὶ μὲν ἀελίου κνεφαίαν ἱππόστασιν, of the western sky. Similarly κάμπτειν βίον οι βίου τέλος.

ἱεράν. Curtius connects the word with the Sanskrit ish-ira-s, = vigorous etc. If this is correct we have a ready explanation of such expressions as ἱερὸν μένος, ἱερὴ ἐλαίη, ἱερὸς ἰχθύς. As applied to νύξ, κνέφας and the like, the meaning vigorous would seem to have developed into mighty, vasty, mysterious; with φάος, ἦμαρ, etc. into glorious, splendid. The later sense sacred, divine, which at last superseded the others, would easily spring out of either of these two classes of meanings.
ἄβατοι, untrodden, because sacred: they could be easily climbed. --κορυφαί: see on v. 714.
ἁψίδα : take literally of the wheel of the sun's chariot. It spoils the picture to import the meaning orb, for which there is no authority.

ἀνύδρου, of the desert: the epithet is transferred from the land where the myrrh is found to the myrrh itself. The myrrh is being burned as incense. It is a bitter aromatic gum exuding from the bark of a shrub (cp. v. 1175), chiefly found in Arabia.
θάσσει. She did not sit on the tripod every day. Cр. v. 419 n. and see Introd. § 3.
ἀείδουσα .. κελαδήσῃ : chanting to the Hellenes the frenzied utterances which Apollo makes ring in her ears. See Introd. § 3. See Introd. § 3. The
θέραπες : noble Delphians. form θέραψ is a rare and poetic variant of θέραπων.
Κασταλίας: see Introd. § 2.

ἀφυδρανάμενοι, when you have bathed. The ἀπο- ex- presses thoroughness, as often: cp. ἀπανδρόω, ἀπεργάζομαι, ἀπευθύνω, ἀποδείκνυμι, ἀποταυροῦσθαι etc. As the simple verb is common, and our word is recognized by Hesychius (ἀφυδραίνεσθαι. περιραίνεσθαι, ἀπολούεσθαι), the correction φαι- δρυνάμενοι is unnecessary. The practice of bathing or sprinkling oneself with water before performing an act of worship or sacred duty is natural and almost universal.

ἀγαθοί. Ι venture to offer this very slight correction for the MSS. ἀγαθόν, which can scarcely be right. The recurrence of the word in the next line has caused difficulty, and Herm. would omit φήμας τ᾽ ἀγαθάς, but the repetition is intentional. ἀγαθός meant primarily of noble birth, and this remained as one of its commonest meanings through classical times: cp. Od. 15. 324 οἱά τε τοῖς ἀγαθοῖσι παραδρώωσι χέρηες : ΙΙ. 21. 109 πατρὸς δ᾽ εἴμ᾿ ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μητήρ : Soph. fr. 105 οἱ δ᾽ ἀγαθοὶ πρὸς τῶν ἀγενῶν κατανικῶνται. Here Ion, speaking to the masters of the temple, who were nobly-born Delphians (Introd. § 3 and v. 415 sq.), reminds them that, being what they are, they especially should be careful of their speech on a festival day. At the same time, by a skilful little play on the word, he takes occasion to suggest a gracious demeanour towards visitors intending to consult the oracle, whom it would be their business to introduce: noblesse oblige. The play can scarcely be preserved in English, but we may trans- late, Guard your lips from ill-omened speech, gentle lords; and let the gentle speech of a gracious tongue be your utter- ance to those who would consult the god. Of course ἀγαθοί is nom. not voc.

ἱλέας is Dr. Verrall's clever correction of the meaning- less ἰδίαs of the Mss. (Journal of Hellenic Studies, vol. 1. p. 227), and will to most students carry conviction. Wecklein proposes Δίαs, but this does not suit the context; it is the language before consultation of the oracle which is in question. ἀποφαίνειν : inf. for imperative. The construction is rare with a true imperative preceding, but cp. Ar. Ach. 1001 ἀκούετε, λεῴ· κατὰ τὰ πάτρια τοὺς χόας πίνειν, Hdt. 6. 86 σὺ δή μοι καὶ τὰ χρήματα δέξαι καὶ τάδε τὰ σύμβολα σῴζε λαβών· ὃς δ᾽ ἂν ἔχων ταῦτα ἀπαιτέῃ, τούτῳ ἀποδοῦναι.
πόνους, acc. in apposition to the sentence πτόρθοισι...
ἀναθήματα. Some of these adorned the outside walls of the temple.

προπόλευμα, not service (as Lex. s.v.) but instrument of service; cp. δούλευμα, a slave, καλλίστευμα, beauty (see esp. Phoen. 215), κήδευμα, affinis, etc. The use of ἀδίκημα v. 325 is similar. -δάφνας is gen. of material. - Come, thou fresh sprung branch of fairest bay, that servest me in sweeping the temple-steps of Phoibos.'
ἐξ: supply a participle;--- 'brought from the never- fading garden neath the temple-wall.

ἵνα δρόσοι κ.τ.λ. : where the sacred waters, sending forth their gushing ever-flowing stream from among the myrtle-shrubs, water the sacred foliage wherewith etc. Both μυρσίνας and φοβάν are generic sing. for plural. The myrtle and olive are said b by ancient writers to need abundant irrigation. -ῥυτὰν ἀέναον : so Fix from the similar passage Ηipp. 123 ῥυτὰν παγὰν προϊεῖσα. The Mss. give τὰν ἀένναον (a common error for dévaor), showing sho a deficiency of syllable. The construction of ἐκπροϊεῖσαι with μυρσίνας was suggested to me by Dr. Verrall. It is neat, and removes all the difficulty that has been felt about the passage. a

παναμέριος, every day. (The ordinary sense, all day long, is unsuitable here.) So too I should take πανήμερος, Aesch. Prom. 1024 ἄκλητος ἕρπων δαιταλεὺς πανήμερος. -ἅμα κ.τ.λ. : ‘so soon as the sun's swift wing appears': cp. v. 41.
τὸ κατ' ἦμαρ, an adverbial phrase following the analogy of τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦδε, τὸ πρὸ τοῦ and the like.

Ο Healer! Healer! Blessed, blessed be thou, O Son of Leto!' This fine burst of praise (repeated vv. 140-2) forms a fitting prelude and conclusion to the lines in which the young man enthusiastically describes his delight in the service of an immortal master. Note the three consecutive lines, each consisting of two molossi (— — -). The rhythm is characteristic of hymns of praise.
πόνοις, modal dat.
εὐλογῶ, praise (as my father).
That is, τὸ δ᾽ ὠφέλιμον ἐμοὶ (ὄνομα) πατέρος ὄνομα λέγω : another way of saying τὸν δ' ὠφέλιμον ἐμοὶ πατέρα λέγω.

Φοίβου, ‘even Phoibos the temple's lord.' Φοίβου should strictly have been in apposition to ὄνομα, but it has been very naturally drawn into the case of the personal word πατέρος. Cp. a similar attraction, Soph. Εl. 317 τοῦ κασιγνήτου τί φής, ἥξοντος, ἢ μέλλοντος ;
At this point the strophic correspondence ceases.

ὁλκοῖς. ὁλκός, anything which ἕλκει or ἕλκεται " (Badham); so here the thing drawn consisting of laurel. Similarly we speak of cuttings from plants. Translate, with my broom of bay. -ὁλκ. is dat. instr. with μόχθους. Soph. Εἰ. τμητοῖς ὁλκοῖς = smooth-cut reins.
ἀποχεύονται. Note the epic form. The v represents the F of the stem XeF.
ἀγαθῇ μοίρᾳ : εἰρωνεία, in anticipation of his future greatness.
φοιτῶσι, are flocking hither.
μάρψω, catch.-av, as on a former occasion (Paley).

ὅδε πρὸς θυμέλας κ.τ.λ. Here to the temple-steps another oars his way, a swan. The metaphor of ἐρέσσει seems to have been first used by Aesch. : cp. Ag. 52 πτερύγων ἐρετμοῖσιν ἐρεσσόμενοι. He also uses it of persons beating the breast in grief. It is imitated in Lucr.'s remigii oblitae pennarum, Virg.'s remigio alarum, and Milton's oarage of their wings.-ὅδε... ἄλλος : cp. Aesch. Theb. 419 γίγας ὅδ᾽ ἄλλος.
φόρμιγξ... σύμμολπος, that the lyre, Phoibos lyre, makes music with thee.
πάραγε πτέρυγας : otherwhere take thy flight.

λίμνης. This was a circular lake or tank (called λίμνη τροχοειδής by Hdt., and λίμνη τροχοέσσα by Kallimachos), 100 yards in diameter, which supplied the water for the equally famous temple of Apollo at Delos. It is still to be seen.

αἱμάξεις...ᾠδάς: thou shalt raise, and in blood, if thou wilt not heed, that sweet dirge of thine. -τάς, demon- strative. αἱμάσσειν ᾠδάς is an expression similar to μηκύνειν βοήν (to raise a loud cry; not, to intensify a cry already begun), λιγαίνειν μέλος (to sing a song with a clear voice), τήκειν οἰμωγήν (to utter a languishing lament), κλέπτειν μύθους, φλέγειν λόγους, and the like. In these phrases the verb con- tains two predications; e.g. μηκύνειν = to utter, and that loudly, τήκειν = to utter, and that languishly; and accordingly αἱμάσσειν ᾠδάς = to utter, and that amid blood. The swan is not a musical bird, but was fabled to sing at its death. Ion threatens that he will give the bird cause to sing, and to sing in a bloody death. Editors (Kirchoff, Nauck, Paley) have needlessly wished to alter an expression which is as beautiful as it is bold.

εὐναίας καρφηράς, nests of sticks and straws. εὐναία as a subst. = εὐνή (so the Schol.) is rare. It is, however, the reading of M and of the Scholiast in Aesch. Theb. 1007 ἐπ᾿ εὐναίᾳ χθονὸς | θάπτειν (where see Dr. Verrall's note), and is used by Apoll. Rhod. 1. 955 in the sense of anchorage. καρφηράς (so the Mss.) is an adj. derived from κάρφος, for which καρφήρεις (Paley) would be a preferable form.
ψαλμοί, the twang. The proper meaning of ψάλλω is to pluck as one plucks the strings of a stringed instru- ment: cp. Bacch. 783 τόξων χερὶ | ψάλλουσι νευράς.

χωρῶν παιδούργει. Goand breed thy young by theeddy- ings of Alpheios. Supply χώρει with νάπος below. –᾿ Αλφείου. The Alpheios rises in the S.E. corner of Arkadia, and flowing in a westerly direction falls into the Ionian sea. Olympia is on its banks.

νάπος Ἴσθμιον. The grove of pines near the temple of Poseidon on the Isthmus. According to Pausanias ii. 1 an avenue of these trees formed one approach to the temple, while another was through a double line of statues represent- ing victors in the Isthmian games.

αἰδοῦμαι, I scruple. -κτείνειν δέ. As the words are an additional reason for the command preceding, γάρ would be more natural than dé, which, however (as also καί), often replaces it: cp. Aesch. Theb. 120 ᾿Αργεῖοι δέ, 726 παιδολέτωρ δ'. Omit the conjunction in translating. Sometimes in compari- sons δέ and καί are used for ὡς : cp. H. F. 101 κάμνουσι γάρ τοι τῶν βροτῶν αἱ ξυμφοραί, | καὶ πνεύματ᾽ ἀνέμων οὐκ ἀεὶ ῥώμην ἔχει.

Parodos, of which vv. 218-236 form a κομμός. — 'Not in Athens alone, then, are there fair temples of the gods and service of Aguieus of the roadway. See, what sculptures! Here is Herakles slaying the hydra. And here Iolaos. And here Bellerophon slays the chimaera. -Look, the battle of the Giants. - Yes, and Pallas brandishing her aegis against Enkelados. - And Zeus with his double-flaming bolt blasting Mimas.--And Bromios slays another of those sons of Earth. Kommos. The Chorus observing Ion, who has reappeared, ask if they may enter the temple, but are told that they must first have offered sacrifice. Ion in turn asks whose servants they are, and they for reply point to Kreousa, who is seen approaching. It will be observed that the Parodos, including the chorus' share of the kommatic portion (the dialogue with Ion), falls into eighteen sections. The first of these was probably sung by the whole Chorus; the remainder by the performers in turn, the coryphaeus taking the second, the last, and vv.
The paragraphs in the text mark these sections.

εὐκίονες ἦσαν κ.τ.λ.: were there (as I supposed) fair- columned courts of the gods and service of Apollo of the Roadway. The Chorus knew, of course, that there was a temple at Delphi; they are surprised at its beauty.

ἀγυιατ. θερ. Apollo was called 'Αγνιεύς as protector of the streets (ἀγνιαί). Conical pillars were set up before the street-doors of the houses, and on these incense was burned in his honour. The worship, which was performed on solemn occasions, is called κνισἂν ἀγυιάς, Ar. Εq. 1320 etc. stage-direction p. 3, and cp. v. 89. See

καὶ παρὰ Λοξίᾳ κ.τ.λ.: with Loxias too (i.e. on his temple) there is the fair-faced brightness of twin façades. καλλιβλέφαρον, fair-faced. For this extension of the use of βλέφαρον cp. Phoen. 543 νυκτός τ' ἀφεγγὲς βλέφαρον. So ὄμμα frequently means face, appearance, and even sight (thing seen): cp. Iph. T. 110 ὅταν δὲ νυκτὸς ὄμμα λυγαίας μόλῃ, Aesch. Pers. 428 ἕως κελαινῆς νυκτὸς ὄμμ᾽ ἀφείλετο (τὴν μάχην), Soph. Αi. 1004 ὦ δυσθέατον ὄμμα, Εl. 903 ξύνηθες ὄμμα. - διδύμων προσώπων, i.e. the eastern and western faces of the temple. See Introd. § 2. Of course the Chorus cannot see both faces, but the expression is natural, since the sight of one suggests the other. The chief figures in the eastern pediment were Apollo, Latona and Artemis, Apollo occupying the centre. In one angle was the setting sun. The rising sun, Prof. Middleton thinks, probably filled the other. The western pediment had for its subject the worship of Dionysos. 190 ff. The sculptures described are probably imetopes on the front of the temple, but (according to Prof. Middleton, Hellenic Journal, vol. 9, p. 289) within the Pronaos, as those metopes alone appear to have been decorated. It will be noticed that the pervading motif is the destruction of earth- born monsters by gods and heroes, the subjects being (as the same high authority observes) evidently chosen from their relation to the victory of Apollo over the earth-born Python. It has been suggested that Euripides trans- ferred to his stage-scene (representing Apollo's temple) sub- jects taken from a στοά which the Athenians built and dedicated at Delphi in honour of Phormio's victories in the Corinthian gulf at the beginning of the Peloponnesian war (see on v. 1592). It stood near to the temple. This is possible, but it is much more likely that the poet would make his scene a faithful representation of the eastern front of the temple as familiar to hundreds of his audience.
τάνδ', here: δεικτικῶς.
χρυσ. ἅρπαις. The golden scimitar would according to the common practice be of gilded bronze, fitted into the stone-work.
ὄσσοις. The only parts found besides this are ὄσσε (dual) and ὄσσων (gen. pl.).
ἆρ ὃς κ.τ.λ.: Can it be he whose story is told to me at my weaving? Cp. v. 506 and Iph. Α. 789 παρ ἱστοῖς μυθεῦσαι τάδ᾽ ἐς ἀλλήλας. Zeus.

συναντλεῖ: cp. Virgil's haurire labores, bella exhausta. The metaphor cannot be reproduced in English. -Δίῳ, of The word apparently does not occur in this limited sense until the Tragedians: see Lexicon. For Δίος παῖς = παῖς Διός cp. Soph. Ο. Τ. 267 τῷ Λαβδακείῳ παιδί, Αἱ. 134 Τελαμώνιε παῖ, Ιph. Τ. 5 τῆς Τυνδαρείας θυγατρός, and the Latin filius erilis, my master's son: also v. 1144.
καὶ μάν : see detached note A.
πτεροῦντος, contracted form of πτερόεντος from πτερόεις. The adjectives in -ήεις and -bets can be used either contracted or uncontracted. ἔφεδρον, Bellerophon.
τρισώμ. ἀλκάν : Musgr. cp. H. F. 180 τετρασκελές ὕβρισμα, of the Centaurs. So Hor. has forma tricorporis umbrae, of Geryon. - At this point the strophic correspondence ceases.
διώκω properly means to set in quick motion: cp. Od. 12, 182 ῥίμφα διώκοντες (sc. τὴν νῆα, of rowers), Aesch. Eum. 403 διώκους᾽ ἦλθον ἄτρυτον πόδα.

τύκαισιν. So Herm. for τείχεσι of the Mss. The word F does not occur, but is formed from τυκ-, as ταφή from таф- (cp. τύκος, τύκισμα). τύκαισιν λαΐνοισι = stonework. The cor- rection is not required on metrical grounds, though ἐν τύκαισιν gives a better rhythm; but τείχεσιν is impossible in the con- text. τύποισιν has been suggested, but does not account for the corruption so readily as τύκαισιν.
ἐπ' Ἐγκελάδῳ: for the dat. cp. v. 1051: Soph. Ai. 44 ἢ καὶ τὸ βούλευμ᾿ ὡς ἐπ᾿ ᾿Αργείοις τόδ᾽ ἦν; ib. 772 ἐπ᾿ ἐχθροῖς χεῖρα φοινίαν τρέπειν.
τί γάρ ; an exclamation of surprise; literally Why, what?—ἀμφίπυρον, flaming at each end : cp. v. 716.

Βρόμιος. The oldest Greek name for the god is Διόνυσος. Βρόμιος, Βάκχος, and "Ιακχοs are later surnames, all meaning boisterous, noisy. Βρόμιος occurs in Pindar, but Βάκχος is not found earlier than Soph. O. T. 211. Βακχεύς is found only in lyric passages. See on v. 1075 πολύυμνον.

γυάλων, sanctuary, i. e. the temple. γύαλον properly denotes a cup-like hollow: cp. Ι.Α. 1052 ἐν κρατήρων γυάλοις. The application of the word to the Delphian temple here and in vv. 233, 245 and elsewhere has generally been explained by saying (1) that it merely = μυχός, interior, or (2) that γύαλα primarily describing the locality of Delphi can also be used even when the temple alone is referred to. But against (1) it is to be noted (and the fact is remarkable) that γύαλον is used of no other temple than that at Delphi; and against (2) that Delphi is not situated in a γύαλον, but occupies an elevated position overlooking the valley of the Pleistos. The true explanation is to be found in an almost unique character- istic of the Delphian sanctuary. The ἄδυτον was actually a pit or cavern in the earth (see Introd. § 2); and nothing could be more natural than that a name originally describing the primitive sanctuary should afterwards be extended to the temple built over it, and even to the sacred precincts. Indeed ἀδύτων is used in precisely the same manner, v. 1309. So at Kolonos not only the rocky basin or hollow (κοίλου...κρατῆρος Soph. O.C. 1593) into which the brazen steps descended, but also the locality, including the grove of the Eumenides, was called χαλκόπους ὀδός, the brazen threshold. Cp. O.C. 57. From v. 1492 of the same play it appears that the word γύαλον was somehow connected with the Kolonos cavern also. After ποδί a subst. was wanting as object of ὑπερβῆναι, the Mss. showing a lacuna. βηλόν is Hermann's suggestion. The purport of the question asked by the Chorus is doubtless whether they may enter the temple. -λευκῷ ποδί, with bare foot: cp. Bacch. 861 θήσω λευκὸν πόδα, ίδ. 665 λευκὸν κῶλον ἐξηκόντισαν, Cycl. 73 βάκχαις σὺν λευκόποσιν.

οὐδ᾽ ἄν κ.τ.λ. Ion interrupts the question before it is finished.-The Mss. give πυθοίμαν αὐδάν ; ΙΩ. τίνα δὲ θέλεις. This violates the metre seriously and is in other respects objectionable. The text is Hermann's.
ὄμφαλον : see Introd. § 2.

Γόργονες. What these Gorgons were, is uncertain. Paley suggests that they were like the Γοργεῖοι τύποι, Gorgon figures, of Aesch. Eum. 49, i.e. rude antique sculptures. If this is so, the mention of the τύποι in that scene was probably suggested by their actual existence in the temple.

θυμέλας, platform: see on ". 46. As v. 219, σέ τοι τὸν παρὰ ναόν, shows, Ion is nearer to the temple than the Chorus. He is in fact on the top of the steps, and they at the bottom. He invites them, on certain conditions, to mount to where he is himself standing, but they retain their proper place in the ὀρχήστρα. It would appear from this passage that poorer worshippers consulting the god, who were only able to offer a cake, received their response on the steps or platform of the temple. To pass inside the temple (ἐς μυχόν) was a privilege accorded only to those who could offer a sheep. It is highly improbable that any visitor was allowed to enter the ἄδυτον (as some edd. have interpreted μυχόν): its very name implies as much.---Note the dactyl θυσατε preceding the anapaest πέλανον: it produces an un- pleasant rhythm and is of rare occurrence.

ἐπ᾿ ἀσφ. μήλοισι, without sheep slaughtered; lit. on the terms of, etc. Cp. Med. 1103 εἴτ᾽ ἐπὶ φλαύροις, εἴτ᾽ ἐπὶ χρηστοῖς [τέκνοις] μοχθοῦσι, whether they toil having good children or bad, and the common phrase ἐπ' ἐξειργασμένοις, with the deed done.
ἔχω μαθοῦσα: a periphrasis for μεμάθηκα, I have grasped, I understand. The formation of the English perfect is similar.

οὐ παραβαίνομεν, we are not for transgressing. This use of the pres. is common both in Greek and Latin: cp. δίδωμι, I offer: Plaut. Trin. 1062 quid ago, what am I to do?: Verg. Aen. 2. 322 quam prendimus arcem ?
γύαλα: see on v. 220.

Παλλάδος ἔνοικα κ.τ.λ. The order is Παλλ. ἔνοικα μέλαθρά ἐστι τρόφιμα μέλαθρα τ. ἐμ. τυρ. : the home of Pallas is the place of my masters nurturing.' Though using the plural, the Chorus are thinking only of Kreousa, as the next line shows.
παρούσας κ.τ.λ. But she is here of whom thou askest; lit., thou askest about one present here. τᾶσδε, adverbial, δεικτικῶς.

First ἐπεισόδιον. --Kreousa enters. After expressing sympathy for her evident distress, which she refuses to ex- plain, Ion asks of her country and parentage. She tells him; and a long conversation then ensues, in the course of which it transpires that she and her husband have come to Delphi to ask the god whether they may hope for children, being hitherto childless. Kreousa also confides to Ion that she wishes secretly to consult the god on behalf of a friend. This friend many years ago had a son of whom Apollo was the father. She had exposed the child as soon as it was born, and she now wishes to ask the god whether he has pre- served it or left it to perish. Ion replies that she will find no one willing to question Apollo for her on such a subject. Kreousa upbraids the god for his injustice, and reluctantly acquiesces in the abandonment of her purpose. Xouthos now enters, having consulted the oracle in the cave of Trophonios. He has been told that he and Kreousa will not return home childless; but beyond this Trophonios will not anticipate the answer of Apollo. Xouthos then enters the temple to consult the oracle, and Kreousa departs to make supplication at the altars of other deities. Ion left alone soliloquizes on the immorality of the gods, and declares that men cannot be expected to be holy with such examples before them.
γενναιότης σοι, 80. ἔστι: thou hast nobility. Cp. Phoen. 1680 γενναιότης σοι, μωρία δ᾽ ἔνεστί τις.
σχήμα: cp. Soph. Ant. 1169 καὶ ζῇ τύραννον σχῆμ' ἔχων. The proper meaning of the word is outward guise or bearing. It is formed from σεχ-, whence ἔχω, σχεῖν.
μερίμνης, properly distracting care (μερ-).
γύαλα : see on v. 220.

τὸ μὲν σόν κ.τ.λ. : It is feeling of thee to wonder, etc. – With ἐλθεῖν supply σε. ἐς θαύματ᾽ ἐλθεῖν is epexegetic οἱ τὸ σόν. τὸ σόν, τὸ ἐμόν, and the like phrases, though com- monly used by the tragedians as equivalents of σύ, ἐγώ, etc., are not absolute synonyms of these words. τὸ σόν, for in- stance, means thou, in this or that relation, in such or such circumstances, behaving in this or that manner. Thus τὸ σὸν λέγει would not be Greek for σὺ λέγεις, but τὸ σὸν οὐκ ἀπαιδεύτως ἔχει is a neat way of expressing, thou, by speaking thus, showest feeling. Cp. Soph. Εl. 261 τὰ μητρὸς ... ἔχθιστα συμβέβηκεν, 'my mother, behaving as she does. - ἀπαιδεύτως, without feeling. The words ἀπαιδευσία and ἀμαθία imported not only the lack of intellectual culture and manners, but also a want of moral perception, or what we call feeling. Cp. v. 916 ἀμαθής and note there: Εl. 294 ἔνεστι δ' οἴκτος ἀμαθίᾳ μὲν οὐδαμοῦ, σοφοῖσι δ᾽ ἀνδρῶν.
μνήμην κ.τ.λ. : I retraced the path of an ancient memory. Cp. Οr. 14 τί τἄρρητ᾽ ἀναμετρήσασθαι με δεῖ;

ἐκεῖ τὸν νοῦν ἔσχον : I was thinking of other things. --ἐκεῖ is Burgess's suggestion for οἴκoι of the Mss. Besides improving the sense, the correction is strongly supported by Phoen. 360 λόγοισι χαίρει, τὸν δὲ νοῦν ἐκεῖσ᾽ ἔχει, thinks other- wise than he speaks; ib. 1418 τὸν νοῦν πρὸς αὐτὸν οὐκ ἔχων, ἐκεῖσε δέ, thinking of something else; Ι.Τ. 781 οὐδέν· πέραινε δ', ἐξέβην γὰρ ἄλλοσε, I was thinking of something else; Soph. Τr. 272 τότ' ἄλλοσ᾽ αὐτὸν ὄμμα θατέρᾳ δέ νοῦν ἔχοντα.
ποῖ δίκην κ.τ.λ. Το whom shall we refer the award- ing of justice, if the injustices of our masters are to be our ruin?' This use of ἀναφέρω, =refer to a tribunal, is common in the orators.

τί χρῆμα κ.τ.λ. Why this mysterious sadness, lady? Lit., as to what thing, etc. Both χρήμα and ἀνερεύνητα are adverbial. The Mss. have χρῆμα ἀνερ. The Sé was supplied by Matthiae, but perhaps ἄρα is more likely to have fallen out.
μεθῆκα τόξα : I have shot my shaft, have said my say.
τέ ... τε: as I am silent, so do thou think no more. Cp. vv. 72, 309.
τραφεῖσα ἀπο : i.e. born of and reared by.

κεὐτυχοῦμεν. The emphasis given by the kal is best represented in English by a stress on the auxiliary verb; thus far I am happy. Cp. Lys. Or. 24. § 12 τί γὰρ ἂν καὶ ἔλεγεν ; for what could he have said?
πρὸς θεῶν ἀληθῶς. Tell me truly... As Badham observes, Ion speaks with all the simple eagerness of a child. Cp. v. 275.

πρόγονος πατήρ, i.e. grandfather. Erechtheus' father was Pandion. 269 ff. The rationalisers of the myth identify Kekrops with the τέττιγξ (grasshopper), because it was supposed to be born from the earth. They say that the τεῦχος of v. 273 was the folliculus or egg-bag which the insect leaves in the fields. The Athenians used to wear golden cicadas in their hair as a symbol that they were αὐτόχθονες. -For the story see on v. 10.
ὥσπερ ... νομίζεται: i.e. as it is usual to represent the story in painting.
οὐχ ὁρώμενον, because enclosed in a τεῦχος or casket.
οὐ κάμνω σχολῇ: lit. I do not fail in respect of leisure, i.e. I have plenty of time to answer your questions. Cp. v. 363.

Erechtheus when fighting against Eumolpos (king of Eleusis and son of Poseidon) obtained an oracle to the effect that he might purchase purchase vic victory by the life of one of his children. He slew the youngest, and the others destroyed themselves in accordance with an agreement they had made to perish all together. Poseidon afterwards slew Erechtheus by an earthquake. A spring of brackish water and a mark in the rock used to be shown on the Acropolis as having been produced by Poseidon's trident on this occasion.

δαίμων. The Mss. give Πύθιος, contra metrum, since the vis long. Paley thinks there may be synizesis of the -ios, but this is improbable, and the word is in itself objectionable with Πύθιαι following. It looks like a gloss which has sup- planted the word over which it was written. Such an original as that proposed in the text would readily account for the corruption.-Near the Long Rocks stood an altar of Zeὺς 'Αστραπαῖος, between the Πύθιον, a temple of Apollo, and the temple of Olympian Zeus. From this altar on three days and : nights of three months in the year lightnings were watched for in the direction of "Αρμα, a a village vil on the borders of Attica and Boeotia, where Amphiaraos was swallowed up in the earth. When these lightnings, which were called ἀστραπαὶ δί' "Αρματος, were seen a sacred embassy was sent to Delphi. Apollo honoured the place by causing the lightnings to be seen from it. Apollo's bow was supposed to make lightnings, cp. Ap. Rhod. 4. 1708 μαρμαρέην δ᾽ ἀπέλαμψε βιὸς περὶ πάντοθεν αἴγλην : and perhaps Hor. carm. sec. 61 fulgente decorus arcu. (From Musgrave's note.)

The Mss. give τιμᾷ τιμᾷ ὡς. Many corrections have been proposed (ἄτιμα τιμᾷ, τιμᾷ γ᾽ ἀτίμως, τιμᾷ γ᾽ ἄτιμ᾿ ὡς, τιμᾶ. τί μήν; ὡς, τιμᾷ. τί τιμᾷ; and others) but none that is satis- factory. Those which make Kreousa say or imply that Apollo dishonours the place are inconsistent with the next line. Ion's rejoinder would be, What do you mean by dishonour ? not Why do you hate what the god holds dear? I venture to offer the reading of the text, τί μαίει; why this eager questioning? The question (equivalent to Do not inquire further; cp. τί δ' ἱστορεῖς τόδ'; two lines above) suits Kreousa's agitation and her natural wish to pursue a disagreeable sub- ject no further. Cp. Soph. Ο. Τ. 1056 τί δ' ὅντιν εἶπε ; μηδὲν ἐντραπῇς. For μαίομαι see Lex., where, however, the classi- fication of the uses is somewhat confused. The word is not very common, and a scribe might perhaps be ex- cused for blundering over such a sequence of letters as TIMAITIMΑΙΕΙΜΗ.
ξύνοιδα : Tyrwhitt's admirable correction of ξέν' οἶδα (MSS.).
δέ τίς σ'. The τις is indefinite: note the accent on δέ.
Εὔβοι' ἔστι: see on v. 589.
λέχος, a quasi-cognate acc. : takes thee in marriage.
The object of λαβών is λέχος supplied from the previous line, φέρνας being in apposition.

σηκοῖς δ' ὑστερεῖ. P gives σηκός, C σηκούς, both give εὐ στρέφει. From the scholion copied by C from the archetype, ἐνστρέφεται τῶ τοῦ Τροφωνίου σηκῶ, most edd., including Möllend., gather and approve ἐνστρέφει, which they translate versatur in. But the meaning assigned to ἐνστρέφει is very questionable, and, what is more, inappropriate to the context. Dr. Badham proposes ὑστερεῖ, which gains some probability from χρόνιος v. 403. If ὑστερεῖ became ὑστρεεῖ, εὖστρέφει would easily follow. For Trophonios see Introd. § 2.
Φοίβος οἶδε κ.τ.λ. A neat instance of εἰρωνεία, which Ion's question is purposely framed to elicit.

ἀνάθημα πόλεως. ‘In the Phoenissae the chorus con- sists of captive Tyrian women sent as an offering to the temple of Apollo at Delphi, and in the Iphigenia in Tauris the attendants in the temple of Diana are Greek slaves kidnapped from the coasts of the Aegean.' (Badham.)
κατὰ στέγας, in a (private) house, perhaps one attached to the temple.
That is ἅπαν θεοῦ (δῶμά ἐστι) δῶμά μοι.
νοσοῦσα, νόσους, suffering.
προφῆτις belongs to the relative clause ἡ ἔθρεψε in v.

The full construction of a relative sentence is as fol- lows, -φιλῶ τὴν προφῆτιν ἢ προφῆτις ἔθρεψέ με. The sub- stantive in the relative clause is usually omitted; sometimes, as here, it survives and the antecedent is suppressed. Occasionally it is even placed outside its own clause, a con- struction commonly but incorrectly called attraction of the antecedent. Cp. Aesch. Theb. 383 καὶ νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις ἐπ᾿ ἀσπίδι, | τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις ἡ ἀνοία τινί : Soph. Ο. C. 56: Ant. 1156: Plaut. Most. 250 mulier quae se suamque aetatem spernit, speculo ei usus est (i.e. mulieri quae): Trinum. 137 ille qui mandauit, exturbasti ex aedibus? (i.e. eum qui).

The sequence of these lines as given by the Mss. is scarcely satisfactory, and Wecklein, Studien zu Euripides, p. 338, places vυ. 326-7 after v. 323. The order of the text, however, perhaps affords a still better connexion. Other arrangements have been proposed.
So Dobree. The Mss. have τάλαινά σ᾽ ἡ τεκοῦσ᾽, ἥτις ποτ' ἦν ἄρα, which some edd. correct to τεκοῦσα· τίς ποτ᾽ ἦν ἄρα.
ἀδίκημα κ.τ.λ. I was born perchance the (fruit of a) wrong done to some woman. Ion is the wrong in its concrete form.
ἔχεις δὲ βίοτον; and hast thou substance? See on υ. 581. –ἤσκησαι : present-perfect.
οὐδ' ήξας, and didst thou not hasten?

προξενήσομεν, will manage. The uses of this word are interesting, and I make no apology for appending here Prof. Jebb's note on Soph. O. T. 1482-3 αἱ τοῦ φυτουργοῦ πατρὸς ὑμὶν ὧδ᾽ ὁρᾶν | τὰ πρόσθε λαμπρὰ προὐξένησαν ὄμματα. “Construe : αἱ προὐξένησαν ὑμῖν who have effected for you τὰ πρόσθε λαμπρὰ τοῦ φυτουργοῦ πατρὸς ὄμματα ὧδε ὁρᾶν that the once bright eyes of your sire should see thus, i.e. should be sightless Cp. Xen. Apol. Socr. § 7 ὁ θεὸς δι' εὐμένειαν προξενεῖ μοι οὐ μόνον τὸ ἐν καιρῷ τῆς ἡλικίας καταλῦσαι τὸν βίον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ᾗ ῥᾴστα, the god's kindly offices grant to me that I should close my life, etc. προξενεῖν = (1) to be a πρόξενος : then (2) fig., to lend one's good offices: either (a) absol., as Ο. Ο. 465 προξένει, stand my friend: or (b) with dat. and acc., or acc. and infin., to effect a thing, or result, for one: Xen. Απ. 6. 5. 14 ἴστε ... με ... οὐδένα πω κίνδυνον προξενήσαντα ὑμῖν :... Soph. Τr. 726 ἑλπὶς ἥτις καὶ θράσος τι προξενεῖ. In particular, προξενεῖν τινά τινι = συνιστάναι, to introduce one person to another."
ἀργὸς ἡ θεός, sc. Αἰδώς. People who feel shame are slow to act. ἀργός = ἄ-εργος.
καὶ παῖδά γ᾽ ἔτεκε. Ay, and bare a son.

ὁ φησιν κ.τ.λ. ‘By her own statement, she hath also suffered piteously. The relative clause is anticipatory : cp. Lysias Eratosth. § 43 ὅθεν τῆς στάσεως ἦρξαν, πέντε ἄνδρες ἔφοροι κατέστησαν: the appointment of the ephors was the first step in the revolution; Isaeus 6.8 ὅθεν δικαιόταθ' ἡγοῦμαι τὰ τοιαῦτα εἶναι μανθάνειν, τοῦτον ὑμῖν παρέξομαι τὸν νόμον. The words φησὶν αὐτή convey that the statement is a true one, as coming from her own lips: cp. Soph. Tr. 249 οὔκ, ἀλλὰ τὸν μὲν πλεῖστον ἐν Λυδοῖς χρόνον | κατείχεθ᾽, ὥς φησ' αὐτός, and ib. υ. 253 ὡς αὐτὸς λέγει. Some edd. would read oὔ φησιν αὐτή· καὶ..., but this makes a disjointed and foolish line. It is both more natural and more dignified for Kreusa to pass over the suggestion of the previous verse without remark, than to say that it had already been put to her friend and repudiated.

δράσασα: quite unemphatic and simply equivalent to How? But for Ion's interruption, Kreousa would naturally have added a participial clause, τὸν παῖδ᾽ ἐκθεῖσα. Ion, as it were, asks for this participle. (From Dr. Verrall's note.)
ταῦτα καὶ μαντεύομαι. It is this that I am in fact (καί) asking the god: see on v. 264.
ὀυκέτι : take closely with ἔστι ( is no more); other- wise μή would be required.
ἐλπίζει, expects. This neutral sense of the word is common. So Chaucer, Our mancyple, as I hope, wil be deed.
οὐχ ηὐρ᾽ ἔτι, found him not any more.
οὐ φησι, negat.; she says, not.

χρόνος ... διαπεπραγμένῳ; i.e. how long is it since he was made away with? Cp. Thuc. 3. 29 ἡμέραι μάλιστα ἦσαν τῇ Μιτυλήνῃ ἑαλωκυίᾳ ἕπτα. Sometimes the participle is omitted; cp. Hdt. 2. 145 Ἡρακλέϊ μὲν δὴ ὅσα αὐτοὶ Αἰγύπτιοί φασι εἶναι ἔτεα ἐς "Αμασιν βασιλέα, the number of years from Herakles to Amasis; Thuc. 1. 13 ἔτη ταύτῃ τῇ ναυμαχίᾳ ἑξήκοντα καὶ διακόσιά ἐστι μέχρι κ.τ.λ.

The line is a clear disproof of the constant assertion of the grammars that sentences couched in this form imply a belief on the part of the speaker that the condition is unful- filled. Whether the child still lives or not is just what Kreousa has come to ask. The truth is that if the speaker, in conditional sentences, referring to present or past time, does believe the condition to be unfulfilled, he then uses in Greek the imperfect or aorist indicative in protasis and apodosis, in Latin the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. The moods and tenses of themselves, however, imply nothing as to the speaker's opinion; the hearer is guided to this, if guided at all, by some independent knowledge. Here, for instance, the matter is left just as open as if Kreousa had said εἴπερ ἔστιν, ἔχει. The imperfects present the contingency less im- mediately, less directly and vividly than the presents, but that is all. -εἶχ' ἄν. So the Mss.; but elision of the e of the third person sing. before av was very rarely admitted by the tragedians. εἶχεν has been proposed: it could have the same meaning as if the av were inserted. Cp. v. 827 n.

The transposition of these lines was made by Her- mann. In the Mss. they stand according to the numbering, with ἡ τεκοῦσα in v. 355. ἀδικεῖ νιν, 'the god wrongs her, i.e. (as the next words explain) by not allowing her to have other children. Several editors retain the Mss. order, but ἀδικεῖ νιν ὁ θεός is a very unlikely observation in Ion's mouth, besides being inconsistent with his suggestion in v. 357; while there is nothing in the previous hundred-and-twenty lines of the conversation to show that he could be guilty of such a hopelessly stupid remark as ἡ τεκοῦσα δ᾽ ἀθλία. Moreover the οὔκουν οι οὐκ οὖν of v. 356 remains incapable of translation. Herwerden, retaining the Mss. order but changing the speakers, believes a line to have dropped out both before and after these two.

In enjoying alone what belongs to both (Apollo and the mother), he does injustice.' It can scarcely be doubted that this natural rejoinder is what the poet meant. It is questionable whether the Greek would bear the ingenious versions proposed by Badham and Paley, even if the sense given suited the situation. μόνος has been removed from its natural place for the sake of emphasis: cp. for a far greater derangement Ar. Thesm. 811 οὐδ᾽ ἂν κλέψασα γυνὴ ζεύγει κατὰ πεντήκοντα τάλαντα ἐς πόλιν ἔλθοι τῶν δημοσίων, a woman will not (as men do) steal public money to the extent of fifty talents and return (from service abroad) magnificent in a chariot and pair.

προσῳδός. Of all metaphors for expressing agreement and likeness those from music were the most favourite with the Greeks: cp. the uses of συνῳδός, συνᾴδω, σύμφωνος, ὁμόφωνος, ἐμμελής (πλημμελής), etc.
ἃ· μή μ': so Nauck. The Mss. give καὶ μή γ᾽ ἐπ᾿ οἶκτόν μ'. -'λελήσμεθα: so Dobree followed by many edd. for λελήσ. of MSS.

σ' ἀνιστορῶ. Edd. have altered this to ἀνιστορεῖς, but the text will stand. Ion, it is true, is here asking the ques- tions, but these are merely subsidiary to Kreousa's implied inquiry whether she can consult the oracle about her child. Cp. vv. 330 ff. This question is her chief thought.
κάμνει, is amiss.-νοσεῖ in the next line is merely an echo of this word. For the verbal variation, unnatural in English, cp. Soph. Ο. Τ. 54 ὡς εἴπερ ἄρξεις τῆςδε γῆς ὥσπερ κρατεῖς.
8, adverbial; with regard to which. Transl.: a secret he wishes to keep.
προφητεύσει ... θεμιστεύοντα (ν. 371). The words refer to the noble Delphians who delivered the god's answer to the applicant: cp. vv. 94 ff., 415, and Introd. § 3.
οὐ μαντευτέον, thou must not ask: cp. v. 346.

I have bracketed these verses as suspicious. They seem to have been intended to follow vv. 378-80, by which they were evidently suggested. As it is, they interrupt the connection between vv. 373 and 378, and ἐς τοσοῦτον refers to nothing. But even if transposed, the lines have little to re- commend them; Ion has fully expressed himself at v. 380. Moreover the construction of ἐκπονήσομεν is scarcely admis- sible, and δι' οίωνῶν πτεροῖς (= μαντεύμασι δι' οἰωνῶν) is a strange and bold expression, though not perhaps an impossible one.
ἀνόνητα. So H. Stephens for ἄκοντα of MSS. Other edd. correct to οὐκ ὄντα, but ἀνόνητα better suits ὠφελούμεθα following.
πολλαί κ.τ.λ. Matthiae cp. Aesch. Supp. 339 αἰόλ ἀνθρώπων κακά, | πόνου δ᾽ ἴδοις ἂν οὐδαμοῦ ταὐτὸν πτερόν.

ἓν δ' ἂν εὐτυχές κ.τ.λ. Several editors have altered this and the next line from a misapprehension of the con- struction. The sentence is a brachylogy for ἓν δ᾽ εὐτυχὲς μόλις γίγνεται ἀνθρώπων βίῳ, ὡς ἄν τις σκοπῶν εὕροι. Sometimes the brachylogy is very harsh: cp. Η. F. 917 πῶς παισὶ στενακτὰν ἄταν πατέρος ἀμφαίνεις; ἱ.ε. πῶς ξυνέβη ἄτη ἣν ἀναφαίνεις ; Soph. Αἱ. 1144 ᾧ φθέγμ᾽ ἂν οὐκ ἂν ηὗρες : Verg. Ecl. 6. 46 Pasiphaen niuei solatur amore iuuenci (= canit se solantem). The fol- lowing passages will repay examination: Aesch. Ag. 634, 1312; Cho. 444; Pers. 300; Theb. 895 ; Verg. Aen. 10. 565; id. Ecl.
ὀγκωθῇ τάφῳ, be buried in a mounded tomb: a variation, to which there are numberless parallels, for τάφος ὀγκωθῇ αὐτῷ. This is better than taking ὀγκωθῇ = honour.
ἐἂν χρὴ τάδ'. These words, though corrupt, probably give the correct sense, but afford no sufficient data for emendation.
τόνδε, here.

προβῇ λόγος κ.τ.λ.: and the story go forward not as we were unfolding it. λόγος: the story is put for the matters that form the substance of the story. ἡμεῖς, Kreousa and her fictitious friend. She means Ion to understand that if Xouthos learned the story, he would judge her friend harshly and prevent her attempting to assist her any more.

τὰ γὰρ γυναικῶν κ.τ.λ.: the condition of women is hard as compared with men (that of men); i.e. a woman is more likely to be misjudged than a man in the matter of acquaintanceships. This is better than to take πρὸς ἄρσενας = with regard to men, meaning that men judge women harshly; since women are judged quite as harshly by their own sex.
σύ τε. After πρῶτον μέν and πρῶτα μέν this substitution of τε for δέ or δεύτερον δέ is not uncommon.—ὁ θεὸς χαιρέτω, I bid the god hail.
He observes a troubled look on his wife's face.

ἀφίκου κ.τ.λ. This is translated, You have found me in anxiety, and so Dr. Verrall takes the words. Badham offers a very attractive correction ἀφίγμην (I was not afraid,' but I had become anxious). If this was the original word it might well have been altered by a διορθωτής unfamiliar with the expression: cp. Bacch. 610 εἰς ἀθυμίαν ἀφίκεσθε, Phoen. 361 ἐς φόβον τ᾽ ἀφικόμην.
σ'. Elision of of emphatic is rare. Cp. Hipp. 323 ἔα μ' ἁμαρτεῖν, οὐ γὰρ ἐς σ᾽ ἁμαρτάνω : Soph. Ο. Τ. 64 ψυχὴ πόλιν τε κἀμὲ καὶ σ᾽ ὁμοῦ στένει.
Mark the εἰρωνεία of these lines.

συμβόλαια, dealings. Paley cp. Plat. Rep. 1. p. 333 συμβόλαια δὲ λέγεις κοινωνήματα : cp. also Dem. de cor. § 210 τὰ τοῦ καθ᾽ ἡμέραν βίου συμβόλαια. συνάλλαγμα and συναλλαγή (the former in prose, the latter in verse) have the same meaning. συμβόλαιον most commonly = contract, bond.
μεταπέσοι. The μετά, as commonly in compounds, denotes change.
προφητεύει : cp. v. 369.
See Introd., § 3.
ἔχων. So Badham. The mss. give ἔχω with full stop at ἐχρήζομεν.

χρηστήριον, a victim. The word is rare in this sense, but cp. Aesch. Supp. 450 δεῖ ... πεσεῖν χρηστήρια. Sophocles even uses the word of the animals butchered by Ajax, Ai. 220 κείνου χρηστήρια τἀνδρός. -It appears that a general sacrifice was offered for all the visitors inside the temple, in front of the vaós or cella. If the omens derived from this victim were favourable, the god could be consulted, but not otherwise. Xouthos has learnt not only that the victim has been slain (πέπτωκε), but also that the omens from it have made the day aloia or favourable for obtaining an oracle. See Introd. § 3.

Join ἀμφὶ βωμοὺς ... εὔχου: i.e. pray, visiting the altars in succession. The branches used by suppliants were of laurel or olive and twined with festoons of white wool (στέμματα, cp. υυ. 225, 1310: Soph. Ο. Τ. 3 ἱκτηρίοις κλάδοισιν ἐξεστεμμένοι). The suppliant came and laid his branch on the top of the altar and then seated himself on the altar-steps. If his petition was refused he left his branch on the altar; if it was granted he took it away with him. Cp. Soph. O. Т.

143: Verg. Aen. 7. 154 ramis uelatos Palladis omnes. the present case laurel branches appear to be intended, and the altars are called δαφνηφόρους because of the branches laid on them. They may also have been decked with laurel. In
ἔσται. She confidently echoes Xouthos' words, v. 413.

ἀλλὰ κ.τ.λ., at least retrieve his former sins; i.e. if he will at least give me back my child, whether he also grants me fresh children or not. ἀλλά cannot emphasize vûv which precedes it: cp. vv. 978, 1304.
μὲν ... δέ : though he cannot become..., yet, etc. : cp. v. 825 n.
δέξομαι, sc. αὐτόν, I will bow to his will.
κρυπτοῖσιν κ.τ.λ., rail in dark and riddling speech.

ἤτοι φιλοῦσά γε. The particles mark this alternative as the more probable of the two. The καί marks the other sug- gestion as just possible. Paley cp. Rhes. 817 ἤτοι μαραγνά γ' ή καρανιστὴς μόρος | μένει σε δρῶντα τοιάδ', ἢ τὸν ῎Εκτορα | τὸ μηδὲν εἶναι καὶ κακὸν νομίζετε.

προσήκει δ' οὐδέν : She is naught to me. The Sé is for γάρ : see on v. 179. The MSS. give προσήκει τ' οἶδας, for which the text is offered as a correction involving the least possible change. προσήκον and προσήκοντ' have been proposed. —ἀλλά, Nay.

πρόχουσιν is given by the Mss. both here and in Ar. Nub. 272 for the more regular πρόχοισιν. -ἀπορραντήρια, basins of sprinkling; i.e. basins placed outside the temple, containing holy water for sprinkling in lustration on wor- shippers or objects belonging to the temple worship. The water has been brought from Kastalia (vv. 94-7).
νουθετητέος, I must admonish. The freedom of this remark is scarcely in keeping with previous indications of Ion's attitude towards the god; but it is really Euripides who speaks.

τί πάσχει, (asking him) what ails him. Cp. v. 1385. τί παθὼν ἐποίησας; means, what ailed you, had happened to you, that you did it?' τί μαθὼν ἐποίησας; what suggested your doing it? Both expressions are common.
γάρ refers to εἰ preceding. But if, (I say if) for it will not happen, but I will put the case,' etc.

τίνοντες. τίνω (active) = (1) to pay, with acc. of thing paid and gen. of thing paid for; (2) to pay for, with acc. of object; cp. French payer le dîner. The middle voice = (1) to make to pay with the following constructions, τίνομαι σὲ φόνου, τίνομαι σὲ δίκην, τίνομαι σὲ δίκῃ : (2) to revenge, e.g. τίνομαι φόνον.
Connect κακοὺς ... εἰ ... μιμούμεθα, wicked for imitat- ing.
τὰ ... καλά : what the gods think good.

First στάσιμον. -Come, O Athena; thou whose name is Victory, leave Olympos and thy golden bower, and come to Pytho. Come, thou and Artemis, each a maiden goddess, each Phoibos' sister. - Pray, girls, for the blessing of offspring for the house of Erechtheus. A lasting fund of happiness is theirs whose home is made bright by the young; for children are a stay in trouble and a joy in prosperous days. They are better than wealth or the palace of the king. O haunt of Pan and Rock hard-by, where Aglauros' daughters tread the green sward in the dance before the temples of Pallas, while thou, Pan, makest music for them in thy cave below;-thy cave where a hapless maid bare a babe to Phoibos, and then left it to be the food of birds and beasts! Never, never did I hear that the child of a god and a mortal had good hap.

ὠδίν. λοχ. ἀνειλείθυιαν : born without help of Eilei- thuia in pangs of childbirth. λοχιᾶν is gen. pl. fem. of adj. λόχιος. ὠδίνων is gen. of separation, depending on a privative in ἀνειλείθυιαν. Eileithuia was supposed to assist in childbirth. She is sometimes identified with Artemis.
λοχευθεῖσαν, brought to birth. According to some accounts it was Hephaistos who cleft the head of Zeus. - Τιτάνι: Prometheus was son of the Titan Iapetos.

Νίκα πταμένα. Cp. v. 1529: Soph. Phil. 134 Νίκη τ' ᾿Αθάνα Πολιὰς, ἢ σῴζει μ' ἀεί. Athene was often worshipped as a winged Victory, and as a Wingless Victory (Niké Apteros) had a temple on the Acropolis, just at the top of the Propylaea. This temple was adorned with winged Victories, of some of which there are casts in the British Museum. The most exquisite is that of one who stoops to tie her sandal. Euripides may have seen these sculptures before the production of the Ion (circ. B.с. 425); but some authorities place them at the close of the century. -Both P and C give μάκαιρα : ποτνα is a correction in C.
yâs: the gen. depends on the μέσος in μεσόμφαλος.
χορευομένῳ, around which they dance and sing; for the word implies both acts. For the passive cp. Soph. O.T. 1094 χορεύεσθαι πρὸς ἡμῶν, ‘be celebrated in dance and song (Jebb), and see v. 1079.

μαντεύματα κραίνει : makes oracles come true, i.e. gives oracles that do not fail; a brachylogy for δίδωσι μαντεύματα & κραίνεται. So Od. 19. 567 (of the dreams that come through the gates of horn) οἵ ῥ᾽ ἔτυμα κραίνουσι, they give real visions that come true. See on v. 168.
καθαροῖς, clear, not ambiguous: cp. Isocr. 834 λέξις καθαρῶς καὶ ἀκριβῶς ἔχουσα.

ἔχει...: a lasting fund of happiness have they for whom etc. ἔχει means involves, carries with it, and the word should have had for its subject τὸ λάμπειν ἥβας, but this is changed by a common idiom into the personal form ois ἂν λάμπωσι κ.τ.λ. Cp. Thuc. 2. 44 τὸ δ᾽ εὐτυχές, ὃς ἄν..., good fortune is when a man etc. : H.F. 162 ἀνδρὸς δ᾽ ἔλεγχος οὐχὶ τόξ᾽ εὐψυχίας | ἀλλ' ὃς μένων βλέπει τε... bows and arrows are no proof of courage; but if a man stands his ground etc. - ἀκινητὸν ἀφορμάν. A common meaning of ἀφορμή is re- sources, funds, what one has to start from; and κινεῖν was used technically = to disturb invested moneys.

καρποτρόφοι νεανίδες ήβαι : young and vigorous lives with hope of fruitfulness, i.e. giving hope that when grown up they too will have children, the ἑτέροις τέκνοις of v. 480. 478 ff. διαδέκτορα κ.τ.λ. : since they give promise (ὡς) of enjoying the inherited wealth (that comes) from their fathers, with other children to succeed them. διαδέκτορα must be active, receiving successive owners. —ἕξοντες agrees κατὰ σύνεσιν with ἦβαι. -ἐπί, cp. v. 228 ἐπὶ δ᾽ ἀσφάκτοις μήλοισι.
σωτήριον ἀκμάν: saving force. ἀκμάν is Dr. Verrall’s correction of MSS. ἀλκάν, which is certainly intolerable after ἀλκά three lines above.

The nurture of children that are one's own.' τροφαὶ κήδειοι = τροφαὶ τῶν ἐν κήδει, i.e. nurture by real parents, not adoptive ones. The meaning careful lacks both authority and probability. 492 ff. ὦ Πανός κ.τ.λ. Ο haunt of Pan and neighbouring rock by the caverns of the Long Cliffs, where the feet of the maiden triad, Aglauros' daughters, tread in the dance the green levels before the shrines of Pallas to the ever-changing sound of the music of the pipes, when thou, Pan, pipest on the reed in thy grot.' This picture of the daughters of Aglauros returning after death and dancing through the summer night on the top of the Acropolis, while Pan pipes to them from his cave below, is an exquisite invention which we may believe to be all the poet's own. It is a scene of idyllic loveliness unsurpassed even in the lyrics of Euripides, and one that will for the imaginative reader lend some of the colour of its romance even to the severer associations of the spot. The story of the shade of Protesilaos coming from Hades to take part in the Thracian foot-races has been com- pared. See for the topography Introd. § 4, and cf. vv. 936 ff. - πέτρα is the Acropolis. -χόρους is cognate acc., and στάδια direct object of χόρους στείβουσι taken together: cp. Med. 205 λιγυρὰ δ' ἄχεα...βοᾷ τὸν...προδόταν, Aesch. Theb. 289 ζωπυροῦσι τάρβος τὸν ἀμφιτειχῆ λεών, Soph. Εl. 123 τίν' ἀεὶ τάκεις οἰμωγὰν... ᾿Αγαμέμνονα. This seems better than, as Paley, to take χόρους = dancing-rings (a meaning not found in the tragedians) and στάδια in apposition to it. -κόραι, see on v. 10, and for other legends of the sisters Smith's Dict. Myth.

v. Agraulos. ᾿Αγλ. κορ. τρίγονοι=lit. 'three daughters of G Aglauros, born to him. Each part of the compound adj. is equivalent to an independent epithet: cp. Phoen. 174 γῆς φιλαίματοι ῥοαί, streams of blood that the earth loves: Ι. Α. 7 ἑπτάποροι πλειάδες, the seven moving Pleiads: Aesch. Theb. 266 ἑπτατειχεῖς ἐξόδους, the seven portals of the wall : Soph. O.C. 717 τῶν ἑκατομπόδων Νηρῄδων, the hundred dancing nereids. A collection of examples will be found in Prof. Jebb's note on Soph. 0. T. 846. I should add καλλίτοξος from Phoen. 1169 τῇ καλλιτόξῳ μητρί. —ναῶν, the Parthenon and Erechtheum (see on v. 10).

ὑπό, to the accompaniment of, properly of music, but the use was widely extended: cp. v. 1474, Hipp. 1299 ὑπ᾽ εὐκλείας θανεῖν, and a comic instance Ar. Ach. 970 εἴσειμ' ὑπαὶ πτερύγων κιχλῶν καὶ κοψίχων. For the uses of αἰόλος, which are instructive, see Lexicon.

αὐλίοις : on the pipes. Dr. Verrall is no doubt right in taking the word to be from αὐλίον, a diminutive of αὐλός. Previous editors have taken αὐλίοις as an epithet of ἄντροις, but it is impossible to assign any suitable sense to αὔλιον ἄντρον. ·ἄντρον Even if αὔλιος could mean (1) echoing to the pipe (Hermann), it is difficult to believe Euripides would have used the word here; while (2) rustic (so Lexicon) is a doubtful extension of the only natural sense of the word (belonging to the cattle- yard or fold), besides being highly inappropriate to a cave under the Acropolis. Moreover, as Dr. Verrall observes, the position of the adjective would be incorrect. So placed, it would not be an epithet at all, but a predicate.
πικρῶν γάμων ὕβριν : the shameful fruit of a cruel union. ὕβριν is used exactly like ἀδίκημα in v. 325.

οὔτ ἐπί κ.τ.λ. : neither at the loom (have I seen), nor in stories have I heard tell. The κερκίς (radius) was a long reed used (1) as a shuttle, (2) like the modern batten, to close up the threads of the woof or weft (κρόκη). Rich (Dict. Ant. s.v. radius) says it is like a large netting needle, rather longer than the breadth of the web.'

θεόθεν τέκνα θνατοῖς : children born of gods to mortals. For the absence of a participle cp. Plato Rep. 607 A ὕμνους θεοῖς καὶ ἐγκώμια τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς, Phoen. 17 ὦ Θηβαῖσιν εὐίπποις ἄναξ, Οr. 363 ὁ ναυτίλοισι μάντις.

Second ἐπεισόδιον. -Xouthos has been told by Apollo that the first person he meets on going out of the temple will be his son. He comes forth, and meeting Ion hails him as his son and seeks to embrace him. Ion in amaze- ment resists. Explanations follow, and at last Ion is con- vinced that Xouthos is actually his father. Xouthos then proposes that Ion shall accompany him to Athens. To this the youth is at first averse, but in the end consents. After enjoining secrecy on the Chorus as to what he believes to be the truth regarding Ion's birth, Xouthos departs to offer a thank-offering on Parnassos. Ion goes to give a farewell banquet to his Delphian friends. The two have agreed to give out that Ion is no more than Xouthos' adoptive son. Kreousa is to be informed of the truth later at Athens, when a convenient opportunity offers.
ὄντος, sc. τινός.
ἡ γὰρ ἀρχή: for that beginning.
δύ' ὄντε, both of us. The addition of the participle is common with numerals. Badham cp. Plato Gorg. 481 ἐρῶντε δύ᾽ ὄντε δυοῖν ἑκάτερος.

εὐ φρονεῖς μέν. When μέν is thus appended to a ques- tion, an alternative is either expressed or understood. The speaker uses the word to give a slight emphasis to the alter- native he wishes to believe. Cp. Alc. 146 ἐλπὶς μὲν οὐκέτ᾽ ἐστι σῴζεσθαι βίον; Ηipp. 316 ἁγνὰς μὲν, ὦ παῖ, χεῖρας αἵματος φέρεις; Med. 676, 1129 φρονεῖς μὲν ὀρθὰ κοὐ μαίνει, γύναι;

τὰ φίλταθ'. The neuter form gives the force of what is to all men 'nearest and dearest. So in Aesch. Eum. 100 (Klytaemnestra speaks) παθοῦσα δ᾽ οὕτω δεινὰ πρὸς τῶν φιλτάτων, treated thus by my nearest and dearest.-Jacobs' οὐ φρονῶ with interrogation is tempting, but the text is natural Greek. σωφρονεῖν in its most general sense is to behave without extra- vagance.
οὐ ῥυσιάζω. I am no robber. ῥύσιον (ρυ- = draw)= (1) booty seized as reprisals, (2) a thing seized as security, a pledge.
ὡς τί; sc. ποιήσων, = wherefore ?- γνωρίσας : note the force of the aorist, at a moment when thou makest acquaint- ance with.' Cp. Plato, Lach. 181 C σύνισθί τε καὶ γνώριζε καὶ ἡμᾶς καὶ τούσδε.
ἀμούσους ξένους, rude foreigners. -πίμπρη: in burial.
ποῦ is stronger than πῶς and marks greater incredulity.
καὶ τί; Again the formula marks incredulity, as in English.
μαρτυρεῖς σαυτῷ: cp. Eu. Ioann. 5. 31 ἐὰν ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ, ἡ μαρτυρία μου οὔκ ἐστιν ἀληθής.
τὸν συναντήσαντα : cp. vv. 661-3.
συμφορᾶς κ.τ.λ. must meet with what mishap? Ion is still incredulous, and speaks sarcastically.
δῶρον ἄλλως, just a gift: cp. Tro. 476 ἄριθμον ἄλλως, mere units, Soph. Phil. 947 εἴδωλον ἄλλως.
δώρον, because restored to him (as he thinks) by Phoibos.
γῆς ἄρα κ.τ.λ.: i.e. I am a terrae filius, a nobody. Neither Ion nor Xouthos in his reply is speaking seriously. Paley quotes the epic expression for autochthony, ἀπὸ δρυὸς καὶ πέτρης.
νόθον λέκτρον, unlawful union. - τοῦ νέου, from τὸ νέον = νεότης.
οὐ ... πω: see on v. 1278.
ἐλθών, following pl. verb ἀφικόμεσθα : cp. v. 1251. Ion finishes his sentence regardless of the interruption.
φανάς, lit. torches, i.e. torch-light processions and ceremonies. Cp. οἱ Χόες, οἱ Χύτροι, names of the second and third days of the Anthesteria.
ἔν του: cp. ἐν "Αιδου. -κατέσχες, lodge; properly put (a ship) to shore. For the πρόξενοι see Introd. § 3.
ἐθιάσευσε: θιασεύειν is to introduce to a company (θίασος).

τοῦτ᾽ ἐκεῖνο : 'that's it,' meaning that is the occasion we have been seeking. For the phrase, which is common, cp. Med. 98, Hel. 622. —ἵν᾽ ἐσπάρημεν : Ion begins as though he were going to finish the sentence as Xouthos does for him; where I was born there I am found. Supply σε with ἐξηῦρεν.
For the use of δοῦλος as an adj. Paley cites such ex- pressions as τύραννα σκῆπτρα, τύραννον δῶμα, and vv. 675, 819 infra.
& is in effect adverbial, = as.
Mark the εἰρωνεία. Both Xouthos and Apollo were Διὸς παῖδες.
ἡμέρα : supply χαιρέτω. Xouthos gives another turn to the sentence.
πότ' ἆρα; when, I wonder? âpa emphasises the question: cp. Ar. Vesp. 893 τίς ἀρ᾽ ὁ φεύγων οὗτος; who, I should like to know, is the defendant here?
κοιναὶ μέν κ.τ.λ. : the happiness of the (royal) house is ours too.
ὀρθῶς ἔκρανε: gave true oracle; see on v. 464.

ήξας, intransitive, wast eager: cp. Plato Legg. 709 A ταῦτα δὴ πάντα προϊδών τις ἀίξειεν ἂν εἰπεῖν, would hasten to say.-Both & and τοῦτο are adverbial accusatives defining the extent of the verbal action.
χρόνῳ δόντες : trusting to time, lit. yielding. The verb is intransitive; cp. Phoen. 21 ὁ δ᾽ ἡδονῇ δούς. ἐνδιδόναι is common in this sense.

ἀλητείαν, vagabond life. The word must not be pressed beyond the general suggestion of homelessness: Ion was a waif and stray. In the Classical Review, vol. 2, p. 225, Prof. Ridgeway proposes an ingenious emendation; but he forgets that Ion is called ὁ Φοίβειος ἀλάτας in v. 1089. Ср. also Hel. 934 τὴν ἐνθάδ' ἐκλιποῦσ᾽ ἀλητείαν πικράν. Reiske made the same suggestion (δάπεδα λητείαν).

οὐδὲ θάτερον κ.τ.λ. Nor, though thou labourest under one of two misfortunes, shalt thou have the names of "base- born" and "beggar" both; nay thou shalt be called both noble and rich. It is the clumsy attempt of a somewhat coarse nature to encourage one whose finer feelings he altogether fails to appreciate. Xouthos admits that Ion must bear the stigma of ignoble birth, but urges as a consolation wealth, the posses- sion of which, he adds, will cause even Ion's humble birth to be lost sight of. -For νοσῶν cp. v. 364.
κεκλήσει, have the name of. Cp. v. 75 n.: Aesch. Theb. 698 κακὸς οὐ κεκλήσει.

πολυκτήμων βίου : possessed of much substance. The gen. depends on the sense of fulness contained in πολυκτήμων : cp. Soph. O. T'. 83 πολυστεφὴς δάφνης, where Prof. Jebb com- pares Soph. El. 895 περιστεφῆ ἀνθέων θήκην. For ẞlos in the sense of ample means of life, wealth, luxury, cp. Med. 194 βίου τερπνὰς ἀκοάς : Soph. Εl. 362 καὶ περιρρείτω βίος : ν. 326 βίοτον.
πάλιν emphasises the idea of change contained in μεταστάς.

ὧν δέ κ.τ.λ. : hear what is in my mind, my father. The Mss. have πέρι, in which Dobree first detected a corruption of πέρ, the usual abbreviation of πάτερ. Paley indeed defends πέρι, and translates, What I am entertaining an opinion upon; i.e. ἄκουσον ταῦτα περὶ ὧν γιγνώσκω. But γιγνώσκω γιγνώσκω could not be used absolutely in this way. We have always ταῦτα or οὕτω γιγνώσκω, or the like. Even the expressions αὐτὸς γνώσει (see thou to it), ἔγνων (I understand), are no justi- fication for such a use; in these cases the mind readily sup- plies an object to the verb. Besides, what Ion wishes to say is hear what I think on this matter, not hear what matters I hold opinions upon.

εἶναί φασι κ.τ.λ. There exists, as they tell us, famous Athens, sprung of the soil, no immigrant race. This way of taking the words seems necessitated by the emphatic position of εἶναι. It is a formal mode of introducing the place of which the speaker is going to say more. Cp. the opening of Thucy- dides narrative (1. 24) Ἐπίδαμνος ἔστι (not ἐστι, as edd.) πόλις, there is a city called Epidamnos: Soph. Trach. 273 ἀκτή τις ἔστ' Εὐβοιίς, ἔνθα κ.τ.λ.: ίδ. 752; Ant. 968 ἀκταὶ Βοσπόριαι [εἴσι] ἰδὲ ... Σαλμυδησσὸς ἵνα κ.τ.λ. : v. 294 supr.
ἐσπεσοῦμαι, shall intrude. -νόσω, infirmities.
ἀσθενὴς ὤν : if I remain obscure.
The line is so corrupt that it cannot be emended with any certainty.

πρῶτον ζυγόν : the high-raised thwart on which the κελευστής sat at the stern of the ship, steering and giving the time to the rowers. Cp. Aesch. Ag. 183 σέλμα σεμνὸν ἡμένων, ib. 1618 τῶν ἐπὶ ζυγῷ δορός. (Paley.)
τις: cp. Iuv. 1. 73 aude aliquid breuibus Gyaris et carcere dignum, si uis esse aliquis.
μισησόμεσθα: middle form used passively, as in v.
The practice is fairly common in the tragedians and is found even in prose writers; but the student should abstain from using any but those forms which are actually found.

The order is varied for χρηστοὶ σοφοί τε δυνάμενοι εἶναι (cp. Hor. C. 2. 19. 27 sed idem | pacis eras mediusque belli), those who might be able men and accomplished, i.e. who could, if they chose, fit themselves by proper training for a useful political life. χρηστός here has its proper sense of serviceable.
οὐ σπεύδ. κ.τ.λ., non rei publicae inseruiunt.
μωρίαν, 'the taunt of folly. Med. 218 δύσκλειαν ἐκτήσαντο καὶ ῥᾳθυμίαν. For the zeugma cp.
ψόγου. So Musgrave, with a decided improvement to the sense, for Mss. φόβου, which however might be defended.

λογίων. This cannot be genuine. It is metrically impossible, and down to Aristotle the word has no other meaning than full of stories, story-telling. Wecklein with great ingenuity proposes δοκούντων, men of repute. He thinks that this may have been replaced in the text by a very natural gloss ἐλλογίμων, which was itself corrected into λογίων. Verrall conj. λόγῳ, = "thought, learning, in the widest sense."

εἰς ... πλέον : "if I invade their occupied privilege, i.e. official administration, which is already full or filled up." So Dr. Verrall, taking πλέον as neut. of πλέως, though the recog- nized form is πλέων. -For φρουρ. ψήφ. see Appendix D, p. 168.
οὕτω, υίz. as follows.

The somewhat strange expression τὰς πόλεις ἔχουσι is made easier by the addition of ἀξιώματα, which explains it: those who have the cities and the dignities of them in their hands. Perhaps, however, we should read with Stobaeus oἱ τὰς πόλεις ἔχοντες ἀξίωμά τε. Relative clauses preceding the antecedent are rare in Greek, though common in Latin.

ἀπολαχοῦσα = χωρὶς λαχοῦσα, on the analogy of ἀποικέω, ἀπόμουσος, ἀφίσταμαι, finding her life dissevered from thine and isolated. - τύχην is object of ἀπολαχοῦσα, the object of οἴσει is not expressed.
The δé, if genuine, marks the apodosis.
τὰ σὰ φίλα: see on v. 521.-πικρῶς: the word looks suspicious after its occurrence in v. 610.
συγχέας, make havoc of: cp. Med. 794 δόμον τε πάντα ξυγχέασ' Ιάσονος.

Two undoubtedly spurious lines with nothing to recommend them even if we improve the scanning and the sense by inserting te after φαρμάκων. But their author thought the a in θανασίμων was long, and placed διαφθοράς in apposition to σφαγάς, not reflecting that σφαγή is inapplicable to a death by poison. Cp. the spurious lines Phoen. 1235 σπαρτῶν τε νεκρῶν ἑᾶλις ὃς κεῖται νεκρός, Hel. 905 ἐατέος δ᾽ ὁ πλοῦτος "αδικός τις ὤν, Aesch. Theb. 805 ἄνδρες τεθνᾶσιν ἐκ χειρῶν αὐτομάτων.
ἄλλως τε, And besides: see Lex.
ἀπαιδίᾳ. So the edd. for Mss. ἀπαιδίαν.
παραβλ. βίαν: looking askance for violence, in fear of an attack on his life.
Aristotle (Pol. 5. 11. 12) says that τυραννίς iς πονηρό- φιλόν τι.

μισεῖ. The subject is ὁ τύραννος. A succession of relative clauses having the same antecedent was distasteful to the Greek ear, and such an anacoluthon as we have here almost invariably replaces the normal construction. Ср. Thuc. 1. 74 ὅπερ σαφέστατα ἔσωσε τὰ πράγματα, καὶ αὐτοὶ διὰ τοῦτο δὴ μάλιστα ἐτιμήσατε κ.τ.λ. (for καὶ δι' ὅ): id. 4. 67 ἐν ὀρύγματι ἐκαθέζοντο, ὅθεν ἐπλίνθευον τὰ τείχη καὶ ἀπεῖχεν οὐ πολύ.
Grandeur (όλβος) is not worth preserving at the cost of detraction (ψόγοι) and anxiety (πόνοι).
Very probably spurious. The text is that of both mss. The author seems to have scanned μέτρια. See on v. 616.
ὄχλον μέτριον the populace friendly.

ἢ (Att. for ἦν), I was engaged in. For εἶναι ἐν cp. Hdt. 2. 82 οἱ ἐν ποιήσει γενόμενοι, Soph. Ο. Τ. 562 τότ' οὖν ὁ μάντις οὗτος ἦν ἐν τῇ τέχνῃ; Ηipp. 452 αὐτοί τ᾽ εἰσὶν ἐν μούσαις ἀεί. ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ εἶναι is common in Plato. So Hor. S. 1. 9. 2 totus in illis.
A cheerful demeanour was enjoined on all visitors to the temple: cp. vv. 245-6.
τοὺς μὲν ... οἱ δέ: while I was speeding some, other visitors would come.

καιν. ὤν καινοῖσιν : a fresh face meeting fresh faces. This doubling of the adj. is common and should be imitated : cp. v. 652, 713 : fr. inc. ἑκὼν ἑκοῦσαν ἢ θέλουσαν οὐχ ἑκών ; It is more rare in Latin: cp. Verg. Aen. 4. 83 illum absens absentem auditque uidetque.

ὁ δ᾽ εὐκτὸν κ.τ.λ.: what men pray for, though it be against their will. (For the position of the relative clause see on 342.) Cp. S.
