Paul ad Rom. 7. 19 οὐ γὰρ ὁ θέλω ποιῶ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλὰ ὃ οὐ θέλω κακόν, τοῦτο πράσσω, and Plaut. Trin. 304-312 (the scene between Philto and Lysiteles) where animus, inclinations, = φύσις here.

νόμος, φύσις. His own inclinations prompt him to behave with the integrity (δίκαιον εἶναι) which others show only under constraint of the law with its threat of punish- ment. Greek and Roman philosophy awarded the highest praise to instinctive or natural virtue, as opposed to that acquired by self-discipline. Aristotle divides men into four classes: (1) ὁ σώφρων, the moral man, who feels little or no impulse to do evil; (2) ὁ ἐγκρατής, the man who is master of himself: he has a struggle, but generally wins; (3) ὁ ἀκρατής, who has a struggle and generally loses; (4) ὁ ἀσελγής, the profligate, who does wrong with no impulse to do right.- δίκαιον εἶναι ... παρεῖχε is awkward. It was necessary to insert εἶναι in order to explain 8 dé, but the sentence is com- pleted with παρείχε as though the infinitive were not there.

ἐμαυτῷ. Let me live to myself: i.e. free from the cares of a state, in the peaceful retirement of his Delphian home. The expression is natural and easily intelligible, and characteristic of Ion's simple nature. There is no need to read δέ μ' αὐτοῦ with Badham.
μεγάλοισι κ.τ.λ.: to exult in greatness and to be content with little. In the latter case the pleasure is less vivid but not less real.
οὕς, i.e. Kreousa.
εὐτυχεῖν δ' ἐπίστασο : learn to bear thy happiness. Cp. Hor. C. 3. 27. 34 mitte singultus; bene ferre magnam disce fortunam; tua sectus orbis nomina ducet.
ἄρξασθαι simply means 'to make a beginning, but is doubtless used with a recollection of the compounds ἐνάρχομαι and κατάρχομαι in the sense of to begin a sacrifice, as v. 653 shows.
γενέθλια, sc. ἱερά. Sacrifices were offered on the day of the child's birth and also on the fifth day after, at a festival called ἀμφιδρόμια, when the child was carried round the hearth and named.

δή, as I will pretend. So δῆθεν two lines below.- ξένον... ἐφέστιον: to my home as a friend. ξένον is an oblique predicate. Xouthos will pretend that he has found an old friend in Ion, and that as the latter is about to accompany him to Athens, he (Xouthos) is defraying the cost of a farewell banquet to the young man's friends.

τῆς δ' Αθ. χθονός. These words are emphatic, and point a contrast. Xouthos suddenly changes the scene in his mind from Delphi to Athens. When he takes Ion to Athens it will be as one who has merely come to see the country.
πρέπον, sc. ὄνομα.
πρόσειπε, say farewell. The word is common in this sense. See esp. Alc. 195, 610. ---ἐκλιπεῖν. The pres. and fut. are the regular tenses with μέλλω : the aor. is rare.
θάνατον, object of λέγω repeated in sense of threaten. -εἰπούσαισι, participial form of ἐὰν εἴπητε.
ἀβίωτον : cp. Soph. Ant. 566 τί γὰρ μόνῃ μοι τῆσδ᾽ ἄτερ βιώσιμον ;
Note the εἰρωνεία.

καθαράν, of pure blood. The Athenians were pecu- liarly proud of the purity of their descent, and believed themselves to be indigenous. In token of this, almost up to Thucydides' time they used to wear golden grasshoppers in their hair. Cp. Thuc. 1. 6 οὐ πολὺς χρόνος ἐπειδὴ χιτῶνάς τε λινοῦς ἐπαύσαντο φοροῦντες καὶ χρυσῶν τεττίγων ἐνέρσει κρωβύλον ἀναδούμενοι τῶν ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ τριχῶν. See Introd. § 1 and v. 29 n.
τοῖς λόγοισιν, a variation of the commoner λόγῳ. Paley aptly cites from a fragment of the Erechtheus λόγῳ πολίτης ἐστὶ, τοῖς δ᾽ ἔργοισιν οὔ.

πέπαμαι = κέκτημαι, from obsol. πάομαι. The word is rare and poetic: cp. Theocr. 15. 90 πασάμενος ἐπίτασσε (‘give orders when you've bought us') which looks like a proverb. The Lex. gives a warning against confusing ἐπᾶσάμην, πέπᾶμαι with ἐπᾶσάμην, πέπασμαι from πατέομαι, to eat.

Second στάσιμον. - ' Tears I foresee, and lamenta- tions when my lady learns her lord's good fortune and thinks how she is desolate. Who is this child, and who is his mother? I fear there is fraud about the oracle and this chance meeting; no good will come of it. There is deception about this alien boy. Friends, shall we tell our mistress all the truth? What a sad old age remains for her, while her lord is happy and cares naught.-Perish the alien under whom the ancient house declines! Perish the false husband, and may his offerings to Heaven miss their mark! But that my heart is loyal my dear mistress shall know. -Already they are feasting, father and new-found son. O peaks of Parnassos, where Bacchios leaps in the dance, never may the boy come to my city; may he die first! Are we straitened, that we need the foreigner's help? Nay, sufficient is our ancient king Erechtheus.'

ἀλαλαγάς: so Hermann for ἄλλας γε of Mss. The cry is ἀλαλαί, which expresses either anguish, as here, or triumph: cp. Ar. Av. 1763 ἀλαλαί, ἰὴ παιήων ἰή, | τήνελλα καλλίνικος. Tears I foresee and sharp cries of sorrow and lamentations invading the home.'
ᾖ, i.e. learns that she is. For the brachylogy see on ν. 383.
πρόμαντι. Apollo delivers the oracles, but Zeus is the author of them: cp. Aesch. Εum. 19 Διὸς προφήτης δ᾽ ἐστὶ Λοξίας πατρός. The title was also specially applied to the Delphian Priestess.
The suspicion of the Chorus springs from the mystery attaching to the boy's mother.

σαίνει κ.τ.λ. The oracle mislikes me, and I fear etc. On Soph. Ant. 1214, παιδός με σαίνει φθόγγος (greets my ear), Prof. Jebb has the following note. As σαίνω was properly said of a dog wagging its tail or fawning, so it could be said of a sight or sound, which appeals for recognition by vividly striking our senses. [Cp. Rhes. 55 σαίνει μ' ἔννυχος φρυκτωρία.] Like arridere, the word usually implied a sensation of plea- sure (O. C. 319 n.). But it could also denote, as here, a recognition attended by pain. So in Eur. Hippol. 862 f., where Theseus recognizes the seal on the tablets left by his dead wife, he says τύποι προσσαίνουσί με.' -μή depends on the idea of fearing suggested by οὐ σαίνει.
συμφοράν in neutral sense, as often: this hap.

So P and C unintelligibly, and emendation is plainly impossible. The line is, however, probably the wreck of a gloss or glosses, which has crept into the text. The sense of the previous verse is complete without it, and there is no corresponding line in the antistrophe. See on v. 708.
ἔχει δόλον κ.τ.λ. 'There is trickery as well as chance about the boy. The suspicion expressed in v. 686 μή τιν᾿ ἔχῃ δόλον has grown into conviction.
ξυνοίσεται κ.τ.λ. Who will not agree in this? - τάδε adverbial.
δεσποίνᾳ. The middle syllable is sung short. So the α in τλάμον, υ. 698.

τάδε τορῶς κ.τ.λ.: speak out these things clearly in her ear about her husband. See on v. 911. In v. 1521 secrecy is the object. -ποσιν is the obj. of τάδε γεγων. taken together: cp. Med. 205 λιγυρὰ δ᾽ ἄχεα ... βοᾷ τὸν προδόταν, Soph. El. 123 τίν᾿ ἀεὶ τάκεις οἰμωγὰν ... ᾿Αγαμέμνονα;

ἐν ᾧ κ.τ.λ.: who being all in all to her. τὰ πάντα (her whole life) differs from πάντα in expressing that the units. are summed up. - ἐν ᾧ : lit., depending upon whom, a common use: cp. Alc. 278 ἐν σοὶ δ᾽ ἐσμὲν καὶ ζῆν καὶ μή.

ἔρρει συμφοραῖς, is whelmed in misery. In Attic the word has the force of a perfect: cp. Soph. Ο. Τ. 560 ἄφαντος ἔρρει, Ο. Ο. 1775 ὃς νέον ἔρρει (of Oedipus, “who hath just passed away').-ὁ δ᾽ εὐτυχεῖ is parenthetic. -εἰσπεσοῦσα. There is no difficulty in the aorist, any more than in ἔρρει; the Chorus speak of Kreousa's future as a fait accompli.
ἀτίετος φίλων, sc. ἐστί: neglects those [who should be] dear to him, i.e. Kreousa.
οὐκ ἔσωσεν τύχας: has not preserved its fortunes (i.e. those of the house).
μὴ τύχοι : may he fail of his prayer. This absolute use is common : so ἀποτυγχάνω = to fail.
καλλίφλογα, because the cakes were sprinkled with salt.

In the Mss. this line reads τυραννίδος φίλα, which is apparently corrupt, besides showing a deficiency of one foot. It seemed better that the young student should have some- thing that at least makes sense, and I have therefore printed an emendation which, though purely conjectural, may perhaps be thought to account for the corruption. Transl.: But that mine is a loyal heart, my beloved Queen shall know. Or perhaps Xouthos was subject of εἴσεται, and we should read something like τυραννίδος φίλας φίλον. For τὸ δ' ἐμόν see on υ. 247. If v. 691 is not spurious, a whole line has also been lost here; but see note there.

ἤδη πέλας κ.τ.λ. Already the new son and father are come to their new feast. There is no need to change νέων τo νέου : the extension of the epithet to the banquet uet is in Greek natural and idiomatic. Cp. v. 641 n., and for a simple transference Soph. Ant. 239 ἔργων ἀκόντων ἀΐοντες αὐδάν (it was Oedipus who was unwilling).

ἰὼ δειράδες κ.τ.λ. Ο rocky wall that upholdest the cliffs and skyey uplands of Parnassos, where Bacchios' etc. Immediately above Delphi the lower buttresses of Parnassos rise in an almost perpendicular wall of rock. These cliffs, which face mostly southwards and flash brightly against the midday and afternoon sun, were called Phaedriades (Φαιδριάδες, the Shining Rocks). About midway along their length they rise into the two peaks so often mentioned by the poets. (See on v. 1222.) Their height is some 2000 ft. above the sea. In a deep chasm between the peaks (the bed of a torrent which is dry in the summer) the Kastalia springs out of the rock. Beyond these cliffs stretch the highlands or uplands of Par- nassos (the δικόρυφον πλάκα of Bacch. 307), a very extensive tract of irregular hilly country culminating in the true summit of the mountain, Lykoreia (Λυκώρεια), which is over 8000 feet in height and invisible from Delphi. δειράδες would properly denote the ridge or sky-line of the Phaedriades, but is here extended to include the whole of the mass which but- tresses up (ἔχουσαι) the rocky heights (σκόπελον, i.e. look-out place) that crown the cliffs, and the uplands beyond (οὐράνιον ἕδραν). The Korykian cave was situated in this district, about 7 miles N.E. of Delphi. -ἵνα Βάκχιος. The reference is to imaginary revels supposed to be held by Bacchus and his followers on the uplands: cp. v. 1125, Soph. Ant. 1126 σὲ δ᾽ ὑπὲρ διλόφου πέτρας στέροψ ὄπωπε | λιγνύς, ἔνθα Κωρύκιαι | στείχουσι Νύμφαι Βακχίδες, | Κασταλίας τε νᾶμα. Every other year there was actually a torch-light festival held there by women. The festival was called (in accordance with the ancient mode of reckoning) τριετηρίς, trieteris, trieterica: cp. Lucan 5. 73 (quoted by Prof. Jebb on Soph. Ant. 1.c.), Mons Phoebo Bromioque sacer, cui numine misto | Delphica Thebanae referunt trieterica Bacchae.
ἀμφίπυρος, with both ends flaming: but cp. Soph. Τr. 213 ᾿Αρτεμιν ἀμφίπυρον, i.e. with a torch in each hand.
νέαν ἁμεραν, his young life: cp. Med. 648 ἁμέραν τάνδ' ἐξανύσασα, ending this life.

στενομένα... εἰσβολάν. Badham believes that we have lost a line following this and containing a verb governing εἰσβολάν. If the line is sound and the sentence complete as it stands, we can only translate, - for the city, if in distress, might have excuse for importations of foreigners (as in the case of Xouthos). εἰσβολάν is thus an acc. defining the verbal action, as in Or. 286 ὅστις μ' ἐπάρας ἔργον ἀνοσιώτατον, Ar. Ach. 652 ὑμᾶς Λακεδαιμόνιοι τὴν εἰρήνην προκαλοῦνται, Thuc.
15 οἱ στρατηγοὶ σπονδὰς ἐποιήσαντο τὰ περὶ Πύλον. στενομένα may be taken=στένουσα (cp. Bacch. 1371 στένομαί σε, πάτερ) ; or, with Musgr., as = the epic στεινομένη, straitened.

The Mss. give the unintelligible and unmetrical ἁλίσας. Most editors agree that this is a corruption of ἅλις, ἅλις, which has been adopted with Matthiae's addition of ποτ' to complete the metre. Sufficient (for our defence) is our ancient chief the King Erechtheus i.e. we need no foreigners like Ion. But see Appendix D, p. 168.

Third ἐπεισόδιον. - Kreousa and an old servant of her father's house appear on the stage together, and Kreousa asks the Chorus whether her husband has received any answer from the oracle. The women tell all they know, and the old man, indignant at the fraud which he conceives to have been practised on his mistress, proposes to murder both Ion and Xouthos, declaring that he is ready to do the deed himself. Kreousa then delivers a long monody in which she recalls her meeting with Apollo and her child's birth and exposure. She then confesses the whole of her sad story to the old man, who suggests that she should revenge herself on the god's cruelty and indifference by setting fire to the temple. Kreousa shrinks from this, but it is finally agreed that the old man shall attend the banquet which Ion is giving to his friends, and murder him with a poisoned cup.
If the text is sound, we must connect ἡνικα κ.τ.λ. with παιδαγωγέ, and translate, tutor, while he lived, of my now dead father. But v. 726 has been suspected.
εἰς, as to: cp. Thuc. 2. 49 ἐκεῖνο (τὸ ἔτος) ἄνοσον ἐς τὰς ἄλλας ἀσθενείας ἐτύγχανεν ὄν : Soph. Ο.Τ. 980 σὺ δ᾽ ἐς τὰ μητρὸς μὴ φοβοῦ νυμφεύματα.
ὅμως belongs to ἀντικηδεύω, but (as often) has found its place in the protasis: cp. Hel. 728 ἐγὼ μὲν εἴην, κεἰ πέφυχ᾽ ὅμως λάτρις, ἐν τοῖσι γενναίοισιν ἠριθμημένος.

φυλάσσεις, holdest fast: cp. Soph. O.C. 1212 σκαιοσύναν φυλάσσων, holding fast to folly. οὐ καταισχυνασ' ἔχεις : lit. art not (in a state of) having disgraced, a common periphrasis for the perfect tense.

τοὺς σοὺς κ.τ.λ. : thine ancestors, descendants of the earth itself. Nearly all editors think the line corrupt. Of the few who defend the text Barnes thinks the sense is τοὺς πάλαι ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς χθονὸς γεγεννημένους. So Seidler. This of course the Greek will not stand, and σούς is not accounted for. Heath supplies προγόνους, but a word cannot be sup- plied which is not virtually in the sentence already, without being supplied. The view taken above was suggested to me by Dr. Verrall. He urges that οἱ παλαιοί being a common expression=maiores, the poet may well have coined from it the phrase οἱ σοὶ παλαιοί=maiores tui. I confess this seems to me unimpeachable. It cannot be denied that Eur. might have invented such a phrase, and the Mss. are evidence of a certain value that he did. For αὐτόχθονας = αὐτῆς τῆς χθονός cp. v. 200 Δίῳ παιδί, η. Of corrections of the text Bothe's τοῦ σοῦ παλαιοὺς ἐκ γένους has alone met with general acceptance, being adopted by Herm., Dind., Badham; but the objections to it are serious and manifest. τοὺς ἐκ παλαιοῦ σου γονεῖς αὐτόχθονας is perhaps more likely. If this became τοὺς ἐκ παλαιοῦ (or παλαιοὺς) ἐκ γονεῖς, the supposed corruption of our texts would easily follow: cp. the next line but one, where the Mss. give αἰπεινὰ δὲ μοι...δέ μοι. But the case for corruption has scarcely been made out.
τοι, as thou seest. - αἰπεινά, on a steep.

ξυνεκπονοῦσα κώλον : assist my toiling limbs, lit. jointly toiling at. Theocr. 16. 94 has veioὶ δ' ἐκπονέοιντο ποτὶ σπόρον of fallowland being worked; but it cannot be denied that in using such an exaggerated expression as ἐκπονεῖν κώλον (as indeed in the whole of this part of the scene) Euripides' eagerness for realism has caused him to descend considerably from the dignity of tragedy.
ἴχνος κ.τ.λ. : mark carefully where thou placest thy step.

βάκτρῳ κ.τ.λ. 'Press the path firmly with thy circling staff. Literally, the circled path, περιφερῆ being passive. (So Dr. Verrall.) The old man is to try the ground as he goes. Paley translates winding path, giving to περιφερής a meaning for which there appears to be no authority. Moreover this path itself is an improbability. The scene represents the steps and platform of the temple. See on vv. 46, 847.
ὅταν and ὅre are frequently used in a causal sense. Cp. Plaut. Trin. 505 quom adfinitate uostra me arbitramini | dignum, habeo ... gratiam. same latitude. We use when with almost the
μή παρῇς, sc. σεαυτόν : cp. Phoen. 21 ὁ δ᾽ ἡδονή δούς.
τοῦ δ' ἀπ. κ.τ.λ.: I am not master of what is not here.
δούλευμα, see on v. 113.
τίνα τυχ. παίδων : what fortune with regard to off- spring. Cp. Thuc. 8. 15 ἀγγελία τῆς Χίου ἀφικνεῖται, news about Chios: Xen. Comm. 3. 5. 10 τὴν τῶν θεῶν κρίσιν, judgment about the gods. So
εἰς δεσπότας κ.τ.λ. Cp. Π. 4. 16 ὅπως φιλότητα μετ' ἀμφοτέροισι βάλωμεν. βάλλειν εἰς θυμόν is a common expression.

νοσεῖ, is aught amiss with: cp. vv. 364-5. I venture to conjecture for Mss. νοσῶ. The intrusion of the servant's personality is out of place and the sentence, with νοσῶ, somewhat unnatural, apart from the absence of ἐγώ, which is needed to point the sense. The mistake apparently arose from an erroneous reference of τλάμον to the old man, instead of to Kreousa, to whom it is of course addressed. See next note.
εἶεν expresses impatience, Well! Cp. Ar. Nub. 176 εἶεν· τί οὖν πρὸς τἄλφιτ᾽ ἐπαλαμήσατο. The Chorus do not notice the questions put to them, but speak to one another till υ. 761.
τίς ἥδε μοῦσα : what strain is this?
ἔχεις γε, thou art possessed of.-εἰς, cp. v. 729 n.

A metrical correspondence between the lines begins here and is continued to v. 799. The lyric κόμματα or periods (which are almost entirely of dochmiac measure, suited to the agitation of the speakers) have been marked in the margin of the text after Schmidt. At intervals iambic trimeters are inserted in pairs of couplets: these are marked as ἐπεισόδια.
ἄχος ἄβιον, a sorrow I cannot live through.
ἔτυπεν. The strong aor. act. does not occur elsewhere in Attic: τυπείς however is found some half-dozen times.
ταὐτὰ πράσσων, faring like thee.
ἄκρον, crowning.
ἐκτελῆ, grown up. Hes. Op. 466 has ἐκτελέα βρίθειν Δημήτερος ἱερὸν ἀκτήν, of ripened corn. ἐντελής is commoner.
ἄρρητον. So Badham and Dindorf metri gratia. The MSS. give ἄφατον ἄφατον. Scan ἄρρή τον ἀναύδῆ τον.
ἐκπεραίνεται, carried out. Kreousa inquires as to the manner of the boy's delivery to his father.
ξυναντήσειεν, orat. obl. for ἂν ξυναντήσῃ, the words of the god.

τὸ δ' ἐμόν. The periphrasis implies more than the simple ἐγώ: see on v. 247. Here it is my side (party). -ἄτεκνον ἄτεκν. ἔλ. ἔλ. Aristophanes, Ran. 1352-55, very funnily parodies Euripides' practice of thus repeating words in his lyrics.
τίς... ἐχρήσθη; of whom, then, did the oracle speak?
πῶς δέ ποῦ: cp. v. 948. So τίς πόθεν ; frequently: cp. ν. 683-4.

ἀμπταίην. Cp. Hipp. 732 ἀλιβάτοις ὑπὸ κευθμῶσι γενοίμαν κ.τ.λ., where the Chorus wish they could fly away to the ends of the world and forget their troubles. So David, Ps. 55. 6 And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove, for then would I flee away and be at rest!'-ὑγρὸν —ὑγρὸν αἰθέρα, Milton's buxom air. Cp. Verg. Aen. 7. 65 liquidum trans H aethera uectae. Pindar finely says of an eagle ὑγρὸν νῶτον αἰωρεῖ, Pyth. 1. 17.

οἷον κ.τ.λ. to be taken with the preceding. I wish I might fly away (when I think) what pain etc. The latter clause gives the ground for the former. Cp. Ι. Τ. 147 σύγγονον ἀμὸν κατακλαιομένα, οἵαν ἰδόμαν ὄψιν ὀνείρων, Η. F. 816 ἆρ' εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν πίτυλον ἥκομεν φόβου, | γέροντες, οἷον φάσμ᾽ ὑπὲρ δόμων ὁρῶ. The following passages will repay examination: Hipp. 845, ib. 878, Soph. Ai. 945, Ar. Nub. 1157, Aesch. P. V. 908. It is better to explain the construction as elliptical than to say οἷος = διότι τοιοῦτος.
τἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ: all I have to tell.

παιδός depends on προ- in προθύσων : ‘to make, on the boy's behalf, sacrifices that seal friendship, and birthday offerings.' ξένια, because Xouthos was pretending that Ion was really a stranger to him, and his son only by adoption.

σκηνὰς ἐς ἱεράς, with φρούδος. Xouthos in fact climbs Parnassos (vv. 1125 sqq.) and sacrifices ὀπτήρια to Dionysos in thankfulness for having found, as he thinks, his own son, and does not return in time to offer the ξένια and γενέθλια in the festal tent. This Ion does for him, and proceeds with the banquet according to his father's instruc- tions (v. 1130). -τῆσδε with λαθραίως.
ἐξενωμένον, sent abroad: cp. Soph. Τr. 65 οὕτω δαρὸν ἐξενωμένου, having been abroad so long.

ἄφετος came to mean consecrated from being pri- marily used of sacred animals who were let go to wander at large over the sacred pastures. -λάθοι: the opt. is regular because παιδεύεται is hist. present.

θεὸς οὐκ ἐψεύσατο in saying he gave Xouthos a son, since he was really (as the old man thinks) giving Ion back to him. The deceiver is Xouthos, who pretends it is an original gift. -κάτα strictly goes with the second ἐψεύσατο, the inter- vening words being logically parenthetical. A clause thus inserted is usually marked by μέν : cp. v. 427, Thuc. 2. 40 ὁ τοῖς μὲν ἄλλοις, —ἀμαθία μὲν θράσος, λογισμὸς δὲ ὄκνον φέρει, whereas with most men,-while courage attends on ignor- ance, reflection makes them falter. The second clause is the important one. So Dem. de cor. § 160.

ἔπλεκεν κ.τ.λ. : ' was weaving a web of trickery like this:-if discovered he intended to lay the responsibility on the god (ἀνέφερεν, sc. τὴν αἰτίαν); but if he escaped detection, wishing als also (καί) (καί) to prevent the chances of time, he pur- Xouthos (he says) was prepared for either event. If detected in rearing the boy, he would still have introduced him into Kreousa's house, relying on Apollo's express com- mands. If on the other hand he should bring his son to Athens undetected, since the secret would always be liable to discovery (or he himself might die), he intended to parry these assaults of time (ἀμύνεσθαι τὸν χρόνον) by making the youth king at the first convenient moment. His position would then be secure against all accidents. - λαθών is a generally accepted correction of ἐλθών (Mss.). The latter word looks like a correction of θέλων erroneously written at the beginning as well as end of the line. See v. 737 n. ad fin. The passage has much perplexed the editors, and the pre- sent explanation is offered doubtfully. Paley takes χρόνον of Xouthos' possibly prolonged life; but under the circum- stances and as an alien, Ion's chance of the succession would be decidedly better during his father's lifetime than after. ψόγον and φθόνον have been proposed for χρόνον.

ἀνέφερεν. Not to be explained as put for ἀνέφερεν ἄv. There is no need of the particle; the imperfect has a meaning of its own in such apodoses, and it is to be noted that this supposed omission of av does not occur with the aorist. Cp. Lysias Or. 7, § 32 ταῦτα δὲ πράξας... ἐκέρδαινον μὲν οὐδέν, if I had done this, I was not likely to gain, was not by way of gaining: Plato, Symp. 190 ο αἱ τιμαὶ γὰρ αὐτοῖς... ἠφανίζετο, ‘for (if they had killed them) they were likely to lose their honours: Dem. contr. Onet. § 22 τοῦτον μὲν γὰρ τὸν τρόπον πράξας ὅλου τοῦ πράγματος ἀπηλλάττετο. (These passages are cited by Mr. Shuckburgh in his note on Lysias l.c. in support of the opposite view.) So in Latin Verg. Aen. 4. 604 quem metui moritura? 830 f. καινὸν δέ κ.τ.λ. And the name is a new one, in- vented as time went on,--Ion, to suit the pretence that he met him [accidentally] as he went. Note that strangely enough ἰόντι refers to Xouthos: cp. v. 662 ἐξιόντι μοι. The lines are no mere repetition of vv. 787-8, 802, as commonly supposed. The Chorus have said nothing to Kreousa about Ion's parentage, and their language to the old man implies a belief that the meeting of Xouthos and Ion, though designed by the god, was accidental so far as Xouthos was concerned, and that the name was suggested to him by this accident. The imagination of the old servant has throughout the scene travelled far beyond the brief statements of the Chorus, and he concludes his account of the matter by declaring that neither the meeting nor the name was accidental: Xouthos maturing his plans as time went on (ἀνὰ χρόνον) had pre- arranged both. It is remarkable that we are not told by what name Ion was known before meeting his father.
φαῦλον χρηστόν : simple, if only good. So

τῶνδ'... ἔσχατον: superlative for comparative, as often; worse than all these. Cp. Thuc. 1.1 ἐλπίσας μέγαν τε ἔσεσθαι καὶ ἀξιολογώτατον τῶν προγεγενημένων : Π. 2. 671 Νιρεύς, ὃς κάλλιστος ἀνὴρ ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἦλθεν τῶν ἄλλων Δαναών. Milton, who frequently affects classical constructions, Adam, the goodliest man of men since born, | His sons, the fairest of her daughters, Eve.

ἀναρίθμητον, a cipher, one who does not count: cp. Ει. 1054 οὐδ᾽ εἰς ἄριθμον...ἥκει, nullo est in numero. Though arrived at differently, the meaning is practically the same as that of ἄριθμος used of persons, = units, items, having no value individually, but only when taken in the gross. Hor. Epp. 1. 2. 27 nos numerus sumus et fruges consumere nati. So
ἄγειν would in prose be τὸ αγειν. The subject is αὐτόν (Xouthos) understood.
πιθών. The common and prose form of the aor. act. is ἔπεισα. -λέγων, alleging.
τῶν Αἰόλου, i.e. his own people.
δή, inferential: in consequence of this thou must, then etc.
ἢ γὰρ κ.τ.λ. : supply δεῖ.

σὺ φείσει : so Badham. Phas γ' ὑφήσεις, C has no y, but leaves a space. The stages of the corruption were pro- bably ΣΥΦΕΙΣΕΙ, ΣΥΦΗΣΕΙ, ΣΥΦΗΣΕΙΣ, ΥΦΗΣΕΙΣ. ει, η, and i were pronounced alike and are often confused in Mss. See on v. 743.
δυοῖν neuter.
τε...τε. It is according to Greek idiom to say I am ready for both of two alternatives; we say I am ready for either. Of course ... ἤ is often used, cp. v. 858.
οὐδεὶς detached note B. ὅστις ᾖ: 'no slave that's honest.' See

Monody by Kreousa. Kreousa was a heart-broken woman when she came to Delphi. Her girlhood had been embittered by shame, and her married life had been a dis- appointment. Two hopes made it possible to live. She thought she might some day find the babe she had lost, or if not that, that at least she might have another child. After her conversation with Ion the first hope was unwillingly abandoned, but only for the second to become doubly precious. While she smarted under Apollo's injustice about the past, she built all the more securely on the belief that he had in store for her some compensation; a belief that was strength- ened to conviction by the favourable answer which her husband brought from Trophonios. In a moment this last hope is rudely torn from her, and with insult. Not only is she to have no child herself, but the son of another woman and her faithless husband is to be intruded into her home. It is more than she can bear, and her patient but proud heart is stung to rebellion. Though it means tearing the veil from what she would fain hide, she will hold up her god-lover to scorn and contempt in the face of heaven and before his own temple. She will indeed cover herself with shame, but she feels with Dido, quae me ad maiora reseruo? The worst has been endured already. Kreousa's monody occurring just in the middle of the play, is important as being the hinge on which all the subsequent action turns; for it is the indignant disclosure of her wrongs which prompts the old servant to suggest his scheme for revenge. The passage is also perhaps the finest in the play. The pathos is true and noble, and is heightened by the felicity of the language. Although, with the exception of four lines, the metre is throughout anapaestic, the rhythm is continually varied in harmony with the subject matter, and with an effect that even an untrained ear will recognize as exquisitely musical. At vv. 894, 905-6, 908-9, the bitterness of the injured woman's feeling can find expression only in the wilder dochmiac measures. 'O my soul, how can I keep silence? Yet how unveil my vol ang rang shame? Nay, what matters shame to me? Is not my hus- band false? I am left without home, without children; and the hope I had that I might find my babe and yet keep my secret,-that is gone too! No; by the starry heavens, I will speak out and lift the load from my breast. My heart is broken; gods and men alike compass my ruin, and I will show them to be thankless traitors to those they loved. Hearken, god of the sweet lyre! Hearken, Son of Leto; before this sun I will utter my reproach to thee. Thou camest with the sun- light in thy golden hair, when I was gathering the yellow flowers in my lap, and didst seize me by the wrists and lead me off, heedless of my cries. And I bore thee a child, and I set my babe in the cave where thou hadst lain; and-oh, the pity!-now he is gone, the fowls of the air have devoured him,-my son and thine, cruel god; -while thou makest music on thy lyre, and art glad and gay!- What, ho! thou Son of Leto, that givest answer to men from the golden throne, I will shout a word in thine ear. Dost hearken? Thou'rt a base lover! For thou bringest home a son for my husband, though thou owest him naught; but my boy and thine, thou heart of stone, has been made meat for the birds. Thy Delos and the laurels and the palms and the garden of Zeus where thou wast born, they hate thee!'
ὦ ψυχά. So Orestes addresses his own heart, Or. 466, ὦ τάλαινα καρδία ψυχή τ᾽ ἐμή, and Medea, Med. 1056, μὴ δῆτα, θυμέ, μὴ σύ γ' ἐργάσῃ τάδε. σιγάσω : of course aor. subj.
σκοτ. εὐνάς, my secret union. The inadmissible hiatus ἀναφήνω εὐνάς seems to demand some correction : Barnes suggests ἀναφήνασ', omitting δ'.
αἰδοῦς δ᾽ ἀπολειφθῶ : and resign my claim to modesty. Cp. Med. 35 olἷον πατρώας μάπολείπεσθαι χθονός, not to have lost etc.

πρὸς τίνα κ.τ.λ. With whom am I to enter the lists προς of virtue, when my husband etc. Hitherto she had felt she must not appear less virtuous than her trusted husband.- τιθέμεσθα. The present is frequently thus used both in questions and statements for the delib. subjunct. or future: cp. v. 232 οὐ παραβαίνομεν, n.--ot, lit. in a case where.
οἴκων: because Ion will supplant her. -παίδων, the children she had hoped she might yet have. no, see

ἐλπίδες. Kreousa had hoped to receive news of her child from Apollo without having to disclose her secret. She now resolves publicly to shame the god into showing her some consideration.-ἃς διαθ. She speaks of disposing her hopes, line 870 meaning the matter of her hopes. The compound διατίθημι is elsewhere found only in prose, excepting Ar. Av. 439. The ων έσομαι poets use the simple verb.
With a negative μá is generally added. Its absence, however, is common: see Lexicon.

λίμνης κ.τ.λ. : 'and the holy shore of the waters of Triton's lake.' Barnes cp. Luc. Phars. 9. 350 sqq. :- Hanc et Pallas amat, patrio quod uertice nata terrarum primam Libyen-nam proxima caelo est, quod probat ipse calor, -tetigit, stagnique quieta uoltus uidit aqua, posuitque in margine plantas, et se dilecta Tritonida dixit ab unda. Tritonia is a common epithet of Pallas.

οὐκέτι κ.τ.λ. : no longer will I conceal my union, for when the load is lifted from my breast, I shall be easier. There are four verbs νέω: (1)=to go (used mostly in middle voice); (2)=to swim; (3)=to spin; (4)=to heap up. Our word is a compound of the last. -ῥᾴων εἶναι is a phrase from the sick-room.

κακοβουλευθεῖσ'. So the Mss., but the form is in- correct; compound verbs are not formed by merely prefixing a noun-stem or adverb to the simple verb. Thus κακο-λέγω, εὐ-πράσσω, δυσ-μανθάνω would be wrong. The verb required must be formed as a derivative from a noun, and the normal termination for such verbs is éw. Accordingly we have κακολογέω (from κακολόγος), εὐπραγέω (εὐπραγής), δυσμαθέω (δυσμαθής). κακοβουλευθεῖσ' has on these grounds been changed by some edd. to κακοβουληθεισ', to which however it is some objection that κακόβουλος only occurs as=(1) ill-advised, (2) ill-advising. Others read κακὰ βουλευθεῖσ', but this gives βουλεύω the sense of ἐπιβουλεύω. In favour of the Mss. it may be urged that the irregular forms δυσ-θνήσκω, δυσ-οίζω are found, and the poet may have intentionally though incorrectly formed κακοβουλεύω on the analogy of ἐπιβουλεύω, wanting a stronger word, and wishing at the same time to avoid the confusion of sound with the pass. aor. of βούλομαι which κακοβουληθεῖσ' (κακοβουλέω) would cause.
λέκτρων προδ. : traitors to their loves.

ὦ τὰς κ.τ.λ. Ο thou that makest music from the seven voices of the lyre, which sounds forth on the lifeless ox-horn to the country-folk the muses' sweetly-echoing min- strelsy.' -ἐνοπάν, cognate acc. -ἅτε, fem. of epic ὅστε, com- mon in lyrics, and even found (though very rarely) in senarii. -κέρασιν stands probably not for the two horn-like points of the lyre (which appear to be called πήχεις, not κέρατα), but for the horn sounding-board. As κέρας means a horn, not being used to express the material, the plural was necessary : cp. Od. 19. 563 αἱ μὲν γὰρ [αἱ πύλαι] κεράεσσι τετεύχαται. Similarly Cicero Nat. Deor. 2. 59 (quoted by Musgr.) uses the plural: cornibus iis quae ad neruos resonant in cantibus. He also is speaking of the sounding-board of a lyre. The epithet lifeless is added merely because sounds generally come from living things.

ἦλθες κ.τ.λ. 'Thou camest to me with the sunlight in thy golden hair, when I was gathering the yellow flowers, golden mirrors, into the bosom of my robe, to deck it. Take φάρεσιν with κόλπους, dat. for gen., as often. -ἀνθίζειν is very difficult to construe, and is perhaps corrupt. Musgr. proposes ἀνθισμόν. -χρυσανταυγῆ, gold-reflecting, is a beauti- ful word that has been needlessly suspected. Paley reads ἀνθίζοντα χρυσαυγή. For the picture cp. the scarcely less beautiful one of Proserpina and her companions, Ovid Fast.
ἐμφύς, clinging to: cp. the Homeric phrase ἐν δ' ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί.
θεὸς κ.τ.λ. : a god and yet my lover, in shameless submission to the goddess of love.-ἀναιδείᾳ : modal; with shamelessness.-χάριν πράσσων, obtemperans.
φρίκᾳ ματρός, in fear of my mother.
ἵνα με κ.τ.λ.: the cruel couch where thou didst cruelly wed me, miserable maid.
ἔρρει κ.τ.λ.: And now my boy is gone, fowls of the air have torn and devoured him, -my boy and thine, cruel god; but thou dost shout and sing songs of triumph to thy lyre! -τλάμων, nom. for voc.
ὃς ὀμφὰν κληροῖς : who givest holy answer. κληροῖς, lit. givest by lot: cp. Thuc. 6. 42 τρία μέρη νείμαντες ἕν ἑκάστῳ ἐκλήρωσαν.
εἰς οὓς, that there may be no mistake about his hear- ing. I will shout a word into thine ear.' Cp. v. 696 : v. 1521 is different.
ἰὼ κ.τ.λ. Ho, ho! Thou art a base lover!
νυμφεύτᾳ, Xouthos.
προλαβών, i.e. from Xouthos. In

καὶ σός γ': ay and thine. -ἀμαθής, unfeeling. Dr. Verrall in a very instructive note on Med. 223 (q. v.) remarks that ἀμαθia and ἀμαθής denoted deficiency in moral feeling rather than in intellectual power; 'a want of feeling for others in all shades from cruelty down to rudeness. proof of this he gives several citations from the tragedians, among which H.F. 347 ἀμαθής τις εἱ θεος is an exact parallel to our passage. Zeus is reproached for indifference to his offspring. Dr. Verrall adds that the purely intellectual sense, ignorance, is rare. Cp. v. 247 ἀπαιδεύτως and note.
ἐξαλλάξας, having left: cp. I.T. 135 ἐξαλλάξασ’ Εὐρώταν.
λοχεύματα...σε: the cognate acc. and acc. obj. are combined, as often; bare thee in a holy birth. Cp. Plat. Αροί. 39 τιμωρία ὑμῖν ἥξει...πολὺ χαλεπωτέραν ἢ οἵαν ἔμε ἀπεκτό- νατε, and v. 931.

Δίοισι κάρποις : by the fatherhood of Zeus: literally, fruits. "For the metaphor of κάρπος applied to children see νυ. 476, 815. κάποις (in the garden) Badham, Kirchoff, and others, but without reason." (Verrall.)--At this point, over- come by her emotion, Kreousa falls down upon the steps.
οἴκτου : so Nauck. The Mss. οὔτοι gives an unsuitable sense.
φρενί, from my soul; lit. for.
Note the change of subjects, [ἐγὼ] ὑπεξαντλῶν... ἄλλο κῦμα αἴρει με. Such anacolutha are very common : cp. Hipp. 23 τὰ πολλὰ δὲ | πάλαι προκόψασ᾽ οὐ πόνου πολλοῦ με δεῖ. ---ὑπό, because of.

οὓς κ.τ.λ. : lit. after speaking which about the already present troubles, thou didst pursue a fresh path, etc. For the gen. κακῶν = περὶ κακῶν (a very common construction both with nouns and verbs of speaking) cp. Soph. Τr. 1122 τῆς μητρὸς ἥκω τῆς ἐμῆς φράσων. Εl. 317 τοῦ κασιγνήτου τί φής; Paley gives θέσφατα κόρης, oracles about a maiden; τέκνων ἐπιστολάς, injunctions about her children ; ὀξεῖα γὰρ σοῦ βάξις, a report about thee. Cp. v. 749 η.
For the cognate acc. and gen. obj. cp. v. 921 n.

ποῖον. Not to be taken simply = what kind of a child ? The word expresses astonishment (sometimes incredulity or derision): what is this child thou sayest thou hast borne? In Ar. Ran. 529, to Xanthias' declaration ταῦτ᾽ ἐγὼ μαρτύρομαι καὶ τοῖς θεοῖσιν ἐπιτρέπω, Dionysos wittily replies ποίοις θεοῖς ; gods indeed!

θηρσὶν κ.τ.λ.: a welcome thing for beasts to bury, i.e. by devouring him; cp. Aesch. Theb. 1020 οὕτω πετηνῶν τόνδ᾽ ὑπ᾽ οἰωνῶν δοκεῖ | ταφέντ᾽ ἀτίμως κ.τ.λ. Badham cp. Soph. Ει. 1488 καὶ κτανὼν προθὲς | ταφεῦσιν ὧν τόνδ' εἰκός ἐστι τυγχάνειν ἄποπτον ἡμῶν, and Herwerden Byron, Bride of Abydos, 2. 26:- 'What recks it, though that corse shall lie Within a living grave? The bird that tears that prostrate form Hath only robb'd the meaner worm'...
αἰσχ. σε. I am ashamed before thee: cp. Plato Symp. 216 в тὸ αἰσχύνεσθαι ὁντινοῦν, and v. 1075.

I have followed Badham in bracketing this line. It interrupts the στιχομυθία, and the cave was certainly not called Μακραί. The line has been said to be necessary because Κεκροπίας πέτρας does not sufficiently describe the place to elicit the answer ἔνθα Πανός κ.τ.λ. But the Μακραί forming the highest cliff of the Acropolis might well have been called The Rocks par excellence. Or it may be urged that the old man having knowledge of some occurrence connected with the cave of Pan, anticipates further description of the place intended, especially as the mention of an ἄντρον in v. 892 must have been significant to him. Such anticipations are not uncommon.
The γε, though placed after the first word, emphasises the whole expression & ᾐσθόμην : could this have been what I heard?
φαίημεν ἄν, I should acquiesce.
νόσον, malady.
ἀνάσχου. At the word έτεκον the old man must be supposed to have visibly started. Paley.
ποῦ τίς; cp. v. 793.-λοχεύει σ': aids thee in the birth.
κατ' ἄντρον. But in v. 16 the child is said to have been born in the house.
ἵνα σὺ κ.τ.λ. He wishes to find the child, that Kreousa equally with Xouthos may be relieved from the reproach of childlessness.'
παιδεύεται (mid.), spends his boyhood; on the analogy of ὀρφανεύομαι, παρθενεύομαι, as Paley points out. Cp. υ. 1084 κορευόμεναι and note.
αἱ ξυμφ. κ.τ.λ.: my misery and secrecy alone.

καὶ πῶς; expresses incredulity or amazement: cp. v. 973 and Plato Alc. 1. 1340, ΣΩ. Δύναιτο δ' ἄν τις μεταδιδόναι δ μὴ ἔχει;-ΑΛ. καὶ πῶς; How could he? Ιn πῶς καί, on the other hand, the kal, emphasizing the words that follow, marks that a fact is assumed: cp. Hec. 515 πῶς καί νιν ἐξεπράξατ᾽; How did you (actually) despatch her?: Phoen. 1354 πῶς καὶ πέπρακται διπτύχων παίδων φόνος;

πῶς δ'; This may be taken (1) (dost ask) how?, πῶς being for ὅπως, which though strictly correct, would, accord- ing to Paley, be scarcely suited to tragedy: (It belongs rather to the language of everyday : cp. Ar. σὺ δ' εἱ τίς ἀνδρῶν ;— Ὅστις εἴμ᾿ ἐγώ; Μέτων.) or (2) a pathetic repetition, How indeed! In either case the Sé merely gives force; see Ellendt Lex. Soph. s. v. δέ, § 7. For (1) Paley cites Aesch. Cho. 766-7 XO. πῶς οὖν κελεύει νιν μολεῖν ἐσταλμένον ; ΤΡ. ἡ πῶς;
τλήμων, 'hard-hearted."
εἰ y': i.e. thou wouldst have said so, if etc.
With πεσεῖν supply ἐπιθυμοῦντα from διώκοντα.

ὡς σώσοντα κ.τ.λ.: acc. absol. The addition of ὡς with acc. or gen. absol. gives the force of in the belief that, on the ground that, marking the statement as subjective: cp. Soph. O. T. 101 ὡς τόδ' αἷμα χειμάζον πόλιν, Thuc. 6. 24 ὡς οὐδὲν ἂν σφαλεῖσαν μεγάλην δύναμιν. Cp. v. 18 n.
Note the awkwardness of the rhythm caused by com- posing a tribrach of a trisyllable. Badham reads πάτραν σὴν δυστυχούσαν. ---Both P and C read εἰσορῶ, not εἰσορῶν.
μὴ νῦν ἔτ' κ.τ.λ. So Mary Queen of Scots after the murder of Rizzio is reported to have said to her women, No more tears, girls; let us think of revenge.
ἀπορία κ.τ.λ. : misery is resourceless.
καὶ πῶς; see on v. 958.
καὶ νῦν, even now.
αἰδούμεθ' κ.τ.λ. I respect the love that was once ours.
ἀλλά, at anyrate: see on v. 426. -ἐπὶ σοί: to sup- plant thee.

ἐπίσημον κ.τ.λ. Men mark a deed of blood, and slaves are irresolute: i.e. the attempt will be noticed, and the slaves will be too cowardly to carry it through. She thinks poison will be safer than the dagger. ὁ is generic. If the poet had meant this murder, we should have had ἐπίσημος. Cp. Virg.'s triste lupus stabulis.
κακίζει, thy courage ebbs.

καὶ μὴν κ.τ.λ. Oh, I have a plan cunning and effectual. Supply βουλεύματα from βούλευε. The effect of καὶ μήν is to draw attention sharply to the statement that is to follow. This is here further emphasised by γε: cp. Dem. Meid. § 56 καὶ μὴν ἴστε γε τοῦθ᾽ ὅτι κ.τ.λ. Soph. Αi. 531 καὶ μὴν φόβοισί γ᾽ αὐτὸν ἐξελυσάμην, Oh, in my anxiety etc. See detached note A.
τοῖνδ', gen.
Φλέγρᾳ, the district of Thrace, afterwards called Pallene. Paley erroneously takes it of the Phlegraei campi (Solfatara) in Campania.

Γόργον'. Hesiod speaks of three Gorgons (Stheino, Euryale, and Medusa, of whom Medusa alone was mortal), daughters of Phorkys and Keto. Euripides here follows Homer in recognizing only one. Her birth from Ge seems to be the poet's own invention.

ποῖον κ.τ.λ. What appearance did her monstrous form present? μορφή denotes the essential and real form of a thing; σχῆμα its appearance to the eye. It is obvious that the two may not always be identical, so that σχῆμα sometimes means a deceptive appearance or disguise.

θώρακα κ.τ.λ. Her breast was armed with the en- velopment of a snake. For θώραξ of the breast itself cp. H. F. 1095 νεανίαν θώρακα καὶ βραχίονα. —ἐχίδνης is practically equivalent to an adj. = snaky. The Gorgon's own skin was like that of a snake: cp. v. 955 ταύτης δέρος.
The sentence is epexegetic of μύθοs in the previous line: yes, the story that etc.

ἣν αἰγίδ᾽ ὀνομάζουσι. Herodotus (4. 189) says that the alyis as a decoration of Athena was borrowed from Libya, where the women wore tasselled goat-skins, αἰγέας θυσανωτάς (cp. v. 1423 and note). Whether this is so or not, he is probably giving the derivation of the word commonly ac- cepted in his day (cp. νεβρίs, fawn-skin). Homer regards the αἰγίς as properly belonging to Zeus, though worn at times both by Apollo and Athena, and bearing the Gorgon's head. It is the work of Hephaistos, and is called χρυσέη. A mytho- grapher of the Christian era, writing under the name of Hyginus, says that Zeus being warned that he must wear a goat-skin if he would conquer the Titans, took for a corslet the skin of the goat Amalthaea. Whether Euripides in the present passage is following authority or not, it is impossible to say; but it is clear that his account of the aegis is quite distinct from those given above. Whereas the common story tells how Perseus slew Medusa assisted by Athena, Euripides makes Athena herself slay the creature. She then takes the tough snaky skin of the Gorgon's breast and makes it into a corslet for herself, placing the monster's head in the centre. He has now to account for the name aἰγίs. He derives it from ἀίσσω. The war with the Giants was of considerable duration. On the first occasion when Athena, after slaying the Gorgon, dashed into the fight wearing the snake-skin on her breast, the object obtained the name aiyis. See next note. The use of αἰγίs for a hurricane (Aesch. Cho. 592) and the existence of the words καταιγίς, αἰγίζω, ἐπαιγίζω, must leave us still in doubt as to the true origin of the word. Some statues show the aegis scaly, others smooth; but probably in the case of the latter the scales were represented by painting.

ἔσχε, got, obtained: the proper meaning of this tense as distinguished from εἶχε. -ᾐξεν : so Paley, from the suggestion of an anonymous friend. The Mss. ἦλθεν is doubt- less a gloss. A meaning for aἰγίs, other than the commonly received goat-skin, is an indispensable part of the poet's version of the story. That he should have left this, the key of the whole passage, to be unearthed from ἦλθεν is incredible. Perhaps we should also read τότ' for τόδ'.
μέλλεις, sc. εἰδέναι.
μέλλον ... ἔπος, a word that hesitates. Kreousa naturally pauses when about to name the deadly thing that is to be the instrument of her murderous deed.
ἐν τῷ; in what? Take σώματος with καθάψασα. Cp. v. 1065 n.
δεσμοῖς, bracelet.
αὔτ᾽, i.e. αὐτά, the δεσμά of v. 1007.
πῶς οὖν κ.τ.λ. How, then, has the twofold gift been ordered? That is, as he afterwards asks, how is it to be used?

κοίλης ... φλεβός, the vena cava, by which the blood returns to the heart. Musgrave quotes Apollodorus 3, 10, 6 παρὰ γὰρ ᾿Αθήνας λαβὼν (Cheiron) τὸ ἐκ τῶν φλεβῶν τῆς Γόργονος ῥυὲν αἷμα, τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῶν ἀριστερών (i.e. from the aorta) ῥυὲν πρὸς φθορὰν ἀνθρώπων ἐχρῆτο, τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῶν δεξίων πρὸς σωτηρίαν, καὶ διὰ τούτου τοὺς τεθνηκότας ἀνήγειρεν. -ὅστις (sc. σταλαγμός) here differs from os in that it marks a difference of kind, a common use of the pronoun. -φόνῳ, modal: in slaying her, in her slaying. Cp. a similar use of povaîs Soph. Ant. 1003 καὶ σπῶντας ἐν χηλαῖσιν ἀλλήλους φοναῖς (murderously) | ἔγνων.

χρῆσθαι is accommodated to κέκρανται in v. 1010. –τι in this common phrase is a quasi-cognate (adverbial) acc., = τίνα χρῆσιν. For the double construction see on v. 921.- ἐκφέρει, exhibit: cp. v. 1352. -δύνασιν is poetic and rare.
ὁ δευτ. άρ. So we say number 2, meaning the second thing.
The meaning is φορεῖς τὸν δεύτερον (αὐτόν) κραθέντ᾽ εἰς ἓν ξὺν τῷ πρώτῳ; The Mss. give εἰς ἓν δὲ κραθὲν ταυτὸν ἰχῶρ εἰσφορεῖς. The emendation, which is clever, is by Snape.
κακῷ γὰρ κ.τ.λ.: a general maxim, but pointed by the instance in question.
σὸν λέγειν κ.τ.λ.: cp. Verg. Aen. 1. 76 Tuus, o regina, quid optes | explorare labor, mihi iussa capessere fas est.
γάρ. The meaning is, I criticize your proposal, for you find fault with mine.
ἆρ' ὑπείδου κ.τ.λ. I wonder, hast thou suspected (guessed) what occurs to me too?

μητρυιάς. The cruelty of stepmothers is a common- place with the ancient writers. Aesch., P. V. 727, boldly calls treacherous waters μητρυιὰ νεῶν. Barnes quotes an epigram of Kallimachos :- Στήλην μητρυιῆς, μικρὰν λίθον, ἔστεφε κοῦρος, ὡς βίου ἠλλάχθαι τὸν τρόπον οἰόμενος. ἡ δὲ τάφῳ κλινθεῖσα κατέκτανε παῖδα πεσοῦσα· φεύγετε μητρυιῆς καὶ τάφον, οἱ πρόγονοι.

προλαζ. κ.τ.λ. At least I taste the pleasure so much earlier; lit. by means of the time. χρόνῳ χρόνῳ is dat. instr., but its effect is that of a dat. of measure (which is in fact instrumental), ἀπολαύω. -ἡδονῆς, gen. obj. or partitive. -λάζυμαι (with its compounds) is an epic and Ionic synonym of λαμβάνω.

&, adverbial acc. defining extent of verbal action. Transl., where; lit. in a matter in which, i.e. about Ion. He thinks he has been rearing Ion without your knowledge; he himself will not know that he has to thank you for the boy's death.

οἶσθ' οὖν ὁ δρᾶσον ; ‘Know'st thou, then, what thou must do?' Prof. Jebb on Soph. O. T. 543 gives the following account of the expression. In more than twelve places of the tragic or comic poets we have this or a like form where a person is eagerly bespeaking attention to a command or request. Instead of οἶσθ᾽ ὡς δεῖ σε ποιῆσαι ; or οἶσθ' ὥς σε κελεύω ποιῆσαι ; the anxious haste of the speaker substitutes an abrupt imperative: οἶσθ᾽ ὡς ποίησον ; That the imperative was here felt as equivalent to you are to do, appears clearly from the substitutes which sometimes replace it. Thus we find (1) fut. indic. Eur. Cycl. 131 οἶσθ' οὖν ὁ δράσεις; Med. 600 οἶσθ᾽ ὡς μετεύξει καὶ σοφωτέρα φανεῖ; (2) a periphrasis ἀλλ' ... οἶσθ᾽ ὁ δρᾶν σε βούλομαι τούτων πέρι; Only a sense that the imper. had this force could explain the still bolder form of the phrase with the 3rd pers.: Eur. I. T. 1203 οἶσθα νῦν ἃ μοι γενέσθω = ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι μοι : Ar. Ach. 1064 οἶσθ᾽ ὡς ποιείτω ;= ὡς δεῖ ποιεῖν αὐτήν.᾿
χρύσωμά κ.τ.λ.: this gold thing that Athena gave, this ancient pyx. She probably detaches from her wrist only that portion of the bracelet which formed the receptacle of the poison.
ἡμῖν, ethic dat.
βαλών suggests the notion of haste: drop it hastily, i.e. the contents of the ὄργανον. For κάθες cp. δρόσον καθήσω v. 436.

Rejected by Paley, Dindorf and Möllendorf. The omission of the τι (wanting in the Mss.) is, however, ver, easily accounted for by the following, and other objections urged against the line are not insuperable. For μή τι Soph. Τr. 383 ὅλοιντο, μή τι πάντες κ.τ.λ. is cited: cp. v. 1113 οὔ τί που.
εἴσω προξένων, sc. οἴκων. Without doubt the Athenian θεωροί were regularly provided for by an officer appointed at the public cost. Paley.
ἄγ', ὦ γεραιὲ πούς κ.τ.λ. Observations such as this, far beneath the dignity of tragedy, deservedly exposed Euripides to all the punishment ridicule could inflict.
δεσποτῶν, Kreousa.

τὴν δ᾽ εὐσέβειαν ... τιμᾶν. This may (1) be taken literally = to honour piety, viz. by acting piously; or (2) the expression may be classed with those given v. 168 note. The translation would then be, to render the observance (τιμή) of piety; but the absence of a dat. (e.g. τοῖς θεοῖς) is perhaps against this view here. The old man's words express the average morality of the poet's day.

Third στάσιμον.- O Hekate, queen of guile, speed thou the fatal cup to its work upon him that would usurp Erechtheus' throne. Never may any but the ancient stock reign over us! If she fails of her purpose, my mistress will take her own life and pass to the other world, making pain pain's antidote. Never will the daughter of kings suffer aliens to rule her home. -Horrible, that this youth should see that holy night when starry sky, and moon, and the daughters of the sea dance to the dread Mother and gold- crowned Maid by the river, where this temple-vagabond hopes to reign, entering on other men's labours. - Mark, ye poets that love to sing slanderously of women's wickedness, mark how far less innocent are men. Let your song be rather of their discreditable loves; for one of your sons of Zeus deserts my lady for another love, and gets him a base-born child.'

Εἰνοδία θύγατερ Δάματρος. O queen of the cross- roads, daughter of Demeter.' εἰνοδία (epic and Ionic for ένοδ.) might be substantival, but is better regarded as adj. with θύγατερ. The goddess appealed to is Hekate, who is, as often, iden- tified with Persephone or Kore, the daughter of Demeter : cp. Soph. Ant. 1199 ἐνοδίαν θεὸν | Πλούτωνά τ'. 'She was regarded as a spectral being who at night sent from the lower world all kinds of demons and phantoms, who taught sorcery and witchcraft, who dwelt at places where roads crossed each other [hence the name Ἐνοδία, Triuia], on tombs, and near the blood of murdered persons. She herself too wanders about with the souls of the dead, and her approach is an- nounced by the whining and howling of dogs.' (Dict. Myth.)
ἐφόδων 'assaults, rather than merely visitations.
καὶ μεθαμ. κ.τ.λ.: in the noon-day also guide the contents of the deadly bowl. For πληρώματα cp. v. 1412.
ἐφ' οἶσι, against those against whom etc. Ion is meant. For the dat. cp. v. 209 η.
λαιμ. σταλαγμ. : blood-drops that fell from the severed throat. For the adj. cp. Soph. Ant. 1216 ἁρμὸν χώματος λιθοσπαδή, an opening made by by tearing away the stones.
τῷ ... ἐφαπτ., him that grasps at: the words explain ἐφ' οἶσι above.
εὐγενετᾶν, a by-form of εὐγενής, employed only by Euripides.
σπουδαί, purpose.

4 τε κ.τ.λ.: and the hope wherewith she is now borne on. For the synizesis-ται ἐλπ. Paley cp. Soph. Tr. 216 ἀείρομαι οὐδ᾽ ἀπώσομαι τὸν αὐλόν, Aesch. Ρ. V. 834 ἡ Διὸς κλεινὴ δάμαρ μέλλουσ᾽ ἔσεσθαι, εἰ τῶνδε προσσαίνει σε τι, Ι. Τ. 679 δόξω ... προδούς σε σῴζεσθαι αὐτὸς εἰς οἴκους μόνος. Add Aesch. Theb. 402 τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις ἡ ἀνοία τινί.
λαιμῶν with ἐξαψ.: fasten to her throat, about her neck. Cp. v. 1006 n.

εἰς ἄλλας κ.τ.λ.: will go down to another phase of life, i.e. the life beyond the grave: cp. v. 953: Med. 1039 ἐς ἄλλο σχῆμ᾽ ἀποστάντες βίου : fr. 830 τίς οἶδεν εἰ ζῆν τοῦθ, δ κέκληται θανεῖν, | τὸ δὲ θνῄσκειν ἐστί; (wittily quoted by Dionysos against Euripides himself in the Ranae). We say, though with more meaning, mors ianua uitae.

αἰσχύνομαι κ.τ.λ. 'I feel awe before the much-sung god, if by the springs of Kallichoros this boy keeping vigil through the night shall look upon the torch of the twentieth day's sacred mission. -αἰσχυν, as in v. 934. The chorus tremble at the insult that will be offered to the god, if a foreigner is allowed to take part in his worship. πολύυμνον is practically equivalent to the πολυώνυμε of Soph. Ant. 1115. The much-sung god' is Dionysos, to whom worship was addressed under many different names and titles (see on v. 216). In the Eleusinian mysteries, here referred to, he was associated with Demeter and Koré (Persephoné) under the name Iacchos. This lacchos was said to be the son of Koré or Demeter (the two are sometimes identified) and Zeus. Prof. Jebb, in his note on Soph. O.C. 682 mentions a relief found at Eleusis in 1859, and referable to the period between Pheidias and Praxiteles, which shows Persephone with her right hand on the head of the young Iacchos (a boy of some fifteen years), who is facing Demeter. Virgil G. 1. 7 speaks of Liber et alma Ceres, doubtless identi- fying the god with Dionysos. But though Ceres was identi- cal with Demeter (whose worship, with a change of the name, the Romans imported from Sicily), Liber is entirely distinct from the Greek god. He and Libera, who was associated with him, are ancient Italian divinities having under their protection the vine and the fruits of the earth in general. The confusion of both with the Greek deities (for Virgil's Ceres represents the Libera of the old religion) is due to this similarity in their office. εἰκάδων. The greater Eleusinia was a festival lasting nine days, from the 15th to the 23rd of Boedromion. The 20th, the sixth day of the festival, was called "Ιακχος, and was the most solemn of all. The statue of Iacchos, adorned with a garland of myrtle and bearing a torch in his hand, was carried along the sacred road amid joyous shouts (ἰακχίζειν) and songs, from the Kerameikos to Eleusis.' (It was nothing uncommon for this procession to number 30,000 persons.) During the night the mystae remained at Eleusis, and were initiated into the last mysteries (ἐποπτεία. Cp. Soph. Ant. 1115, πολυώνυμε,...μέδεις δὲ παγκοίνοις Ἐλευσινίας Δηοῦς (Deme- ter) ἐν κόλποις. -The Καλλίχορος was a well or spring at Eleusis, so called because the women used to dance round it. -The subject of ὄψεται is easily easy supplied, though not actually expressed till v. 1089 ὁ Φοίβειος ἀλάτας. The sh shortening of final -ai before a vowel in lyrics, as in epic poetry, is common. Not infrequently the syllable is shortened in the middle of a word: cp. El. 497 παλαιόν (beginning an iambic line), Soph. Ant. 1140 βιαΐας, ίδ. 1310 δείλαῖος. - λαμπάδα θεωρόν is a torch belonging to the θεωρία or sacred visit to Eleusis.

ὅτε καὶ κ.τ.λ. The awfulness of their power is finely expressed by the idea that the very elements unite with mortals in the service of Demeter and Cora. (Paley.) -ἀστερωπὸς... αἰθήρ : i.e. the stars in heaven dance. The addition of Σελάνα makes this certain, or we might have com- pared Aesch. Theb. 155 δοριτίνακτος αἰθὴρ δ᾽ ἐπιμαίνεται. – ἀνεχόρευσεν... χορεύει. These words govern κόραν and ματέρα below: cp. Soph. Ant. 1153 αἵ σε μαινόμεναι πάννυχοι χορεύουσι τὸν ταμίαν "Ιακχον. In H.F. 871 the word=make to dance, τάχα σ᾽ ἐγὼ μᾶλλον χορεύσω καὶ καταυλήσω φόβῳ.

The Mss. give Νηρέος, so that, as compared with v. 1098, the line wants a syllable. For κόραι Νηρηίδες, offered in the text, cp. v. 200 п. The adj. would be easily corrupted into the gen. of the substantive. Several edd. accommodate ข. 1098 to this by changing ἀμφί into περί, but this is to play at emendation.

The Mss. give ἀεννάων, i.e. ἀενάων (see on v. 118). But v. 1099 (δείκνυσι...) having the anacrusis, there must be one here also.---ἀμφ' in the text is from Hartung. The false spelling ἀεννάων was apparently intended to supply the miss- ing syllable.

κορευόμεναι, spend their maidenhood: cp. Alc. 313 σὺ δ᾽, ὦ τέκνον μοι, πῶς κορευθήσει καλῶς ; and v. 953 n. It is extraordinary that this admirable correction of Musgrave's for the corrupt χορεύομεναι of the Mss. should have remained unnoticed by all subsequent editors. It was again proposed by Dr. Verrall (evidently in ignorance that he had been anticipated) in the Journal of the Hellenic Society vol. 1, p. 283, and is strongly supported by the κόραν which echoes it in the next line.

ἄλλ. πόν. εἰσπεσών : entering on others labours'; i.e. obtaining a kingdom which he had done nothing to advance. There is a suggestion of violence in the participle. -ἀλάτας, vagabond: cp. v. 576 ἀλητείαν.

ὁρᾶθ' ὅσοι κ.τ.λ. Mark, all ye that pursue poesy and sing slanderous songs of our loves and unholy unions of lawless passion. -κατὰ μ. ἰόντες: lit. going after song. The expression has caused difficulty, but cp. Hel. 164 τίνα μοῦσαν ἐπέλθω ; Alc. 965 διὰ μούσας ᾖξα : Ηipp. 452 ἐν μούσαις εἶναι, where the thought is the same though differently expressed. -I have ventured to write ἀθέμιτος, because if Κύπριδος is not generalized by an adj., γάμους Κύπριδος can only mean marriages of the goddess Kypris, as Badham points out. The a of αθέμιτος is lengthened according to epic usage. The Mss. give ἀθεμίτους (by assimilation to ἀνοσίους?), which does not correspond properly with v. 1077.-The whole passage, υν. 1090-1100, is closely similar to Med. 414. sqq. τὰν δ᾽ ἐμὰν εὔκλειαν ἔχειν βιοτὰν κ.τ.λ.
ἄροτον, race; lit. crop: cp. Med. 1281 τέκνων ὃν ἔτεκες ἄροτον.
παλίμφαμος κ.τ.λ. Let a song of contrary strain go forth against men, speaking evil of their loves.

δείκνυσι κ.τ.λ. : for here one of your children of Zeus shows neglectfulness (of his wife). That is, here is a case of masculine infidelity. "According to the traditional genealogy of the bards, as we see it in the Theogonia of Hesiod, the female sex were not children of Zeus at all. While men, in the tables of these partial antiquaries, were allowed to trace their pedigrees through this or that god to the father of gods and men, Ζῆνα θεῶν πατέρ' ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν (Theog. 47), women (that is, the sex in general) were thought too wicked and mischievous for so respectable an origin, and were derived according to the famous legend from a deceitful temptress fashioned by Hephaestus to humour the wrath of Zeus against mankind (Theog. 570 ff.)." Thus Dr. Verrall explains and justifies his admirable correc- tion (EIC for EK), proposed in an article (On some Ionic elements in Attic Tragedy) in the Journal of the Hellen. Soc. vol. 1, which older students should by all means consult. He further suggests τe (epic) where I have offered ώδε. The metre would admit either word, but ὧδε seems to me to account better for the corruption ὁ Διός (ΩΔΕΔΙΟC became ΟΔΙΟΣ). The Mss. reading is ὁ Διὸς ἐκ, which does not accord with the metre of v. 1083, and there is a further difficulty in the sense. ὁ Διὸς ἐκ παίδων can only refer to Xouthos' relationship to Zeus through Aiolos and Hellen. But as Dr. Verrall shows (ubi supr.) this reference takes the whole point out of the passage. "It is Xouthos the man, not Xouthos the grandson of Zeus, whose infidelity has given the women occasion to retort." See further in the article referred to above.
οὐ κοινὰν κ.τ.λ.: 'in not becoming the father, with happy fortune to the house, of children that are also my lady's: lit. the (good) fortune of children common to my mis- tress.

πρὸς δ' 'Αφρ. κ.τ.λ.: and indulging passion for another, found a base-born son; lit. doing a favour towards another passion. 'Αφροδίταν is put generally, like Κύπριδος υ. 1093. –θεμ. χάριν, cp. v. 895 Κύπριδι χάριν πράσσων.

Fourth ἐπεισόδιον. - One of Kreousa's servants rushes in and asks for his mistress, whom he has been seeking all over the town. An attempt has been made to murder the young man Ion, and the enraged populace are looking for Kreousa that they may put her to death for having instigated the crime. At the request of the Chorus the man tells the story of the attempted deed and its strange detection in a long speech of much beauty. At its conclusion he hurries away to search further for Kreousa and warn her of her danger.

κεδναί is offered for the inappropriate κλειval of the MSS. It gives just the meaning wanted, and will account for the corruption. Paley and Dind. read ξέναι, but the women were the men's own fellow-servants (cp. υ. 1110). κλεινήν also (several edd.) is inadmissible: the word obtains an un suitable emphasis, and the sentence becomes (as Paley says) very unlike the style of Euripides.
ἐξέπλησα, I have gone over, lit. completed. The object of this verb must be found in πανταχῆ ἄστεως taken κατὰ σύνεσιν as = πᾶν τὸ ἄστυ. Cp. Tib. 1. 4. 69 et ter centenas erroribus expleat urbes.
τί δ'; for the addition of dé see on v. 959.--ἔχει σε : possesses thee, a favourite use of ἔχω: cp. Ι. Α. 837 ἀφασία μ' ἔχει, γύναι.
θηρώμεθ'. They are chasing us.
πετρουμένη : cp. v. 1222 n.
που, surely.
ἔγνως. Thou hast hit it. Note two important meanings of this tense: (1) to come to know, to learn; (2) to come to a decision, to resolve.
ὤφθη : cp. v. 1215 n.

τὸ μὴ δίκαιον κ.τ.λ. The attempt of right to defeat wrong the god exposed, not willing to be defiled; lit. dis- covered the wrong when being defeated. On the lips of Kreousa's servant τὸ μὴ δίκαιον is Ion's cause, τῆς δίκης his mistress' righteous attempt to murder the boy.

πεπυσμέναι κ.τ.λ.: for if I had learned this, I should die more happily, if die I must, or still see the light: lit. or if I must see the light (should live more happily). The latter alternative must not be pressed. It is irrelevant to the speaker's thought, which ends at θάνοιμεν, and its addition is due to a confusion of ideas. The chorus believe they must die. Examples are common; e.g. υν. 853, 858, Aesch. Ag. 634, Phoen. 533.
ἔνθα πῦρ. Lights were said to be seen at night on Parnassos, and were supposed to be made by the lighted torches carried by Bacchus and his train: cp. v. 716 n.

ἀντ' ὀπτηρίων : as offerings for the sight of his child. Xouthos'sacrifices are described as substitutes for (ἀντί) ὀπτήρια, because these offerings were properly made immediately after the child's birth: see on v. 653.

ἀμφ. σκηνάς, the enclosure of a tent. The meaning well-fastened for ἀμφήρεις (Lex.) has no probability. The word means going all round (ἀμφί and √ AR, unless -ήρης be supposed to contain a suffix whose meaning is lost).
μοχθήμασιν, labours, i.e. things made: dat. of instr.
γενέταις, that preside over birth, as Bacchus, Eileithuia, Zeus, Hera.
παροῦσι, emphatic: let the feast be for the friends who are there.

σεμνώς, religiously. Paley suggests that some pre- liminary ceremonies were observed. -ἀτοίχους κ.τ.λ. : the wall-less frame-work of his tent he set firm on uprights.' The περιβολάς are the cross-pieces connecting the upright baulks or posts, and marking the dimensions of the tent. They culminated in a gable, cf. ὀρόφῳ v. 1143. The epithet ἀτοίχους is happy, because the absence of walls at this stage would be conspicuous. The uses of περιβολή are various: Ι. Τ. 903 χειρῶν περιβολαί = embraces ; Tro. 389 περιβολὰς χθονός = α grave; Phoen. 276 φέρ᾽ ἐς σκοτεινὰς περιβολὰς μεθῶ ξίφος, of a scabbard; ib. 1078 τί δ', ἐπτάπυργοι πῶς ἔχουσι περιβολαί ; of the walls of Thebes.

ὀρθοστάταις: cp. Hel. 547 τύμβου 'πὶ κρηπῖδ᾽ ἐμπύρους τ' ὀρθοστάτας, where the shafts at the corners of the tomb are meant. They are called ἐμπύρους because burnt-offerings were made at tombs. See Paley ad loc. -ἡλίου κ.τ.λ. The Mss. give ἡλίου φλογός ... μέσας βολάς, which is just capable of translation as follows: (he set up the framework) neither towards the midday shafts of the sun's flame, making careful observation, nor again towards his rays when ending their life.' Paley alone of the edd. defends the Mss. He constructs καλῶς φυλάξας ὥστε ἱδρύεσθαι οὔτε κ.τ.λ.: but if ὥστε ίδρ. could be supplied thus, anything could be supplied anywhere. Dindorf boldly reads ἡλίου φλόγα ... μέσας θεοῦ ... τελευτώσας βολάς, which is almost guess-work, and other alterations have been proposed. The objections to the Mss. reading are mainly two: (1) καλῶς φυλάξας is awkwardly interposed between φλογός and its governing words; and (2) ἀκτῖνας, being a mere repetition of the idea contained in βολάς, could not bear the emphasis it obtains by beginning the line. It must undoubtedly be constructed with the preceding verse. Herwerden records, though without remark, an extremely م simple remedy proposed by A. Schmidt, viz. the transposition of φλογός and βολάς. With this change (which has been adopted in the text) the Greek reads well and gives excellent sense:-'he set firm his frame-work, --having carefully ob- served the sun's shafts, -to face neither the midday rays of his flame, nor again the dying ones.'-For μέσας cp. Soph. Ο. Ο. 1247 ἀνὰ μέσσαν ἀκτῖν᾽. - The description implies that one side of the tent was open. Ion is careful that this side shall not face any points of the compass between S. and W. because the heat of the afternoon sun would have been intoler- able to the feasters. The detail is introduced probably because the precaution was generally necessary, and its insertion gives reality to the narrative.

πλέθρου κ.τ.λ. : measuring it (his framework) to the length of a plethron with angles regular (i.e. equal to each other). The mention of only one measurement of length shows that the tent was equilateral; the addition of εὐγώνιον shows that it was rectangular. It was therefore a square. 1138 f. Two lines have been omitted from the text : μέτρημ' ἔχουσαν τοὺν μέσῳ γε μυρίων | ποδῶν ἀριθμόν, ὡς λέγουσιν οἱ σοφοί. Paley writes, 'These two lines are undoubtedly spurious. The γε is alone a sufficient proof of this. The Athenians were not so ignorant of arithmetic as to require to be told that 100×100=10,000, and Euripides was not the man to call those who could perform that feat in multiplication οἱ σοφοί.’
καλῶν, fut.
λαβών κ.τ.λ. He was keeper of the treasures: cp. v. 54f.
κατεσκίαζε, hung as a screen (from the sun, over his framework): see on v. 1159 ἤμπισχεν.

πτέρυγα πέπλων : a fold of drapery. Xen. uses πτέρυξ of the flap or skirt of a coat of armour, and a fragment of Aristophanes shows that it had the general meaning of lappet. Here it aptly describes the piece of drapery doubled over the roof-ridge.
Δίου: cp. v. 192 n.

One of the labours imposed on Herakles by Eury- stheus was to obtain the girdle of Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons. The Amazons were said to inhabit the region S. of the Caucasus, and as all Asiatics are skilful in weaving and embroidery, they could well be supposed to have possessed rich stuffs such as are here mentioned. It has been suggested that the poet is actually describing spoils taken by the Athenians from the Persians.

ἐνῆν κ.τ.λ. And there were among them webs woven with figures like these. ἐνῆν, sing. for pl. (σχῆμα Πινδαρικόν), cp. Soph. Τr. 520 ἦν δ᾽ ἀμφίπλεκτοι κλίμακες. The figure though well-established in Attic is not common. Note that the verb must precede the subject. --- γράμμασιν, rare as = designs or pictures: cp. Theocr. 15. 81 ποῖοι ζωογράφοι τἀκριβέα γράμματ᾽ ἔγραψαν ; Plat. Crat. 430E ἆρ' οὐκ ἔστι προσελθόντα ἀνδρί τῳ εἰπεῖν ὅτι Τουτί ἐστι σὸν γράμμα, καὶ δεῖξαι αὐτῷ, ἄν μὲν τύχῃ, ἐκείνου εἰκόνα...;
Οὐρανός, personified. ἀθροίζων, as a chieftain gather- ing his forces, or as for a dance; cp. Shelley, I sang of the dancing stars, I sang of the daedal earth.
εἰς τελ. φλόγα: to the place where his flame dies, lit. last flame.

ἐφέλκων, bringing in his train: cp. Med. 462 πόλλ' ἐφέλκεται φυγὴ | κακὰ ξὺν αὐτῇ, and Milton, Comus, v. 188, 'They left me then when the grey-hooded Even, Like a sad votarist in palmer's weed, Rose from the hindmost wheels of Phoebus' wain.'

μελάμπεπλος κ.τ.λ. And the chariot of sad-robed Night swung onward, drawn by steeds twain with none beside them in the traces.-ἀσείρωτον, lit. having no traces. A two-horse chariot was drawn entirely by the yoke and pole. When four horses were put in abreast, the outside ones drew only by traces. These formed their sole attach- ment to the car, and they were not connected in any way with the inside pair. -ζυγοῖς is dat. instr. and poetic pl. for sing. Translate literally, made her car, that had no traces, swing forward by means of a pair. Or take ἀσείρ. ζυγοῖς = having no trace-horses added to the pair. -In Or. 1004 The Dawn is called μονόπωλος. This is commonly taken as = with one horse; but a much more satisfactory sense is obtained, if with Prof. Jebb we assign the adj. to the class mentioned in the note on v. 496 fin.
ᾔει κ.τ.λ. : was moving along her path in mid-sky. μεσοπόρου = lit. offering a path in its midst. -Πλειάς: one of them is put for all.
Ωρίων. Note the i: Eur. always scans it thus.

στρέφουσα κ.τ.λ., wheeling round by the tail in a golden heaven: cp. Soph. Tr. 131 ἄρκτου στροφάδες κέλευθοι, the circling path of the Bear,' fr. 379 ἄρκτου στροφαί. For στρέφειν intrans. cp. Xen. Ages. 2. 3 στρέψαντες ἀνεχώρουν, Soph. fr. 771 τὸν στρέφοντα κύκλον ἡλίου. I take οὐραῖα to mean literally by the tail, the adverb being equivalent to the dat. of a subst. used instrumentally, as in πύξ, ὀδάξ, λάξ. For οὐραῖα as an adv. cp. πυγηδόν, used by Aristotle = (1) tail- foremost, (2) tail to tail. The sky is called golden because of the other stars; of course the groundwork of the design could not be golden. This But to χρυσήρει is Stephens' correction for Mss. χρυσήρη. some edd. retain, taking οὐρ. χρυσ. = 'golden tail. add an attributive adj. to an adj. used as a subst. is doubtful Greek, except in such a case as πολλὰ κακά, where the adj. has become firmly established as a subst.; and the bear turns round not merely his tail but his whole body. One might as well speak of a horse turning his tail round a race-course. - Paley (reading χρυσήρει) renders turning its tail-stars round (lit. by) the axle of the spangled sky. He would either (1) supply ἄστρα with οὐρ. (which is surely impossible), or (2) take οὐρ. = τὰ οὐρ. ; but this would be a very exceptional use, while the objection to the sense obtained has been already stated. Badham renders turning tail-wise to the golden Pole. Against this Paley justly urges that στρέφω can only mean to turn on an axis; i.e. it cannot like τρέπω = to point in a certain direction. We have also a doubtful use of the dat.

ἠκόντιζ᾽ ἄνω, was shooting her arrows upwards. Cp. Hor. C. 3. 28. 12 celeris spicula Cynthiae, and Matthew Arnold, Mycerinus, 'While the deep-burnish'd foliage overhead Splinter'd the silver arrows of the moon.'

μην. διχήρης, dividing the month, because the moon was full. Υάδες (ὕειν, to rain): three stars in the head of Taurus. The constellation is visible in the northern hemi sphere from Sept. to March; and its first rising in Sept. accordingly marked (σημεῖον) the beginning of the rainy season. Horace calls them tristes Hyadas, and Virgil pleon- astically pluuias Hyadas.

τοίχ. ἔπι : upon the walls, i.e. on what would have been walls, if the framework had been filled in. – ἤμπισχεν, an aorist. The construction is a variation for τοίχους ἠμπ. ὑφάσμασιν : cp. κατεσκίαζε υ. 1142. Such variations are much affected by Virgil, e.g. Aen. 4. 172 hoc praetexit nomine culpam.
This verse has been supposed to represent a Persian design made in anticipation of the battle of Salamis, and captured on that occasion. The anachronism is no objection to this.

μιξόθηρας: cp. Phoen. 138 μιξοβάρβαρος half a bar- barian. -ἱππ. ἄγρας ἐλάφων, hunting of stags on horseback. The sports of an oriental king are depicted. Some edd. place a comma at ἄγρας and interpret of the horses of Diomede, the brazen-hoofed stag and the Nemean lion. But this makes ข. 1162 read awkwardly, and ἱππείας ἄγρas becomes a very obscure expression.
Κέκροπα: see on v. 10.
ἐν ἄκρ. ποσί: cp. Soph. Αi. 1230 ὑψήλ᾽ ἐκόμπεις κἀπ᾽ ἀκρῶν ὡδοιπόρεις. A proud walk is meant, like that of the Highland piper.

στέφανοισι, wreaths of flowers. -εὐόχθου, abundant. The origin of the word is obscure. Its use as an epithet of γῆ in the Epigr, Hom. points to its being a compound like those given in the note on v. 496, so that εὔοχθος γῆ = rich swelling land. Its transference to a banquet piled high with cates divine would be easy and natural. Bacchylides has εὔοχθαι δαῖτες.
δαιτός : so Verrall fills up a lacuna in the Mss. - πέδον, floor.

χεροῖν with νίπτρα, which is a supplementary pre- dicate. ἔπεμπε, with its suggestion of πομπή, seems to imply ceremoniousness. It was customary to wash the hands before and after eating: cp. Ar. Vesp. 1216 ὕδωρ κατὰ χειρός· τὰς τραπέζας ἐσφέρειν· | δειπνοῦμεν· ἀπονενίμμεθ᾽· ἤδη σπένδομεν. — There is no reason for supposing with Paley that the old man blundered in doing all this, as by using drinking-water for the hands and wasting the incense. He may have been awkward; but it was his eager fussiness in doing services for which there were servants properly appointed (πρόθυμα πράσσων), which roused the hilarity of the guests. His interference in the earlier stages of the banquet was intended to disarm sus- picion when he should present the poisoned cup.
σμ. ἱδρῶτα, the oozings of the myrrh: cp. v. 89 n.

ἦρχε, ordered, took the management of. The χρυσ. ἐκπωμ. are the τεύχη σμικρά mentioned below. Their mention at this point implies that wine was on this occasion drunk during the δεῖπνον. At Athens at least, ordinarily no wine was drunk until the δεῖπνον was over and the συμπόσιον began. To preserve the sequence of time these cups should have been mentioned before the νίπτρα. The usual order of events was as follows: -First came the πρῶται τράπεζαι [pl. because each guest had a table to himself], the δεῖπνον or dinner proper, at which no wine was drunk. When this was over, water for cleansing the hands was passed round (cp. v. 1173 n.) with soap (σμήγμα), perfumes were burned, and flowers and garlands were distributed. Then came the cup called μετανιπτρίς or μετάνιπτρον. It was of undiluted wine, and was drunk as we drink a loving-cup. Each guest before he sipped said ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος or ὑγιείας and passed the cup to his right-hand neighbour. This libation concluded the δεῖπνον. The δεύτεραι τράπεζαι were now brought in bear- ing τραγήματα (dragées, dessert), the musicians were intro- duced, and the συμπόσιον began. It was inaugurated by three solemn libations: (1) to Zeus and Hera, (2) to the Heroes, (3) to Zeus Soter alone. A large bowl of wine mixed with water (cp. δρόσου ν. 1194) was prepared, and from it the cups of the guests were filled and handed to them by the slaves. This is the κρατὴρ κοινός of v. 1177. A fresh bowl was mixed for each libation (cp. Soph. fr. 375 Διὸς Σωτηρίου | σπονδὴ τρίτου κρατῆρος). It is at this point that the old man proposes the τεύχη μέγαλα, υ. 1179. The guests drank simultaneously and poured what they did not drink on the ground. Imme- diately upon the third libation, to Zeus Soter, the Paean or song of thankfulness to him was sung (cp. Aesch. Ag. 245 τριτόσπονδον εὔποτμον παιᾶνα: Plat. Symp. 176 Α ᾄσαντας τὸν θεόν), after which the merriment of the feast was resumed.
οἵδε, these gentlemen. The word marks the line as a quotation of the old man's words.
φιάλας, goblets, beakers. The shape was that of a saucer on a stem, like the modern champagne glass.
δραστήριον, potent.

ᾔδειν, 3rd pers. metri grat. for ᾔδει: cp. ὅς ἔμ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ἂν ζῶντ᾽ ᾔδειν, εἰ μή ...: Ραx 1182 οὐ γὰρ ᾔδειν ἐξιών. Note that the true Attic form of the 1st pers. is ἤδη (not ᾔδειν); the 3rd pers. always ᾔδει (never ᾔδη, as was formerly supposed).
ἔχοντι δέ, ethic dat.: and as he (i.e. Ion) held it.
An evidently interpolated line.

βλασφημίαν, a contrary word; any chance word that might be taken by the hearer as crossing or interfering with his religious act. The general use of the word favours its derivation, as if βλαψί-φημος, from βλαβ-. This itself is from AAB, and its proper meaning is hinder.

οἰωνὸν ἔθετο. ὄρνις is also, though less commonly, used = omen. Aristophanes is very amusing on this use of the word Av. 721 φήμη γ᾽ ὑμῖν ὄρνις ἐστὶ, πταρμόν τ' ὄρνιθα καλεῖτε, ξύμβολον ὄρνιν, φωνὴν ὄρνιν, θεράποντ' ὄρνιν, ὄνον ὄρνιν. And in Aesch. Theb. 1011 there is grim jesting on the two meanings of ὑπ' οἰωνῶν :-οὕτω πετεινῶν τόνδ' ὑπ᾽ οἰωνῶν δοκεῖ | ταφέντ᾽ ἀτίμως τοὐπιτίμιον λαβεῖν.

γαίᾳ. Some edd., pressing this word, have inferred that but for the βλασφημία the libation would have been poured on the table. This is, however, uncertain; δίδωσι γαίᾳ may not mean more than that Ion pours out the wine without using the form of words which usually accompanied a libation.
δρόσου, water, as often.

κρατήρας ἱρούς. The pl. seems to imply that they were still occupied with the first libation, having two more to make. If this is so, θεοῦ in v. 1192 is to be taken generally. If θεοῦ is taken of Zeus Soter, κρατήρας must be regarded as poetic pl. for sing. Βυβλ. τε πώμ.: and liquor of Byblos, a town, river, or district in Thrace. The wine was famous: cp. Hes. Op. 207 εἴη πετραίη τε σκιὴ καὶ Βύβλινος οἶνος : Theocr. 14. 15 ἀνῷξα δὲ Βύβλινον αὐτοῖς | εὐώδη τετόρων ἐτέων σχεδὸν ὡς ἀπὸ λανῶ.

κάν ... μόχθῳ: and amid this business, the contre- temps caused by the βλασφημία and the work of mixing fresh bowls. -στέγην: so Paley. The Mss. give δόμοις copied by error from the next line. So in v. 649 for λόγοις both Mss. give φίλοις.

κῶμος, troop; properly a troop of revellers. The sudden inroad of a party of κωμασταί (as in the Symposium of Plato ad fin.) was expressed by ἐπεισκωμάζειν, ἐπεισπηδᾶν, ἐπεισπίπτειν. Compare Andr. 603 ἐξεκώμασε | νεανίου μετ ἀνδρὸς εἰς ἄλλην χθόνα.' (Paley.) Cp. also Hor. C. 4. 1. 9 Tempestiuius in domum | Paulli, purpureis ales odoribus, | comissabere Maximi.

ἀτρ. ναίουσ'. The church of S. Mark at Venice and the buildings in the immediate neighbourhood are the haunt of countless pigeons, so tame that they will come and perch on the hand or shoulder of any one who will feed them. - ἀπέσπεισαν, sc. the guests. There is no difficulty in the omission of the subject.
κεχρημέναι, eager for: cp. Cycl. 98 βορᾶς κεχρημένοι. The word is also used absol., = needy, Plat. Legg. 7170 ἀποδι- δόντα δὲ παλαιοῖς ἐν τῷ γήρᾳ σφόδρα κεχρημένοις.
καθῆκαν, rare for the regular form καθεῖσαν. Paley cp. παρέδωκαν, ἔθηκαν, ἀνῆκαν, all from Eur.
ἔσεισε κἀβάκχ. κ.τ.λ.: quivering through all her plumed body, staggered and screamed with an unintelligible note, a cry of anguish.
θάμβησεν. The augment is not infrequently omitted in long speeches: cp. Soph. El. 714 κόνις δ' ἄνω | φορεῖθ᾽· ὁμοῦ δὲ πάντες ἀναμεμιγμένοι | φείδοντο κέντρων οὐδέν.
πόνους, agonies.
θνῄσκει δὲ κ.τ.λ. : and dies at last in convulsions, her pink claws and legs relaxed.

γυμνὰ ... πέπλων: bared of his cloak; lit. bare out of. He threw off his ἱμάτιον and leapt (μέλη ἧκε) over the table. Imagine the couches as forming three sides of a square, and the old man standing opposite Ion and offering him another cup over the small round table in front of him; this time a poculum innocens.
τίς. He rightly guesses the old man to be but a minister sceleris.
ἐρευνᾷ, searches him, scrutatur.
ἔχοντα, 'with the poison (or its receptacle) on him. -ἕλοι, convict.
ὤφθη, manifestus fit (Paley). Cp. v. 1116 : Thuc. 474 εἰδότες ὅτι ὤφθησαν, had been detected. - κατεῖπε, con- fessed: the prep. denotes completeness. μόγις, with κατεῖπε.
κοιράνοισι, see Introduction § 3.

πετρορριφῆ, flung from the rock (cp. v. 1268) after being stoned (cp. vv. 1112, 1239). Originally criminals were hurled from the peak Hyampeia, but after Aesop's murder (middle of sixth century B.C.: see Dict. Biogr.), the height Nauplia was chosen. Hyampeia was the right-hand of the two peaks of Parnassos that rise immediately over Delphi. Nauplia may have been the name of the other, but its identi- fication is uncertain. See on v. 714.
οὐ ψήφῳ μιᾷ, but by many, i.e. the votes of all: cp. Aesch. Theb. 103 πάταγος οὐχ ἑνὸς δορός.
τὸν ἱερόν, the holy youth.-ἀνακτόροις : the word is extended to include the precincts; cp. v. 1309 n.
