φόνον τιθεῖσαν : attempting to do murder. 'This comparatively rare use of τίθημι by the tragedians has been insufficiently recognised. Both in act. and mid. the verb can stand with a subst. as a mere periphrasis for a verb cognate to the subst., the middle being used where the effect of the action begins and ends with the agent. Thus in Aesch. Ag. 1583 λάκτισμα δείπνου ... τιθείς, λάκτ. τιθ. = λακτίζων, and - the line needs no correction (as Herm. Paley, others). Again ibid. 1029 μὴ σχολὴν τίθει = μὴ σχόλαζε (not do not cause delay, Paley). So Eum. 217 πόνον πλέον τίθου. In Soph. the usage is confined to the mid. voice. The following reff. will repay the trouble of looking out: Rhes. 827, Eur. Or. 1510, Med. 66, Alc. 424, Andr. 828; Soph. O. T. 134, О. С. 1139, Ai. 13. Cp. Virgil's use of dare, e.g. Aen. 4. 604 lam Deiphobi dedit ampla ruinam | Volcano superante domus.
ὁδόν : (1) the journey from Athens to Delphi, (2) the path of crime. So Paley, citing Med. 1067 ἀλλ᾽ εἶμι γὰρ δὴ τλημονεστάτην ὁδόν, | παῖδας προσειπεῖν βούλομαι.

These lines sadly disturb the effect of the fine line preceding, which forms an admirable conclusion to the speech, and it is difficult to believe they are genuine. εἰς ἔρον is in- correctly used as a synonym for δι' ἔρωτα, and the second line expresses the writer's meaning very awkwardly. The edd. indeed have corrected Φοῖβον into Φοίβου, but this only makes matters worse. The point of the lines depends upon ἐλθοῦσα explaining ὁδόν. But ἐλθοῦσα εἰς ἔρον can only mean becoming desirous, so that the point is lost. The use of σῶμα = life may be paralleled by Soph. Ant. 676 τῶν δ᾽ ὀρθουμένων | σῴζει τὰ πολλὰ σώμαθ᾽ ἡ πειθαρχία. - Verr. defends the lines.

Fourth Stasimon. - 'There is no escape for me from death. All is now betrayed, and I must perish; and my mistress they will stone to death. Oh, that I might soar into the air, or plunge beneath the earth, or speed over seas. None can escape when the gods refuse their aid. -Ah, hapless lady, what doom awaits thee? Must we ourselves suffer the fate we had prepared for others? Indeed, twere just.

σπονδᾶς κ.τ.λ.: through the violent death (φόνῳ) caused by the libation made out of the clusters of Dionysos mingling with the blood-drops of the swift-working viper. The key-word φόνῳ finely closes the sentence. Οι σπονδᾶς μιγν. may be taken as gen. absol., and φόνῳ as adverbial, mingled... in murder. - θοᾶς refers to the rapidity of the poison's working.
μυχῶν: the acc. would be more natural, but cp. Hes. Theog. 717 τοὺς μὲν ὑπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης | πέμψαν, Od. 9. 375 μοχλὸν ὑπὸ σποδοῦ ἤλασα πολλῆς.
τεθρίππων... ἐπιβᾶσ': a bold expression, mounting a chariot sped by four steeds of swiftest hoof.

ὅτε μὴ κ.τ.λ.: except when a god is willing to steal a man away; lit. steals away, desiring it. Cp. Od. 16. 197 οὐ γάρ πως ἂν θνητὸς ἀνὴρ τάδε μηχανοῴτο | ᾧ αὐτοῦ γε νόῳ, ὅτε μὴ θεὸς αὐτὸς ἐπελθὼν | ῥηϊδίως ἐθέλων θείη νέον ἠὲ γέροντα.
δρᾶσαι ... πεισόμεθ'. They recall the proverb quoted Aesch. Cho. 313 δράσαντι παθεῖν· τριγέρων μῦθος τάδε φωνεῖ: cp. Ag. 1540 μένει δὲ ... παθεῖν τὸν ἔρξαντα.

Exodos. The recognition. - Kreousa rushes in and takes refuge at the altar. She is rapidly followed by Ion, who bids his attendants to seize his would-be murderess. Kreousa warns them not to incur the wrath of Apollo by violating his sanctuary. While Ion hesitates how to act the Pythia comes in, and after warning the youth not to stain his hands with murder shows him something she carries in her arms concealed by a covering. It is the cradle in which she found him, a new-born infant, laid on the temple-steps, and which she had preserved at Apollo's command. She bids Ion now seek his unknown mother and departs. After she is gone Ion opens the bundle and discloses the cradle. This Kreousa immediately recognizing, claims Ion as her child, and declares Apollo to be his father. As Ion, doubting this, is about to enter the temple to question the god on the point, Athena appears; she confirms Kreousa's statement, and all ends happily.
διωκ....κρατηθεῖσ': for the pl. and sing. cp. v. 549.— Πυθίων. Both Mss. (according to Möllendorf) give Πυθίῳ.
τῷ νόμῳ. She fears it will be useless to plead the sanctity of the temple, when the law of the god who inhabits it demands her punishment.
χειρ. γ' ἁλοῦσα. Yes, if caught in their hands.- οἵδ', here: she points.
πυρᾶς ἐπί: at the altar: cp. Tro. 484 κατασφαγέντ' ἐφ᾽ ἑρκείῳ πυρᾷ, of Priam; I.T. 26 ὑπερ πυρᾶς | μεταρσία.

προστρ. κ.τ.λ. : thou wilt bring on them the guilt of thy blood; lit. thou wilt establish against them blood that cries for vengeance. Cp. Gen. 4. 10 What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground.' To kill even a guilty person in sanctuary was murder. For the various and important meanings of προστρόπαιος see Lexicon.

ταυρόμορφ. ὄμμα, bull-shaped form. So rivers were commonly represented: cf. Soph. Τr. 508 ὁ μὲν ἦν ποτάμου σθένος, ὑψίκερω τετραόρου | φάσμα ταύρου, ᾿Αχελώος : Hor. C. 4. 14. 25 sic tauriformis uoluitur Aufidus: Verg. G.
371 et gemina auratus taurino cornua uoltu | Eridanus.- For ὄμμα see on v. 189. –πατρός. Kephisos was a maternal ancestor of Kreousa.

τήνδε, in this woman. ἔχιδναν. The image is a favourite one for treacherous women: cp. Andr. & δ᾽ ἔστ᾽ ἐχίδνης καὶ πυρὸς περαιτέρω (of a γυνὴ κακή): Aesch. Cho. 249 θανόντος ἐν πλεκταῖσι καὶ σπειράμασι | δεινῆς ἐχίδνης (Klytaem- K nestra). The young vipers were fabled to destroy their mother in being born.
φοινίαν, deadly. It was an ancient belief that one might be blinded by the lightning-like flashing of a serpent's eyes.

The rearrangement of the lines is that suggested by Kirchoff. The improvement on the disjointedness of the Mss. order is manifest. - ἔκυρσα κ.τ.λ. There is a slight incoherence, due to the speaker's excitement. A clause like ἐν τῷ ἀναμετρήσασθαι κ.τ.λ. is required before πρὶν ἐς πόλιν... πεσεῖν, but it is omitted from its place and added afterwards in the form of an explanation (cp. γάρ υ. 1271).
ξυμμάχοις, his friends. Ion guesses (what we know to be the truth) that if he had been friendless, Kreousa would have employed the more certain dagger.
εἴσω γὰρ κ.τ.λ. This sentence explains (γάρ) the mention of ξύμμαχοι two lines above.

ἄρδην, with a high hand, i.e. powerfully, with complete success, utterly. ἄρδην (ἰ.ε. ἀερ-δην : cp. ἀείρω, αἴρω) properly = lifting high: cp. Alc. 608 νέκυν...φέρουσιν ἄρδην, Soph. Ant. 430 ἔκ τ᾽ εὐκροτήτου χαλκέας ἄρδην πρόχου κ.τ.λ. In Αἱ. 1279 πηδῶντος ἄρδην "Ἕκτορος τάφρων ὕπερ we seem to have the transition to the figurative sense, which is the commoner of the two.
πανούργον, jade.-ἐκ τέχνης τέχνην. She first attempted murder and now cunningly seeks to evade justice by taking sanctuary.
All the edd. omit or emend οὐ. But the rhetorical question makes Ion's point more effectively than the tame statement βωμὸν ἔπτηξε κ.τ.λ.

ὁ δ' οἶκτος κ.τ.λ.: and the pity thou claimest touches me (πάρα) more powerfully for myself etc. -καὶ μητρί. His thoughts revert to his mother-of whom he had lately been talking with Kreousa-and her suffering if she had had to mourn for a murdered son. Note how the refer. ence heightens the dramatic force of the situation.
πω accentuates the denial. We say not yet in exactly the same way. Cp. v. 546 οὐ γὰρ ὕστερόν γέ πω : Soph. Ει. 403 μή πω νοῦ τοσόνδ' εἴην κενή : v. 1435 οὐ ποτ' and note.
λαζυσθ' : see on v. 1027.
καταξήνωσι, may card, as it were wool.-πλάκες, levels.
πετραῖον κ.τ.λ. : shall be flung like a quoit, bound- ing from the rock. The edd. quote Tro. 1121 πύργων δίσκημα πικρόν, i.e. Astyanax flung from the walls of Troy.
κοιν. ἐν μέσῳ: in common between thee and Phoibos. Note the εἰρωνεία that adds significance to every line here.

ἀλλ' ἐγεν., sc. Λοξίου. 'But the god adopted me: I speak of (the time of) my father's absence. The Mss. give δ᾽ οὐσίαν. Some edd. simply omit the d. The letter, how- ever, is not likely to have been gratuitously inserted either by a scribe or διορθωτής; it disturbs the metre and is no assistance to the assumed sense of the passage. Seidler's π ἀπουσίαν (ΑΠΟ, perhaps ДО, becoming AO) is much better, and is even required to point the τότε of the next line.
τότ' (emphatic), viz., ἐν ἀπουσία πατρός : see previous note. A clever retort of his own argument. - εἶ: sc. Λοξίου.
οὐκ εὐσεβεῖς. This Kreousa admits v. 1256.-τἀμά, my manner of life: cp. v. 247 n.
8'. She continues her previous remark without noticing the interruption.
ἐπίμπρᾶς, imperf. from a rare form πιμπράω used by later writers: cp. Xen. Hell. 6. 5, 22 ἐνεπίμπρων τε τὰς οἰκίας.

I have followed Nauck, Kirchoff and Wecklein in placing vv. 1296-9 after v. 1303. The result is a gain in coherence at vv. 1299-1304 and at vv. 1295-1300, while the disjointedness exhibited by the old arrangement at vv. 1299- 1300 disappears. This last objection to the old arrangement is not, it is true, an insuperable one; but as a rule dialogue by στιχομυθία is like a chain, each line is somehow linked on to the preceding one, and this even though a new subject is introduced. -τοῦ μ. φόβῳ : for fear of my intending.

ὡς μὴ κ.τ.λ. Yes, to forestall my death [which would have happened], in case thou shouldst cease intending' (while I continued to intend instead of acting.) She means that in this ἀγὼν περὶ ψυχῆς all depended upon who should strike the first blow. -For the ellipse cp. Thuc. 4. 86 οὐ γὰρ συστασιάζων κ.τ.λ., a difficult passage.
φθονεῖς ... εἰ : thou art jealous that.
ἀναρπάσεις : like a bird of prey.

γῆν ... ἐκτήσατο. This can scarcely refer to property given to Xouthos as part of Kreousa's dowry. Aliens were not allowed to possess either land or houses at Athens (a point made by Kreousa in v. 1299), and in a passage reflecting with such unmistakeable intention the mistrust and dislike felt towards them in the poet's own time, we should be sur- prised to find any inharmonious detail. The interpretation also fails to provide a proper retort to ἀναρπ. δόμους. It is better to take γῆν of the kingdom, which Xouthos won back as it were (ἐκτήσατο) from the enemy: cp. ἐῤῥύσατο, υ. 1298. It is not unnatural that Ion should suppose his father to be more than a reigning consort, but Kreousa bluntly undeceives him, vv. 1299, 1305.
τῆς π., sc. γῆς.
οὐ λόγοις. Hermann thinks Kleon is glanced at. Some political allusion must be intended, for without it the antithesis lacks point.
ἐπίκουροs, the hired soldier, soldier of fortune. The word as a subst. was in Attic used especially of mercenary troops, and is here used in disparagement: see Xen. Hell.
1. 12. -οἰκήτωρ, an owner. The word seems to be used in the sense of the Latin dominus as opposed to possessor.

ἡμῖν δέ κ.τ.λ. But we, we aliens, had we at least (ἀλλά) no patrimony?: lit. no portion consisting of ancestral wealth. πατρικῆς, sc. οὐσίας is gen. of definition like θανάτοιο τελευτή. -ἦν : sc. always, even before Xouthos came to Athens. -ἡμῖν, Ion and his father. Ion asks whether they had not at least some wealth inherited from their family. (Aliens at Athens were often very rich.) Kreousa curtly replies that his father had been a penniless flibustier.
παμπησία : from √πα, whence πέπαμαι. See on ข. 675.

θεηλάτους ἕδρας, holy seat. compound nd is not to be pressed; The latter part of the cp. Aesch. Ag. 1297 θεηλάτου βοός, an ox for sacrifice. Some edd. would read θεοδμήτους, but this is no better. The altar was not built by Apollo. It so happens that θεόδμητος itself occurs twice in Pindar similarly used: Ol. 3. 11 θεόδματον χρέος, holy duty ; Isthm. 6. 11 θεοδμάτους ἀρετάς.
ὅπου ... ἐστί, wherever she is (now). Distinguish this from ὅπου ἂν ᾖ, may be at any time. For the extra- ordinary hyperbaton cp. Soph. Ο. Τ. 1251 χὤπως μὲν ἐκ τῶνδ᾽ οὐκέτ᾽ οἶδ᾽ ἀπόλλυται.
κτείνουσ', for seeking to kill.

ἔντος ἀδύτων : within this sanctuary. Note this extended use of the word (limited probably to the plural) and cp. vv. 662, 220 γυάλων η. Kreousa chooses the word which most enhances the sacredness of the spot where she has taken refuge.
στέμμασι : see on v. 422.
τιν', Apollo. Note the pl. ὧν following. Ion thinks of Xouthos.
φεῦ, expresses impatience: Out upon it!
ἐξελαύνειν : note the change of subject.

τοῖσι δ' ἐνδίκοις. Prof. Jebb on Soph. Ant. 736 takes this = in the interest of the just. We might say that two constructions are fused. The sentence begins as though ἐστί or the like were going to complete the construction, but as it proceeded the poet found it convenient to write ἐχρῆν. It seems difficult to separate ἐνδικοῖς from ἱερὰ καθίζειν. -The construction ἐχρῆν τοῖς ἐνδίκοις (dat. for acc.) could not be paralleled by any certain example in Attic. -ὅστις ἠδικεῖτο, "the victim of injustice. The imperf. indic. must not be taken as a mere alternative for ἀδικοιτο. The opt. is the only correct form for an indefinite sentence (i.e. a sentence of indefinite time) in historic sequence. If the indic. is used, the time is definite; e.g. ὅποι ποτε ἡγεῖτο can only mean whithersoever he was then leading. The apparent excер- tions are to be explained as follows. For ὁ κλέπτης we have two synonyms, ὁ κλέπτων and ὅστις κλέπτει. But though in both cases the present tense of a participle or verb is used, the time-notion is entirely absent; the translation in each case is equally the thief. If ὅστις κλέπτει, in the sense of ὁ κλέπτης, needs to be accommodated to historic sequence, it becomes ὅστις ἔκλεπτε. In fine, such a sentence as ὅστις ἡδικεῖτο in v. 1317 struck the Greek ear as a mere periphrasis for a substantive. Regarded as an indefinite' (time) sentence it is a barbarism.
The ταινía mentioned in the stage-direction is a long ribbon which passes round the forehead and fastens the hair in a knot behind; the ends hang down on the shoulders.

θριγκοῦ τοῦδ' with ὑπερβάλλω = step over. The construction with the gen. is rare, but cp. Theogn. 673 в ὑπερβάλλει δὲ θάλασσα | ἀμφοτέρων τοίχων. The θριγκός over which the Prophetess stepped was a low wall (μικρὸν τειχίον, Phot.) running round the ἄδυτον and serving to protect it from intrusion. τοῦδε implies that it was visible to the spectators through the large central doors, which are left open. We might have supposed that the σκήνη or back-scene was now changed so as to represent the interior of the temple, but the mention of the ῥόπτρα υ. 1612 is conclusive against this.
τρίποδος ... σῴζουσα: 'preserving the tripod's im- memorial use,' i.e. maintaining its rites and ceremonies, as priestess. The words are epexegetic of προφῆτις.
ἐξαίρετος : 'the god's special choice.' The word means more than merely αἱρεθεῖσα: cp. Hdt. 6. 130 ἕνα ὑμέων ἐξαίρετον ἀποκρίνων.
οὐ περ : howbeit thou didst not bear me. The participle alone contains the concession. περ never, as be- ginners sometimes think, = although; it only adds emphasis. See on v. 17.

ἀλλ᾽ οὖν ...: True, but the name was mine. Cp. Hdt. 3. 140 (Darius speaks to Syloson) ἀλλ᾽ ὧν ἴση γε ἡ χάρις ὁμοίως ὡς εἰ νῦν κοθέν τι μέγα λάβοιμι: but all the same, the favour etc. See detached note A.
προγόνοις, step-sons; lit. those born previously.
μὴ ταῦτα. Say not so.

νουθετούμενον, hearkening to thy counsel, i.e. obey- ing, morigerantem. In the pass. the word sometimes imports willing acceptance of correction: cp. Soph. O. C. 1193 νουθετού- μενοι φίλων ἐπῳδαῖς ἐξεπᾴδονται φύσιν, they hear advice, and are charmed from their mood by the gentle spells of friends (Jebb).
ὑπ᾽ οἰωνῶν : cp. νν. 499 (note), 1191.
καθαρὸς κ.τ.λ.: cp. vv. 1045-7.
335. μὴ σύ γε. This use of the nom. of the pronoun to give force to injunctions is equally common in Latin: cp. Hor. S. 1. 4. 85 hic niger est; hunc tu, Romane, caueto.

ὑπαγκαλισμ' ἐμῆς. So Elmsley for MSS. ὑπ' ἀγκάλαις ἐμαῖς. Ср. p. Dr. Verrall's restoration of the simple word Soph. Ο. Τ. 1031 τί δ' ἄλγος ἴσχον τἀγκάλισμα λαμβάνεις, where ΙΣΧΟΝΤΑΓΚΑΛΙΣMA became by successive corruptions corru ICXOΝΤΕΝΚAΛOICME, and was then variously corrected into ἐν κακοῖς, ἐν καιροῖς, ἐν νάπαις.
στέμμασιν, of wool : see on v. 422. These had per- haps been fastened round the cradle by Kreousa in token of supplication.
The order is πῶς οὖν τότε λαβοῦσα (τὴν ἀντίπηγα) ἔκρυπτες ἡμᾶς πάλαι ; See on v. 1307.
Scan θεός as a monosyllable.
κατειπών : see on v. 1215.

πόθεν, wherefore?: causal, as also ἐκ. Cp. Aesch. Cho. 315 πόθεν χοὰς ἔπεμψεν ; ἐκ τίνος λόγου ; Like ποῖος (see on v. 932) the word also frequently expresses incredulity and derision: cp. Ar. fr. 723 σὺ δ᾽ ὁμέστιος θεοῖς; πόθεν ;

ἐνθύμιον κ.τ.λ. A secret prompting then came to me from Loxias. The obj. of τίθησι is σῶσαι ν. 1349, and the adj. ἐνθύμιον is a supplementary predicate :- makes the saving ... a matter of scruple to me. Except in Soph. Τr. 110 ἐνθύμιοι εὐναί, the word appears to be always used as a predicate.

δρᾶσαι. So most edd. Paley retains Mss. δράσειν saying, "If right, it will depend directly on ἐνθύμιον, ‘the idea that you should do what?” But ἐνθύμιον is never used as a subst., nor does it ever mean simply thought, suggestion, idea (see last note). In Hdt. 8. 54 (quoted by Paley and Badham) εἴτε καὶ ἐγένετὸ οἱ ἐνθύμιον ἐμπρήσαντι τὸ ἱερόν the subject of ἐγένετο ἰς τὸ ἐντέλλεσθαι supplied from ἐνετέλλετο preceding, and ἐνθύμιον is adj. and predicate.
ζητήματα, supplementary predicate: lit. thou exhibitest these things as means for seeking, i.e. these things... will help me in seeking. He seizes with alacrity on the first clue ever offered to him.
τὴν τεκ. ἐκπ., i.e. labour at finding her: see on v. 740.
There is little doubt that this line belongs to Ion, not (as in Mss.) to the Priestess. Badham with probability proposes πῶς; ἆρ'.
γνώσει κ.τ.λ. : that is for thee to decide. Ср. Aesch. Theb. 652 σὺ δ αὐτὸς ἤδη γνῶθι ναυκληρεῖν πόλιν.
ἀκέλευστον, without express command: see on v.

The Mss. add λέγειν at the end of the line. Several corrections have been proposed, but it is simplest (and per- fectly satisfactory) to follow Möllend. in omitting the un- necessary infinitive. For ἔχω = understand cp. Alc. 51 ἔχω λόγον δὴ καὶ προθυμίαν σέθεν.
ἴσον γὰρ κ.τ.λ. This evidently means that she em- braces him affectionately.

It is difficult to believe in the genuineness of these lines. The Priestess dismissed the matter of Ion's search for his mother with a decisive γνώσει τάδ' αὐτός in v. 1357, and now that she has said goodbye, is little likely to revert to the subject again in five tame and prosaic verses. Other objec- tions are (1) ἄρξαι δ' wants connection with the preceding; (2) υυ. 1365-6 are a recollection of vv. 44, 45; (3) τις Ελλάς leads up very inartistically to Kreousa; (4) μετέσχε τῆς τύχης is a pointless tag that forms a fitting conclusion to the whole.
ἀπημπόλα, made away with; properly, by sale.
ἐπέσχεν, put to my lips: cp. v. 1492, Ar. Nub. 1382 πιεῖν ἐπέσχον, Plat. Phaed. 1170 καὶ ἅμα εἰπὼν ταῦτα ἐπί- σχόμενος (putting the cup to his lips) καὶ μάλα εὐχερῶς καὶ εὐκόλως ἐξέπιε.
τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ : see on v. 247. -δαίμονος, fortune.

χρόνον ... τρυφήσαι ... τερφθῆναι ... ἀπεστερήθην. The aorists, though at first sight strange, are properly used in reference to a completed period of time referred to as a whole. The acc. χρόνον, on the other hand (needlessly suspected by some edd.), elegantly serves to mark that the time is a period and not a moment: cp. Aesch. Eum. 109 ἔθυον ὥραν οὐδενὸς κοινὴν θεῶν.

βίου may be (1) possessive, the gen. depending on the τέρψιν implied in τι: cp. Soph. O. C. 694 ἔστιν δ' οἷον ἐγὼ γᾶς ᾿Ασίας οὐκ ἐπακούω, or (2) the common indeterminate gen. of connexion or reference; cp. Heracl. 379 εὖ χαρίτων ἔχουσαν πόλιν, Soph. Εl. 1096 τῶνδε φερομέναν ἄριστα.
τί πάσχω; What ails me? See on v. 437, and cp. Med. 1049 καίτοι τί πάσχω; βούλομαι γέλωτ᾽ ὀφλεῖν;
Join προθυμίᾳ...ὡς ἔσωσε; his favour, in that (shown in the fact that) he preserved. The Mss. give ős. The correction is Paley's, and is much better than ὅς γ' or σέσωκε.

ὑπερβαίην. The metaphor is from a hunting-net, which the animal enclosed was sometimes able to leap over, ὑπερτελεσαί (Paley). - οὐδ' ... ποτ', = οὐδέποτε, a stronger form of οὐποτε, ας οὐδὲ εἰς οἱ οὐδείς.

We must suppose the ἀντίπηξ to have been enclosed in a covering by the Priestess; otherwise Kreousa would have recognised it at once. The ξύνδετα are the strings of this wrapper. - τἄμ' ... φίλα, these dear tokens. The con- tents are dear to him as ζητήματα μητρός. Paley, understand- ing clothes, ornaments, playthings etc., dear to him in infancy, forgets the child was exposed immediately after birth.
ἰδοὺ κ.τ.λ. Lo, the cradle and its enfolding shelter; lit. the embracing thing consisting of a rounded cradle. ἀντίπηγ., defining gen.

ἔκ τινος θεηλ., by some cause divine: lit., heaven- sent.-τινος. In using the neuter of indefinite pronouns without a substantive both Greek and Latin writers generally confine themselves to those cases which have a distinctive neuter form, viz. the nom. and acc.

πλεγμάτων, the plaitings. - Paley cp. with this scene the opening of the casket in Plaut. Rudens 1140. Recognitions, ἀναγνωρίσεις, played an important part in ancient tragedy. Aristotle Poet. 11, 14, 16 has some in- teresting and instructive remarks on them. He says (ch. 11) καλλίστη δὲ ἀναγνώρισις, ὅταν ἅμα περιπέτειαι (reversals of fortune) γίνωνται· ὡς ἔχει ἐν τῷ Οἰδίποδι. Here the περιπέτεια takes a happy turn converting, according to modern notions, the tragedy into a comedy.
φάσμα τ. ἀνελπ.: a sight (one) of the unexpected sights. Cp. Xen. Symp. 2. 1 ὀρχηστρίδα τῶν τὰ θαύματα (jugglers' tricks) δυναμένων ποιεῖν.

This line reads in the Mss. σίγαν (or σιγᾶν) σὺ πολλὰ καὶ πάροιθεν οἶσθά μοι. The text is Paley's unexceptionable emendation. It proceeds on the supposition that πολεμία became πολια by omission of a syllable. This was corrected into πολλά and oύ added metri grat. The confusion of oa and η is common, owing to the similarity of their pronunciation. In modern Greek they represent resent the same sound.
οὐκ ἐν κ.τ.λ. My case knows not silence! Chide me not.

Cobet and Badham reject this line and read οὐξέθηκ᾽ (δ ἐξέθηκ') in the previous one. Badham says 'the unmeaning supplements ye and μοι sufficiently betray its spuriousness. Let us say rather that they are marks of tenderest pathos.

A spurious line Κέκροπος ἐς ἄντρα καὶ Μακρὰς πετρηρε- φεῖς has been omitted from the text. The child was exposed in the cave of Pan (cp. v. 938) : but Κεκρ. ἄντρα must be meant for the cave of Aglauros. See Introduction § 4.
θεομανής. He thinks she is mad, and that her hallu- cination has been inspired by the god in order that she may be tempted to leave the protection of the altar which she is wrongfully enjoying.
ξοανά, carven images forming part of the altar.
σφάζοντες κ.τ.λ. Slay and desist not. Cp. v. 527.
ῥυσ. λόγῳ. I am being seized by fraud. Ficta uindicatione corripior. That is, she is laying a fraudulent claim to me. Cp. v. 523 and Aesch. Supp. 423 μηδ᾽ ἴδῃς μ᾽ ἐξ ἑδρᾶν | πολυθέων ῥυσιασθεῖσαν.

ληψ. κ.τ.λ. I shall catch thee finely; i.e. he will convict her of falsehood by questioning her as to the contents of the cradle. She intentionally misunderstands him, as though he meant he would take her to himself and acknowledge her. - With πλέκουσα supply πλοκάς.
τόλμη a by-form of τόλμă: cp. δίψα and δίψη, πρύμνα and πρύμνη, πεῖνα and πείνη. The Mss. give ἡ τόλμα γε.

σκέψασθ' κ.τ.λ. Search for a web that once I wove when a little maid. A somewhat rare use of σκοπέω, but found both in act. and mid.: cp. Isocr. 403 Α ὅτανπερ ἀδικεῖν ἐπιχειρῶσιν, ἅμα καὶ τὴν ἀπολογίαν σκοποῦνται.
οἷον δ' ἐκδ.: 'as it were, prentice-work of the loom. ἐκδίδαγμα is properly work done under instruction, a sampler. For κερκίδος cp. v. 506 n.
ἠτρίοις, threads; properly the threads of the warp, stamina.
In constructing the aegis Pallas placed the snakes of the Gorgon's hair round the edge.

θέσφαθ'. So the Mss. The word is beyond a doubt corrupt. Several edd. accept Musgrave's δεσμά θ', but then ὡς εὑρίσκομεν is intolerably flat. We want something like λεχθὲν ὡς εὑρίσκομεν, described as I find it. If this (or the like) were misunderstood to mean how clearly I now understand what was said (τὸ λεχθέν) by the oracle, the gloss θέσφατα would readily follow. Hermann indeed translates θεσφ. ὡς εὑρ. by nam inuenimus significata ab oraculo, but the Greek will not bear it.
παρθένευμα, 'maiden's work.'

The Mss. give δράκοντες ἀρχαῖόν τι πανχρύσῳ γένυι, which all edd. agree in rejecting. The text is Paley's sug- gestion, and seems the most natural of all the corrections proposed. He cp. Aesch. Αg. 579 ἀρχαῖον γάνος, of bright armour.
ᾖ, as. So I have accented for the MSS. ที.
See on v. 10.
τί χρ. χρυσ. Compare the common phrase τί χρησώμεθ' αὐτῷ; What are we to do with him? The Ti = τίνα χρῆσιν.
Note the pathos of τέκνον.

ἀμφέθηκα. The olive was called παιδοτρόφος (cp. Soph. Ο. Ο. 701 γλαυκᾶς παιδοτρόφου φῦλλον ἐλαίας). Paley has the following note : - It was probably a custom of the Athenians to place an olive wreath on the head of newly-born children, because this would supply a motive to the poet for attributing it to their remote ancestor Ion.
᾿Αθάνα κ.τ.λ. These words do not necessarily con- tradict the ordinary legend, which says that the goddess caused the olive suddenly to spring out of the rock.

οὐ ποτ' ἐκλ. χλόην: in no wise forsakes its green- ness. The ποτε, which should be written separately, adds force to the negative: cp. v. 1278 n.: Aesch. Αg. 1139 οὐδέν ποτ᾽ εἰ μὴ ξυνθανουμένην, for nothing, nothing but to die with him: Cho. 16 οὐδέν ποτ' ἄλλο: Soph. Αi. οὔ ποτε γὰρ φρενόθεν γ᾽ ἐπ᾿ ἀριστερὰ ... ἔβας τόσσον, surely not of thine own heart: Verg. Aen. 2. 670 nunquam hodie moriemur inulti. In each case a definite time is referred to. So τίς ποτε; who in the world?

ἀκηράτου (κεράννυμι), unpolluted by human touch, and so sacred. A certain number of olives (μορίαι) belonged to the state and were sacred. They were under the protection of Zeus Morios: cp. Soph. O. C. 704 ὁ γὰρ αἰὲν ὁρῶν κύκλος | λεύσσει νιν Μορίου Διός.
ὁ θεός, Helios: see on v. 6. -ξυγγνώσεται, sc. the words she has just uttered.
ἀμπτυχαί, expanse, lit. unfoldings.
ἀύσω, βοάσω, delib. subj.-πόθεν μοι : cp. Eu. Luc.
43 καὶ πόθεν μοι τοῦτο ἵνα ἔλθῃ ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Κυρίου μου πρός με ;
συνέκυρσ' with μοι, crossed my path (not = συνέβη). Cp. Soph. O. C. τῇδε συγκύρσαι τύχῃ: Andr. 1172 εἰς ἓν μοίρας συνέκυρσας.
πάντα. We should say, anything.
οὐκ ἔχειν, sc. δοκοῦσα.
ἀπέβαλον : aor. for pluperf. by the common idiom.- γύναι, the absent priestess.
τίν' ἀνὰ χέρα, by what hand: ἀνά = via. The expression is not paralleled, but nothing could better express the poet's meaning.

Note how τέκνον beginning the sentence bespeaks his attention to her confession. Mark too the timid vagueness of her first words, and how as soon as she has begun her courage fails, and she takes refuge in language dwelling on her present happiness. -ἐκλοχεύει : for the tense cp. Phoen. 55 τίκτω παῖδας παιδί.
ματρός with γόοις.
The accent of παρά does not suffer ἀναστροφή because σέθεν is equivalent to σαῖς.
τοὐμὸν κ.τ.λ. περιπέτεια. There has been for me too the same

δῶμ᾽ ἑστιοῦται. The house becomes a home; lit. receives a hearth. As the hearth was the symbol of family life, the expression is easily intelligible. Paley cp. Aesch. Supp. 958 δεδωμάτωμαι, I have had a house built for me. Several other verbs in -ów are similarly used: cp. Xen. An.
3. 28 διηγκυλωμένους τοὺς ἀκοντιστὰς καὶ ἐπιβεβλημένους τοὺς τοξότας, the javelin-men with their javelins grasped by the thong, and the archers with their arrows on the string.
νύκτα, quasi-cogn. acc. Cp. Phoen. 377 σκότον δεδορκώς : Aesch. Theb. 53 λεόντων ... "Αρη δεδορκότων, and the comic expressions νᾶπυ, κάρδαμα, ναύφρακτον βλέπειν, in Aristophanes.

ἀναβλέπει κ.τ.λ.: recovers sight with the shining of the sun. For this sense of ava cp. Med. 1183 ἡ δ᾽ ἐξ ἀναύγου καὶ μύσαντος ὄμματος | δεινὸν στενάξασ᾽ ἡ τάλαιν᾿ ἀνωμμάτου, ἱ.ε. brought back sight to her eye. So ἀναπνέω, for which πνέω is used v. 1460.-λαμπάσιν, dat. instr.
After all it is left to Ion definitely to broach the subject of his parentage.
ἄλλοθεν, an untranslateable euphemism. is secret, is secret.'
παρθένευμα, maiden estate.
ὑπό: see on vv. 499, 1191. Thy birth
σὸν κάρα = σέ. Cp. Soph. Αnt. 1 ὦ κοινὸν αὐταδελφὸν Ἰσμήνης κάρα.
ποθέν ; note the accent.

ἀηδόνιον πέτραν. The neighbourhood of Athens was famous for nightingales. Cp. Soph. O. C. 16 Χώρος δ᾽ ὅδ᾽ ἱερὸς, ὡς σάφ' εἰκάσαι, βρύων δάφνης, ἐλαίας, ἀμπέλου· πυκνόπτεροι δ' εἴσω κατ᾿ αὐτὸν εὐστομοῦσ᾽ ἀηδόνες.
κεδνόν, good news: cp. Aesch. Ag. 623 πῶς δῆτ᾽ ἂν εἰπὼν κεδνὰ τἀληθῆ τύχοις ; ... ,
σε κρύφ. ὠδῖν', ‘thee, a secret birth. For the ap- position cp. Aesch. Ag. 1417 παῖδα, φιλτάτην ἐμοὶ ὠδῖνα. Aristotle calls eggs ὀρταλίχων ἁπαλὴ ὠδίς.

παρθένια δέ μου κ.τ.λ. The Mss. give δ' ἐμᾶς, which is untranslateable. The reading in the text occurred to me before I saw that Barnes proposed δ' ἐμοῦ. The unemphatic form would, I suppose, be more regular. If δέ μου was the original, it probably became δ' ἐμοῦ, and then ἐμοῦ was erroneously made to agree with ματέρος. Translate, 'And maiden's work of mine are these mother's swathing bands that wrapped thee, that I folded round thee, my shuttle's wander- ings. παρθένια seems to stand for παρθενεύματα (ν. 1425). ἔργα might be supplied, but it is unnecessary; the word was used by itself for παρθένια μέλη, to denote maidens songs.
ἁνῆψα (i.e. & ἀνῆψα): so Dind. for MSS. ἀνῆψα. Α long syllable is required by the metre. -χειροῖν : dat. instrum.

γάλακτι κ.τ.λ. ‘And I put to thy lips no mother's γάλ. οὐδὲ μαστῷ is a The verb is sometimes ὁπόταν ᾖ πέπων, ἐσθίω nourishment with milk or breast. hendiadys.-ἐπέσχον : cp. v. 1372 n. used absol.: cp. Ar. Pax 1165 εἰθ κἀπέχω.
οἰωνῶν γαμφ. κ.τ.λ.: a thing for birds with their talons to slay and eat. φόνευμα seems to be ἅπαξ λεγόμενον.
ἐκβάλλει. For the tense cp. v. 1458 ἐκλοχεύει.

ἑλισσόμεσθ': a metaphor from the heeling of a ship to port or starboard according to the wind. Cp. Ar. Ran. 536 μετακυλινδεῖν αὐτὸν ἀεὶ | πρὸς τὸν εὐ πράττοντα τοῖχον (the snug side). Or. 1293 ἀλλ᾽ αἱ μὲν ἐνθάδ', αἱ δ᾽ ἐκεῖσ᾽ ἑλίσσετε (im- perative) is different; the metaphor there is from dancing.
δ€. We should expect γάρ as the sentence gives an explanation of the preceding; but see on v. 179 κτείνειν δέ.
μενέτω, sc. τὰ πνεύματα. For the simile cp. Aesch. Theb. 705 ἐπεὶ δαίμων λήματος ἂν τροπαίᾳ χρονίᾳ μεταλλακτὸς ἴσως ἂν ἔλθοι θελεμωτέρῳ πνεύματι.
πρός, in view of.

Cp. fr. 152 ὁ μὲν ὄλβιος ἦν, τὸν δ᾽ ἀπέκρυψεν | θεὸς ἐκ κείνων τῶν ποτε λαμπρών. | νεύει βίοτος, νεύει δέ τύχη | κατὰ πνεῦμ᾽ ἀνέμων : Hor. C. 1. 34. 12. Valet ima summis mutare et insignem attenuat deus obscura promens; hinc apicem rapax Fortuna cum stridore acuto sustulit, hic posuisse gaudet. Carm. 1. 35 is addressed to Fortuna.

παρ' οἵαν κ.τ.λ. The difficulties felt about this pas sage vanish, if we regard βίου as no more than a poetical addition, serving to mark that στάθμην is used figuratively. It is a possessive gen., but has the force of a descrip- tive adj. Instead of παρ' οἵαν στάθμην ἤλθομεν, the poet writes παρ' οἴαν βίου-στάθμην ἤλθομεν, without any appreciable addi- tion to the meaning. Transl., Within what a narrow line (in my life) I came of slaying etc. There is a precisely similar addition of βίου in Med. 1245 ἄγ᾽, ὦ τάλαινα χεὶρ ἐμή, λαβὲ ξίφος, | λάβ᾽, ἔρπε πρὸς βαλβίδα λυπηρὰν βίου, where I take the meaning to be (not come to the starting-line of a painful life,' but) come, my hand, take up the dagger, begin thy painful task. Medea is in fact literally encouraging herself to come up to the scratch. The writer adds βίου, but the sense is complete without it. Cp. Ηipp. 785 τὸ πολλὰ πράσσειν οὐκ ἐν ἀσφαλεῖ βίου: ίδ. 678: Alc. 292 καλῶς αὐτοῖς κατθανεῖν ᾖκον βίου. Paley's explanation would make the expression a most confused one. Badham gives up βίου.

ἆρα, for ἆρα οὐ: Is it (or is it not) possible ?-φεῦ : impatient, as in v. 1312. Bah! Is it not possible within the shining embraces of the sun to hear of all this day by day?— φαενν. περιπτ.: i.e. within what his embraces enclose, throughout the world. - τάδε: these reversals of fortune.
μέν answers to δε below. οὖν = now.
ὡς ἡμῖν, methinks; dat. of person judging. Cp. Soph. Αi. 396 ἔρεβος ὦ φαεννότατον ὡς ἐμοί: Ant. 1161 Κρέων γὰρ ἦν ζηλωτός, ὡς ἐμοί, τότε.
ἐς οὓς : for secrecy, note as in vv. 696, 911.
σφαλεῖσα κ.τ.λ. : erring with that weakness as to secret unions that besets maidens.
προστίθης. The indic. gives a hint of the speaker's opinion; the subj. would leave it open. Cp. Plat. Theaet. 145 Β ὅρα μὴ παίζων ἔλεγε.
τοὐμὸν αἰσχρόν, the shame of me, i.e. the shame 1 should in that case bring.
See on v. 996. –Νίκην : see on v. 457. It was flatter- ing to Athenian pride to be reminded that Zeus' victory over the giants was not won without the help of their patron goddess.
The construction is πότερον ὁ θεὸς ... τοῦτο ταράσσει.

ὄνομα πατρός. 'Without this an Athenian citizen could not secure any political rights; for by the name of his father, and that of the deme or parish, he was enrolled in the ληξιαρχικὸν γραμματεῖον [see Lex.], and it was by this process only that he became entitled to enter upon an inheritance. (Paley).-πῶς γάρ : sc. ἔσχες ἄν κ.τ.λ. The argument is as follows:- If you had been called (i.e. had been left to be called) the god's son, you could not have inherited; for I should never have revealed the god's name and you would have remained an οὐδεὶς ἐξ οὐδένων. The words τοῦ θεοῦ λεγό- μενος must be taken as meaning οὐδενὸς ἄλλου λεγόμενος ἢ τοῦ θεοῦ. -The clause καί σ' ἀπέκτεινον λάθρα is not part of the argument, but merely amplifies ἀπέκρυπτον. Besides conceal- ing her union with Apollo, she had almost killed their son in consequence.
φαύλως, lightly, indifferently: cp. Aesch. Pers. 520 ὑμεῖς δὲ φαύλως αὔτ᾽ ἄγαν ἐκρίνατε.
ἀντήλιον. The Ionic form (not ἀνθήλιος) is preferred by the Attic writers. Appearing above the eastern façade of the temple the goddess faces the morning sun.
μολεῖν οὐκ ἠξίου κ.τ.λ. The god's timidity is some- what droll, as are also the rather lame explanations put into the mouth of counsel, vv. 1566 ff.
ἐς μέσον, between him and you: cp. v. 1284 ἐν μέσῳ.
τοὺς λόγους (note the art.) his message.
ἐπεὶ δ' κ.τ.λ. And since this matter has been opened and laid bare. At this point there is an ellipse, —(I go on to explain that) fearing thou shouldst die etc. A

χθονός depends on λαῶν, λαῶν on ἐπώνυμοι. --κἀπι- φυλίου. This is taken to mean εἰς φύλας διαιρεθείσης, appor- tioned to the tribes. more satisfactory expression would be ἐπιφυλίων λαῶν, proposed by Paley, the tribal peoples. Badham ridicules the reading ἐπιφυλίου and all interpretations of it. But ἐπί compounded with a substantive commonly implies nothing more than mere connexion ; cp. ἐπικίνδυνος, ἐπίδικος, ἐπίψογος, ἐπίδοξος, ἐφίμερος, ἐπαφρόδιτος, ἐπαίτιος. He himself reads ἐπιφύλιοι, which he translates giving (i.e. originating) tribes, on the analogy of ἐπώνυμος, giving a name. This is very unlikely. 1579 ff. Down to the revolution of Kleisthenes (509 в.с.) the inhabitants of Attica formed four tribes bearing the names Τελέοντες (alias Γελέοντες, Γεδέοντες), Ὅπλητες, ᾿Αργαδεῖς (alias Ἔργαδεῖς), Αἰγικορεῖς. Euripides here traces these titles to four sons of Ion. This is of course romance. On the other hand the origin of the names is very uncertain, and their derivation from four tribal chieftains is at least possible. The words have been supposed to denote occupations of the four classes, as Τελέοντες=taxpayers or priests, "Οπλητες = fighting-men, 'Αργαδεῖς=artizans or labourers, Λἰγικορεῖς=goat- herds. These etymologies, however, together with the theory that the words denote castes or professions at all, are entirely rejected by Grote. He sums up the question, on which much has been written without any conclusive result, as follows :- 'All that seems certain is that these were the four ancient Ionic tribes (analogous to the Hylleis, Pamphyli and Dymanes among the Dorians) which prevailed not only at Athens but among several of the Ionic cities derived from Athens... The four tribes and the four names (allowing for some variations of spelling) are therefore historically verified. But neither the time of their introduction nor their primitive import are ascertainable matters; nor can any faith be put in the various constructions of the legends of Ion, Erechtheus, and Kekrops, by modern commentators' (Hist. of Greece, vol. ii. p. 427). — The names of the ten tribes formed by Kleisthenes were derived from Attic heroes, and were as follows :- Erechtheis. Aegeis. Oeneis. Pandionis. Leontis. Akamantis. Kekropis. Hippothoontis. Aeantis. Antiochis. Each tribe was divided into 10 δήμοι (demes or parishes), but the local position of these was so arranged that no two demes of the same tribe would be found adjacent to each other. The object and effect of this was to abolish many old associations which might have interfered with the com- pleteness of the revolution. This distribution continued down to the time of the Macedonian supremacy.
ἀπ' αἰγίδος. This derivation is probably all the poet's own.
Κυκλάδας... πόλεις: shall colonize the island towns that lie round (his home). These are the shining Cyclades: cp. Hor. C. 1. 14. 19 interfusa nitentes | aequora Cycladas.

χερσ. παράλους. Barnes cp. Thuc. 1. 12 καὶ Ἴωνας μὲν ᾿Αθηναῖοι καὶ νησιωτῶν τοὺς πολλοὺς ᾤκισαν, and Strabo 8. p. 383 ἔκτισαν δὲ δώδεκα πόλεις ἐν τῇ παραλίᾳ τῆς Καρίας καὶ τῆς Λυδίας. The following cities formed the Ionian confederacy :- Ephesus. Miletus. Myus. Priene. Kolophon. Teos. Lesbos. Erythrae. Phokaea. Klazomenae. Chios. Samos. Smyrna.
ἀντίπορθμα, facing each other across the strait, i.e. the Hellespont.

Δωρίς. The small state so called in Northern Greece. It was the original home of the Dorian conquerors of the Peloponnese: cp. Hdt. 8. 31 ἡ δὲ χωρὴ αὕτη ἐστὶ μητρό πολις Δωριέων τῶν ἐν Πελοποννήσῳ : Thuc. 3. 92 ξυνεπρεσβεύοντο δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ Δωριῆς, ἡ μητρόπολις τῶν Λακεδαιμονίων.

῾Ρίου πέλας. The allusion to Rhium was doubtless intended to remind the audience of Phormio's brilliant vic- tories in the Corinthian gulf B.с. 429, some four or five years before the date usually assigned to this play.-'Αχαιός : see on v. 63.

κάπισημ. κ.τ.λ. : and the folk thereof, his name- sakes, shall be marked as bearing his name. ἐπισημανθ. is used in two senses, (1) shall be marked or distinguished, (2) shall be declared: the construction of κεκλῆσθαι is accommo- dated to (2). For the former sense cp. Thuc. 2. 49 καὶ εἴ τις ἐκ τῶν μεγίστων περιγένοιτο, τῶν γε ἀκρωτηρίων ἀντίληψις ἐπεσήμαινε (left its mark on him); for the latter cp. Xen. Hell.
7. 2 ὁ δὲ θεὸς ἐπεσήμαινεν αὐτῷ ὅσιον εἶναι (signified to him).
ἄνοσον λοχεύει σ': gives thee a harmless birth.
ἡδέως ἔχῃ=τέρπη : lit. may possess agreeably.

εἴδῃς. Both Mss. have εἴη, corrected in C to εἴης. The edd. generally accept Wakefield's ἴns. Mr. H. Macnaghten proposes εἴδῃς (Class. Rev. vol. 2), as affording a forcible and appropriate contrast to δόκησις, and this has been adopted in the text. The sense is (as Mr. Whitelaw points out, Class. Rev. vol. iv. p. 251), "that both he may rejoice in his fancy, and you in your knowledge." I had previously misunderstood Mr. Macnaghten's suggestion, but I now see that it is better than ἥδῃ which was proposed in my first edition.

καὶ...δέ. When καί and dé are so placed the καί = even, and δέ=and. Here, however, the dé comes rather late, and perhaps we should read γε. -ἄπιστον. The thing had never been incredible to Ion, only he had wanted certainty.
παιδός : cp. v. 321 n.
εὐωποί, fair is the face of.

ῥόπτρων. The great ring-knocker on the temple door. Apparently she grasps it by way of taking a friendly fare- well.-χέρας, acc. defining extent of verbal action, commonly called acc. of respect. ἐκκρημνάμεσθα : a rare and poetic by-form = ἐκκρέμαμαι : cp. Η.Ε. 520 ἐκκρήμνασθε πατρῴων πέπλων. - προσεννέπω, of farewell, as προσειπεῖν often. So too ἀσπάζομαι Τro. 1276 ὡς ἀσπάσωμαι τὴν ταλαίπωρον πόλιν.

χρόνια κ.τ.λ. The gods act late, perhaps, but at last with power. πως qualifies: cp. Soph. Αi. 327 τοιαῦτα γάρ πως καὶ λέγει κὠδύρεται : Εl. 372 ἠθάς εἰμί πως | τῶν τῆσδε μύθων, accustomed more or less.
ὁδουρός, guardian of our path: not conductress, as Lex. Athena will accompany' them in the air. She has spoken throughout the scene from above the temple.
ἐλαύνεται, is vexed: cp. Soph. O.T. 28 ἐν δ᾽ ὁ πυρ- φόρος θεὸς | σκήψας ἐλαύνεῖ, λοιμὸς ἔχθιστος, πόλιν.
ὥσπερ πεφύκασ', as their nature is; i.e. as they are κακοί they will ever fare κακώς. - πεφύκασ': elision of the of the perf. is rare.
